- On NVIDIA, `horizon_sky_and_bounce` stored every sector's slope as 0: `sv = mix(sv, x, pick)` from −1e9 evaluates as a + t(b − a) there and loses x to f32 rounding (lavapipe's a(1 − t) + bt is exact). Every consumer of `Surf::horizon_slopes` (this term, `fill_horizon_vis` — Europa's Jupiter-shine behind the trench horizon — and the VT relief path's `horizon_open`) has been a no-op on NVIDIA since it was added.
Decision:
- `sky_excess_hidden` (terrain.wgsl): per horizon sector, the hidden band (horizontal to the horizon slope, 90° of azimuth) through the receiver's view factor (the band vector irradiance already used for the wall bounce) × the sector's low-sky radiance above the four sectors' mean. The low-sky radiance comes from the irradiance map of a vertical face turned to the sector (ground half removed), ×2 for the glow's concentration toward the band (fitted to the tracer). It is subtracted from the seen sky on walls and slopes (n.y < 0.75, full below 0.55); gentle ground keeps the isotropic estimate, as the wall bounce keeps the horizontal receiver's factor there. Zero under an isotropic or airless sky; inside `ambient`, so the Depth probes replace it like the rest of the sky term (no double count).
- `sv` uses `select` instead of `mix`.
Consequences: lavapipe, raster/PT surface light in PT shade, textured PT, base → this lane: wide sun-facing walls 1.49 → 1.16, walls facing away 1.18 → 1.18, mid walls 0.96 → 0.96, shaded flats (wide / mid / close) 1.05 / 0.78 / 0.82 unchanged, sunlit unchanged (≤ 1 %); Europa's three plates unchanged (≤ 0.2 %). On NVIDIA the slope fix also turns on what lavapipe already showed: the Jupiter-shine horizon test and this term. Not yet measured on NVIDIA (the test machine's 5080 dropped off the bus at ~12:20 on 10-09); before the fix the 5080 frames with and without the term were byte-identical, which is how the bug showed. Cost not yet benched (same reason): four fixed-UV reads of the 64×32 irradiance map and ~60 ALU, in a branch taken only on walls and slopes. Open (not this lane): the raster's aerial in-scatter at < 1–12 km is a fraction of the PT's media on Mars (mid's far walls, wide's distant terrain); Mars shaded flats stay at 0.78–0.82 because of the plain ORM AO.

## ADR-155: Glass reflection: roughness floor, glass front layer, SSGI and translucency bias under glass
Date: 2026-10-09   Status: accepted
Status note: accepted 2026-10-21, shipped in v0.1.0. GGX alpha floor (MIN_GGX_ALPHA), glass front layer (fs_glass_add), SSGI transmittance scale and translucency bias shipped in v0.1.0.
Context: In lookdev hero_ref (studio), DO27's X12 / scavenger / turret glass pixels read 4-70x Cycles
(integ/1130). Ablations (`docs/evidence/parity/2026-10-09/glass-reflection/`) found four causes:
(1) GGX α floored at 0.045 — Filament's perceptual floor applied to α — in the forward pass, the
clearcoat lobe, `ferrite_pt` and its CPU mirror, so perceptual roughness < 0.21 surfaces had a wide sun
highlight; (2) transmissive panes behind the nearest one (the far side of a canopy, the inner sheet of
a two-sheet pane) added their reflection unattenuated, because a mesh's multiply covered all its
triangles before its add; (3) the SSGI bounce, added over the composited frame, showed through dark
glass at full strength; (4) the translucency-map compare used the opaque map's receiver offsets, so a
panel 1.1 cm under glazing counted as in front of it.
Decision:
- α ≥ 0.002025 (perceptual 0.045²) everywhere the forward pass and the PT evaluate GGX
  (`pbr_lighting.wgsl` `MIN_ALPHA`, `hard_surface::MIN_GGX_ALPHA`); the DFG LUT's punctual albedo
  column follows; the LTC table keeps its 0.045 fit limit. Pre-exposed forward output clamped at 6e4.
- With the refraction copy (Desktop High / Ultra), a "glass front layer" pass draws the transmissive
  panes (`fs_transmit`, depth-tested among themselves) into a Depth32 + Rgba8 pair. Consecutive
  transmissive draws multiply first and add after; `fs_transmit_add` / `fs_glass_add` weight a pane
  behind the nearest by the nearest's transmittance (exact for two layers). Group 3 bindings 7/8.
  Frames without the copy keep the per-draw order.
- SSGI gather/upsample scale the bounce by the front layer's transmittance (1×1 white without it).
- Translucency compare: 0.25-texel normal offset, (0.5 + 1.5·slope)-texel depth bias.
Consequences: glass pixels X12 1.9-2.6x (front34 4.7x: the cockpit through the canopy at grazing
angles), scavenger 2.0-2.1x; the glass's own light is 0.8-1.8x Cycles on all three assets. The turret's
remaining 17-24x is the enclosed cockpit lit by the studio IBL (not glass). Smooth materials everywhere get
tight highlights (goldens re-blessed where they moved, see the lane's commits). Cost on the 5080:
X12 frame −0.07 / −0.17 ms. Lower tiers (no refraction copy) keep the old compositing. BLEND (alpha)
glass is not in the front layer. Specs: `book/user-guide/materials.md`.

## ADR-156: Froxel fog keeps a thin haze's light; Mars media parity is limited by terrain-blind media lighting
Date: 2026-10-09   Status: accepted
Status note: accepted 2026-10-21, shipped in v0.1.0. Froxel fog sigma fix and tests/thin_fog.rs shipped in v0.1.0 (merge 8cc62275, named in the v0.1.0 notes). Terrain-aware media lighting stays a follow-up lane, as the ADR says.
Context: mars-shade-fill reported the raster adding ≤ 3 % aerial in-scatter at 150 m–1 km on Mars, against ~30 % in the path tracer. Its "haze off" toggles left the aerial-perspective pass on, so that in-scatter was counted as surface light. Measured cleanly, by skipping only the composite draws and swapping the terrain surface (docs/evidence/mars-haze), the raster's in-scatter was already 0.92 (mid) and 1.00 (wide) of the PT over 150 m–1 km, and transmittance within 2 %. The darkness of mid's shaded walls is surface light (raster 0.66–0.72 of the PT at 150–550 m). Two froxel-fog bugs made the haze term small: (1) the slice integral divided by max(σ, 1e-4) where the CPU mirror `integrate_segment` divides by σ, so a medium thinner than 1e-4 /m kept σ/1e-4 of its light (Mars dust ≈ 2e-5 /m: a fifth); (2) `inscatter_at` skipped the lighting below 1e-5 /m, so the Mars haze (1.2e-5 /m at its base) vanished about 100 m above it. With both fixed, the haze term is 1.05–2.7× the PT's haze and the aerial table 0.84–2.2× the PT's air. On open flat ground the table and the PT agree (0.83–1.11, `ferrite_pt/tests/aerial_parity.rs`), so the excess in DO27's canyon is terrain: the PT's medium sees a sky the terrain mostly hides and air the walls shadow, while the table's multiple scattering and the froxel's ambient assume an open planet.
Decision: Fix both froxel bugs: integrate by σ exactly (floor 1e-20, only guarding the branch `select` discards) and light any froxel with σ > 0. Frames are bit-identical where σ ≥ 1e-4 /m (and where there is no fog: Earth's default, airless). Pin the GPU froxel to the CPU mirror at 1e-5, 2e-5 and 1.5e-4 /m (`tests/thin_fog.rs`, within 3 %, measured 0.2 %). Do not fit the haze density or scale the media lighting to the PT here. No haze density reaches ±15 % at mid 550 m, and a single sky-visibility factor would need 0.2 in one window and 1.2 in another.
Consequences: Mars is hazier in the graded frames: shadow p10 +1 to +4, mid-tones 0 to +2; the ue / nasa / nasa_dark grades need no retune. Raster/PT in-scatter over 150 m–1 km goes 0.92 → 1.36 (mid) and 1.00 → 1.52 (wide). The per-window ±15 % target is not met, before or after. Meeting it needs terrain-aware media lighting: per-froxel sky visibility from the terrain horizon (and the near air moved into the shadowed froxel volume) for the aerial term. That is a follow-up lane, as is the shaded-wall surface light on switchbacks_mid. `pt_plates` gains `PT_PLATES_RT_ONLY`, `PT_PLATES_MEDIA=air|haze` and a per-shot `CAM` line for this kind of split.

## ADR-162: The planet-surface sky composite is off on airless worlds by default (per-sky `planet_surface`)
Date: 2026-10-10   Status: accepted (lane horizon-band)
Context: arena-horizon round 2 (ec26ee1a) made the visible sky composite the planet's surface (inscatter + transmittance × one Lambertian radiance) on every ray below the geometric horizon that no geometry covers, so the view past a platform edge is ground, not the black clear. On Europa (airless) the third morning sheet showed a flat light grey/lavender band across the top of bore_twelve_wide, between the terrain's far edge and space, in Balanced, Depth and on the dim laptop; the second edition (3b54c94f) had black space there. A/B on the rig's RTX 5080, look_r2 --set parity: the parent d621d933 has black (band rows 42–65 mean sRGB 4/4/5), ec26ee1a has the band (150/151/164) over rows 39–88; Mars switchbacks_mid is bit-identical between the two. Cause: the composite is a single colour for the whole planet disc. Under air the aerial perspective fades it into the horizon haze, so on Earth and Mars it reads as distant ground; with no air nothing fades or textures it, and past the edge of a finite map it is an untextured slab at the end of the world.
Decision: `OutdoorParams::planet_surface: Option<bool>` (per sky). `None`, the default, draws the surface on a planet with air and leaves it off on an airless one (`OutdoorParams::shows_planet_surface`); `Some(_)` forces it either way (an airless arena with platform edges can turn it on). Off writes `ground.w = 0` into the sky uniform, which skips the shader's planet hit test, so those rays keep the sky table (black on an airless world, stars above the -0.02 cutoff, sky bodies) exactly as before ec26ee1a. The CPU `sample_sky` is unchanged (its only engine caller integrates the upper hemisphere). A textured far-ground (the map's heightfield or an impostor ring carried to the horizon, shaded like the terrain) is the proper airless answer and is left to a later lane.
Consequences: Europa maps get black space past the map edge again; Earth and Mars skies, the sky_night / sky_dawn / sky_dusk goldens and the arena's below-horizon test are unchanged. `cliff_relief` forces the surface on so its "the planet surface does not move the cliff's depth edge" test still draws it; `horizon_ground` gains `airless_below_horizon_stays_space`. Agent guide: `book/agents/atmosphere.md`.

## ADR-163: Minimum-spec device profiles and capability fallback notes
Date: 2026-10-09   Status: accepted
Context: Ferrite was only ever run on Blackwell (RTX 5080/5090) and lavapipe, but DO27's Steam players have
older cards (Pascal GTX 10xx, Ampere RTX 30xx) and the owner's test box with those GPUs had not arrived. Whether
device creation, pipeline layouts or shaders silently require something those tiers lack was unknown; nothing
reported *why* quality or timings degraded when an optional feature was missing.
Decision: audit every wgpu Feature/Limit the engine requests (against public vulkan.gpuinfo.org reports: Pascal
GTX 1080 Ti 52316/13896/51723, RTX 3080 51786/52370, Mali-G710 51090). Every request stays intersected with the
adapter's capabilities (device creation never fails on a feature), and `RenderCapabilities::fallback_notes()` now
lists each active capability fallback as a stable `fallback_*` code that `render.problems` and the host checklist
carry (informational, not errors). `MinspecProfile::Pascal` / `::Mobile` (`ferrite_render::minspec`) reproduce a
tier's limits/features on any adapter — `RenderDevice::headless_with_profile` — so CI on lavapipe exercises the
exact code path a GTX 1080 Ti or mid-range mobile GPU takes (`tests/minspec.rs`).
Consequences: the desktop minimum spec is proven, not assumed: Pascal/Ampere with the current driver expose every
optional feature the engine requests except ASTC/ETC2 (and 8 bind groups via wgpu — wgpu caps `max_bind_groups`
at 8 even though the raw Vulkan `maxBoundDescriptorSets` is 32 — above the 5 the shared terrain draw needs, its
virtual-texture colour atlas and cascade-shadow view-projection binding at group 4), so no desktop
fallback is expected to fire. The mobile tier exercises eight fallbacks (timestamps, indirect count, first-instance,
RG11B10, float32 filtering, BC-decode, per-mip Hi-Z, forward-only vis-buffer); a device below 5 bind groups turns
the terrain VT and self-shadow cascade off rather than failing its layout. New engine code that needs more than the
profiles allow fails its minspec test on CI instead of failing silently on a player's GPU. Specs: `specs/13` § 2
updated (feature list corrected — `DEPTH_CLIP_CONTROL`/`SHADER_F16` were listed but never requested; minspec
paragraph + the 5-bind-group minimum added).

## ADR-166: Game-frame warm watchdog and device guard
Date: 2026-10-10   Status: accepted; amended by ADR-196
Context: DO27's rc1 candidate (pin green-20261010-0201) drew only the clear colour and the UI on both maps for
the whole run. Its runtime renderer cache stayed at 0. The shell calls `BootSplash::finish()` at sim boot,
before any scene exists, and `GameFrameWarm` (boot-fast lane, extending ADR-093; `on_splash_finish` defaults to true)
requested a warm. A request does not block drawing; only a running warm does. But once the warm had moved
the runtime renderer onto a warm worker, nothing bounded how long it stayed there. The renderer never came
back, so the window drew no scene for the rest of the run. A started warm can wait forever behind another
job that never finishes (workers = cores / 4, can be 1), or hang inside `warm_extracted`. The likeliest cause
there: `settle_material_graphs()` waits for every queued material-graph build, and a build that panicked
(wgpu's default error handler panics on a validation error) killed its worker thread without sending a result.
The queue also keeps the first `RenderDevice` it saw, so a host that replaces the device would warm across
devices.
Decision: `GameFrameWarm` gets a watchdog, `timeout` (default 15 s; `FERRITE_GAME_WARM_TIMEOUT_S`). When a
started warm is older than that, a job still queued is cancelled (`RendererWarm::cancel`,
`PipelineWarmQueue::cancel_queued`; it counts as a failed "cancelled" job) and the runtime renderer comes
back unwarmed. A running job is abandoned: the stand-in, which now shares the runtime renderer's VFX
layers, keeps drawing, and the job's result is dropped when it returns. Both cases log a `warn` with
`PipelineWarmQueue::describe()` (done/total, each running and pending job with tier, label and age) and
leave boot marks `game_warm_cancelled` / `game_warm_abandoned` and `GameWarmReport::timed_out`. A warm is
skipped, and the request dropped with one warning, when the queue's device is not the current
`RenderDevice`; boot-handoff renderers from another device are dropped instead of adopted. Material-graph
build workers catch panics and send an error result that names the graph key, format and panic message
(logged at `error`), so `settle` always ends. A request made before a renderable frame (a view plus a mesh)
does not block drawing until its warm starts. Hard rule: once a game frame can be drawn, the splash's warm
never blanks the window. A splash request that has not started when the splash is gone is dropped, and the
scene draws unwarmed. DO27's log had the request firing 90 s later, at the first gameplay frame, and
blanking the window for 50 s. Only an explicit `request()`, made behind a loading screen, may hold the
renderer. Any request expires after `request_grace` (10 s) without a renderable frame. The warm's speed on
the worker (50 s for 49 pipelines on a DO27 map, against about 2 s on the frame path) is lane warm-speed's.
Consequences: whatever order the host calls things in, the scene draws within `timeout` of a stuck warm
(earlier when the warm finishes). The cost is one compile hitch on the frames after a timeout, which is the
pre-boot-fast behaviour. Frames are bit-identical whenever no timeout fires. The host checklist § Boot says
so and adds that a host replacing the `RenderDevice` must recreate the `PipelineWarmQueue`.

## ADR-158: Native crash bundles through an out-of-process monitor (Embark crash-handler / minidumper)
Date: 2026-10-09   Status: accepted
Context: DO27's alpha needs reports for native crashes (SIGSEGV/SIGBUS/SIGILL/SIGABRT, often inside
the GPU driver), not only Rust panics. The feedback lane's crash bundle came from the panic hook
only. Writing a minidump inside a crashed process is unsafe (heap and locks may be corrupt), and a
signal handler cannot allocate.
Decision:
- Dependencies, Linux only (target-gated; Windows and Android build a no-op that reports
  `NativeCrashStatus::Unsupported`): `crash-handler` 0.8 in `ferrite_platform`, which is already on
  the `unsafe_code` list, so the one `unsafe` call (`make_crash_event`) stays there behind
  `native_crash::attach`. `minidumper` 0.11 (+ `minidump-writer` 0.13) in `ferrite_framework`. The
  reader (`minidump`, `minidump-processor`, `minidump-unwind` 0.27) is in xtask only.
- The monitor is the game's own executable re-launched with `FERRITE_CRASH_MONITOR`. This needs no
  second binary in the package. The host calls `feedback::run_crash_monitor_if_requested()` first
  in `main`. Without that call, capture stays off: a monitor that started as the game and reached
  plugin builds could initialise a GPU or rotate logs, which is worse than no capture.
- The signal path: one `AtomicBool` guard, `try_lock` on the frame ring, the log ring
  (`ferrite_core::log::ring::try_for_each_recent`) and a scratch buffer allocated at startup. The
  data goes out in messages of at most 8 KiB, because minidumper's server reads each message with
  one `recv`. Then `request_dump` runs. The handler returns `Handled(false)`: the previous handlers
  run and the process dies as before.
- A SIGABRT within 5 s of a panic bundle is the `panic = "abort"` abort and writes nothing more.
- The crash context (settings, host fields, problems, GPU) reaches the monitor only when it
  changes, through the same refresh points as the panic hook, plus once after arming. There is no
  per-frame IPC.
- The bundle format gains `minidump.dmp` and a native `crash.txt`. `BUNDLE_FORMAT` stays 1: the
  additions are optional entries.
- Symbolication uses binutils `addr2line` on `ferrite package`'s existing `symbols/<binary>.debug`.
  `minidump-unwind`'s `debuginfo` feature (wholesym) was rejected as too heavy for a dev tool.
Consequences: DO27's `main` needs one line, documented in the host checklist. A release must keep
its `symbols/` directory. Frames in system libraries and the driver stay `module+offset`. Under Yama
`ptrace_scope` 2 or 3, or in a sandbox that forbids ptrace, the dump fails, but the bundle is
still written, with `minidump: not written (...)`. minidumper has no client timeout, so the crash path forks a
watchdog first (raw `clone`, no atfork handlers) that `SIGKILL`s the game after 5 s (`SIGKILL`, not
`alarm`/`SIGALRM`: a monitor hung while it has the game ptrace-attached would hold `SIGALRM` in a
signal-delivery stop); `alarm(5)` is the fallback when the clone fails. The monitor exits when the game's socket closes. docs/03, deny.toml
(two reviewed duplicates), book `user-guide/feedback.md` and the host checklist were updated.

Addendum (v0.1.0 validation, lane v010-minor, 2026-10-10): a SIGSEGV *sent* with `kill` (`si_code` <= 0: SI_USER, SI_TKILL, SI_QUEUE) wrote its bundle but the game lived until the 5 s watchdog's `SIGKILL` (5.2 s measured, exit status SIGKILL): `crash-handler` re-raises a sent signal into the handler it restores, and Rust std's SIGSEGV/SIGBUS stack-overflow handler only resets the disposition and returns, which ends only a real fault (it re-faults). Now, after the callback has requested the bundle (or returned early: not connected, already crashing), a sent signal other than SIGABRT gets `SIG_DFL`, is unblocked on the crashing thread and re-sent with `tgkill`, so the process dies of that signal at once (`SIGKILL` if that ever returns). Async-signal-safe (sigaction, pthread_sigmask, raw syscalls). Real faults and SIGABRT (the panic-abort dedupe) keep `crash-handler`'s path unchanged; the watchdog stays the backstop. A process with no handler attached (opted out, monitor not up) keeps std's behaviour. Test: `xtask/tests/native_crash.rs` sends `kill -SEGV` and requires signal 11 within 2 s and a bundle.

## ADR-159: Engine telemetry: structured `ferrite::*` events; wgpu errors log instead of panicking in release
Date: 2026-10-09   Status: accepted
Status note: accepted 2026-10-21, shipped in v0.1.0. ferrite_telemetry crate and release-build wgpu error logging shipped in v0.1.0.
Context: DO27's alpha needs extensive logging to find bugs and drive engine work, but logging must never slow or crash a player's machine. The shell forwarded only Ferrite's INFO text, so the engine's measurements (GPU timings, frame-path creations, problems, boot marks, streaming state) never reached a file. wgpu's default uncaptured-error handler panics, so one validation error in a release build ends the match.
Decision: New Gameplay-layer crate `ferrite_telemetry` (allowed same-layer edges: → `ferrite_framework` for the frame sampler shared with the feedback ring and `GameSettings`; `ferrite_agent` → it for `telemetry.get_last_summary`), added to `DefaultPlugins`. It emits stable-target `tracing` events (`ferrite::session`, `boot`, `frame_summary`, `hitch`, `gpu_error`, `device_lost`, `surface`, `problems`, `stream`), each with a `data` JSON record. Per-frame work aggregates into buffers allocated once and logs nothing (an allocation-counting test over 1000 frames; ≤ 0.05 ms per frame). RSS and VRAM are sampled on a background thread. Lower crates feed it through `ferrite_core::telemetry` (atomic counters/gauges and a fixed 64-slot note ring; no logging on hot paths). `json_layer(path, opts)` is a bounded, lossy, non-blocking JSONL writer (size cap, drop counter, repeat suppression, fsync ≤ 1 Hz) so the host wires it in one line; the host's subscriber still decides where events go. The plugin installs wgpu's uncaptured-error handler: it logs `ferrite::gpu_error` (kind, frame, the innermost span = the pass), and panics afterwards only when `TelemetryOptions::gpu_error_panics` (default: debug builds). A release build keeps running after a validation error.
Consequences: Release builds no longer abort on wgpu validation errors; CI and dev runs (debug) still panic, so bugs are not hidden in tests. Render gains cheap taps: surface-error and eviction counters, a 32-entry process-wide ring of recent creation labels (`frame_stats::recent_creates`), `boot::mark_count`, `FrameRenderer::texture_budget_bytes`. Assets note slow loads (> 100 ms) and pak corruption; terrain and VFX publish scatter and particle gauges. `ferrite_framework::feedback::FrameSampler` is the one frame sampler (feedback ring and telemetry). Triangles are not counted yet. Specs: book/user-guide/telemetry.md (events and fields), host checklist "Telemetry and the alpha log".

## ADR-157: Automatic quality detection on first launch
Date: 2026-10-09   Status: accepted
Status note: accepted 2026-10-21, shipped in v0.1.0. ferrite_render::quality (QualityTier, gpu_tiers.ron, QualityProbe) and AutoQualityPlugin shipped in v0.1.0.
Context: DO27's alpha needs a good first launch on any GPU without a trip to the options menu (owner request). The engine had render presets (Mobile Low/High, Deck, Desktop Low/High/Ultra) and a persisted `GameSettings.graphics.preset` (Low/Medium/High/Ultra/Clean) that nothing applied, no notion of who set it, and no "Medium" render tier. Measured DO27 frame times now exist on four GPUs: RTX 5090 and 5080 (do27-perf, gpu-farm4), RTX 3080 Ti and GTX 1080 (minspec-hw).
Decision: (1) `ferrite_render::quality`: `QualityTier` (MobileLow, MobileHigh, Deck, Low, Medium, High, Ultra), where Medium = Desktop High at render scale 0.67 with Balanced lighting (≈ half of High's GPU cost at the same output; no new preset row, so no golden changes). `AdapterProfile` reads name, PCI ids, device class, the largest Vulkan device-local heap (via `as_hal`; unknown on DX12), limits and BC support. `detect` walks a RON table compiled into the engine (`quality/gpu_tiers.ron`; first match wins; each row is `Measured(..)` (bench-do27 on that GPU), `ByClass(..)` (table-by-class from the nearest measured row, not measured) or `Guess(..)` (Deck, phones); coverage follows the Steam Hardware & Software Survey, September 2026: its top 40 cards all match a row, pinned by a test; the survey is data only, the engine fetches nothing), falls back by class and VRAM (unknown discrete ≤ High, never Ultra), caps at Low below the ADR-153 no-fallback floor and steps down while VRAM is under a tier's floor. (2) `QualityProbe` (render resource): after the game-frame warm, the window path draws ~3 s of the first scene under the splash with GPU timestamps on, holds the fade until the result is taken, and `judge_probe` steps down one tier when p95 > 1000 / target fps (60 desktop, 40 Deck, 30 mobile). (3) `GraphicsSettings` gains `preset_source` (`Unset`/`Detected`/`Player`; absent in older files = Player when the preset is not the default) and `detected` (the record), and `GraphicsPreset` a `Deck` variant. The settings plugin applies the preset to `RenderSettings` only once a source is known and only when the preset changes, and marks any preset change detection did not make as the player's. (4) `ferrite_framework::auto_quality::AutoQualityPlugin` (in `DefaultPlugins`) detects when the source is Unset or a re-detect was requested, and acts only on apps with `GameSettings`. (5) Agent `quality.get_detected` / `quality.detect`.
Consequences: Games using `SettingsPlugin` get a GPU-matched preset on the first launch, and a ~3 s longer splash on that launch only. Apps without `GameSettings`, and goldens, are unchanged. A preset change re-seeds `RenderSettings.profile` (a game's own scale/upscaler tweak must be re-applied after a preset change; host checklist). Most table rows are estimates until more GPUs are benched; the probe only corrects estimates that are too high. VRAM is unknown on DX12 (Windows can still pick Vulkan; the name rows still match). The book gained user-guide/auto-quality.md and agents/auto-quality.md; spec 13 § 3's presets are unchanged.

Addendum (integration, wave Q, 2026-10-10, from the v0.1.0 feature review): (a) a saved preset is applied to `RenderSettings` in `SettingsPlugin::build`, before any host `Startup` system; the `Update` apply re-applies only a preset that changes. Before this, the first `Update` of every launch re-seeded `RenderSettings.profile` without a `SettingsChanged`, silently overwriting a host's startup tweaks (DO27's 4K render scale / TSR). (b) A probe that only had the wall clock (`ProbeSource::Wall`: under half the frames carried GPU timestamps) never steps down: the render tick's wall time includes the vsync wait (≈ 16.7 ms under Fifo at 60 Hz), which is the 60 fps budget itself.

Addendum v0.1.2 (lane v012-pascal-vt, 2026-10-11, lead look sign-off): the terrain virtual texture on Desktop Low, an ADR-041 exception.
- Context: the GTX 1080, the alpha's min-spec card, gets `Low` from the table. Without the texture, DO27's Switchbacks ran at 39 fps median with a 24 fps 1 % low.
- Decision:
  - `TerrainBudget` gains `virtual_texture: bool`. It is false in every preset (including `OFF` and `MID_RANGE`), so goldens are unchanged.
  - `QualityTier::apply_for_gpu(settings, Some(adapter))` sets it only when `QualityTier::terrain_vt_default` holds: tier `Low`, a discrete GPU, not Android, and known device-local memory of at least 6 GB (`TERRAIN_VT_MIN_VRAM_MB`). `Medium`, `High` and `Ultra` never set it. Since the review of v012-vt-horizon also: a Linux build only (`terrain_vt_default_on(adapter, std::env::consts::OS)`), and not on AMD (`TERRAIN_VT_EXCLUDED_VENDORS` = 0x1002); see the correction below.
  - `SettingsPlugin` applies a preset through `apply_for_gpu`. When there is no render device yet at plugin build, a one-shot system (`decide_gpu_levers`) applies the lever on the first frame that has one; it overrides a host that cleared the lever in `Startup`. The lever is re-applied on every switch to Low (Low → Medium → Low in the options menu turns it back on). To opt out permanently, a host calls `TerrainSharedDraw::set_virtual_texture` (correction from the lane review, v012-vt-horizon).
  - `QualityTier::of_settings` and `RenderSettings::preset` ignore the lever.
  - `TerrainGpu::set_virtual_texture_from_profile` (called from `TerrainSharedDraw::prepare` with `SharedFrameInfo::terrain_budget`) turns the texture on with `VirtualTextureSettings::for_profile()` (the defaults with `stochastic_lod: false`, because Low has no TAA) or off. It does nothing once the host or the agent has called `set_virtual_texture`: an explicit call, `None` included, wins.
- Evidence: `docs/evidence/perf/v012-pascal-vt/` (README, `index.html`). GTX 1080 ms1 at real clocks, 1920×1080 Desktop Low, bench-do27, 1800 frames per map:

  | Map | median fps | 1 % low fps | wall p95 ms | GPU p50 ms | engine GPU memory |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | Switchbacks | 39 → 77 | 24 → 43 | 37.1 → 22.1 | 25.9 → 13.4 | 797 → 1338 MB |
  | Bore Twelve | 75 → 100 | 35 → 57 | 24.1 → 12.6 | 13.9 → 10.5 | 674 → 1215 MB |

  - Card peak (nvidia-smi): 1.15 → 1.66 GB of 8 GB.
  - One segment got slower: the Bore Twelve fight is near ground the texture does not serve, so it only pays the bake (wall p50 9.9 → 11.1 ms).
  - The stochastic LOD pick costs the same as reading both LODs on Pascal (within 0.1 ms per plate), and on Low it shows as grain.
  - Motion (dollies on both maps and a pan): flicker and pop counts are unchanged or lower, with 0 missing pages and 0 frames waited.
- Look: ground nearer than 24 m is identical, and the mid plates are unchanged by eye (SSIM 0.986/0.989). Far ground and slopes past crests are softer. The terrain's relief and self-shadow contrast flattens: shadows are lighter, cracks are lost and edges are smoother. Plate SSIM is 0.957–0.967. Crops: `crops/switchbacks_wide_shadowed_wall.png` and `crops/bore_twelve_flyover_cliff.png`. The lead accepted this at Low for the frame rate.
- Consequences:
  - On Linux, a GTX 1070/1080, GTX 1060 6 GB, RTX 2060 or Intel Arc on Low gets the texture. 4 GB cards, integrated GPUs, AMD cards, lavapipe, the Deck and phones do not.
  - Correction (review of v012-vt-horizon, lead decision 2026-10-11): this line used to say "unknown VRAM (DX12) … do not", implying Windows players were left out. That was wrong: Windows makes a DX12 | Vulkan instance and `gpu_select::enumerate` puts Vulkan first, so Windows players' VRAM is known and they would have got the texture, on drivers it has never run on. The default is now **Linux only** until there is a Windows measurement (the alpha is a Linux tarball), and **AMD (0x1002) is excluded** until a RADV measurement exists (the RX 7900 could not be run that day). Intel stays eligible on Linux: the BMG G31 was measured clean on ANV (0 validation messages, Switchbacks 57 → 93 fps). Tests: `quality::tests::the_terrain_vt_default_is_linux_only_and_skips_amd` (a Windows adapter and AMD 8 GB Low cards get no texture; NVIDIA and Intel on Linux do).
  - Known issue: on maps with hole cuts, the cut nodes draw with the holes colour pipeline, which does not read the texture, so they shade in full next to VT-shaded neighbours: a slight look step at those node edges is possible.
  - The texture's pipelines and its atlas (537 MB; 671 MB with map E since v012-vt-horizon) are built on the first frame that carries the flag, which is inside the game-frame warm. They are not built at `prewarm`. Every Low ↔ other switch in the options menu drops and rebuilds them inside one frame: a one-time hitch there, not a crash.
  - A sun-direction change of more than 0.1° flushes the cache (ADR-117 addendum v0.1.2), so the next frames shade in full until the pages are re-baked. That costs time but never shows. Smaller drift, and any change of sun colour, illuminance, ambient or fill, keeps the pages.
  - Resolved by lane v012-vt-horizon (ADR-117 addendum v0.1.2: map E, Switchbacks 76 fps p50 / 43 1 % low, switchbacks_wide SSIM 0.985). The original note follows. Known issue, follow-up lane: the pages flatten relief and self-shadow contrast compared with direct sampling. A brief investigation (switchbacks_wide plate, same camera) found the cause. In `Surface` mode, `vt_lookup` rebuilds `Surf` with `horizon_slopes = -1000` ("not computed"): the four atlas maps have no room for them. On every VT-served pixel, `fill_horizon_vis` therefore returns 1, so Europa's Jupiter-shine fill is never hidden by the terrain, and `sky_excess_hidden` returns 0, so Mars's circumsolar sky excess is never hidden on walls. Shadowed walls and slopes get light that the per-pixel path takes away, which makes the shadows lighter and the relief flatter. Two control runs ruled out the other suspects: `VtCache::Relief`, which caches the slopes, matches VT-off (SSIM 0.988–1.0, dark shadows, cracks kept); `oversample=2` stays flat (SSIM 0.972–0.993), so texel resolution is not the cause. Lighting baked into the page is not the cause either: sun, sky and fill stay per pixel. The lost crack detail is the separate, known ADR-117 effect of pre-filtering the layer textures at the texel footprint. Likely fix: carry the slopes (a fifth atlas map, ~134 MB at 32 slots, or packed into spare precision) or finish both horizon terms in the bake. The cache already flushes on a sun change, and would also need to flush on a fill change.
- Intel Arc rows (lane v012-vt-horizon, from the arc-sweep report, 2026-10-11): the BMG G31 (8086:e222, Mesa name "Intel(R) Graphics (BMG G31)", 32 GB) matched no row and fell to the VRAM fallback's Medium. Measured on Ferrite it runs at 1.1–1.4x a GTX 1080 (1080p Switchbacks Low 57, Medium 60, High 35 fps), so it gets a `Measured` Low row (`intel_arc_bmg_g31`). `intel_arc_mid` (B580, B570, A770, A750, and now "bmg g21" for the Pro B50/B60, which would otherwise hit the VRAM fallback) drops from Medium to Low, still by class. Rationale (lead decision after the review, which asked to keep Medium): the alpha is Linux/ANV; the measured G31 is the bigger die and reached only ~60 fps at Medium on ANV, so a B580 or A770 at Medium on ANV would do worse. Intel's Windows driver is unmeasured and may not have ANV's terrain cost; revisit this row when Windows ships. All of them are discrete with ≥ 6 GB, so on Linux Low turns the terrain virtual texture on: on the G31, Switchbacks 57 → 93 fps and Bore Twelve 98 → 115, with 0 validation messages. Test: `quality::tests::intel_arc_cards_get_low_with_the_terrain_virtual_texture`.
- Specs: `specs/13` § 3 presets are unchanged; the lever is a detector decision. Book: user-guide/auto-quality.md, agents/auto-quality.md.

## ADR-160: In-game performance overlay — a setting with a host default, no default key; UI pipeline warm from the first frame
Date: 2026-10-09   Status: accepted (lane perf-overlay)
Context: The owner wants DO27's alpha testers to see and report performance themselves. The brief
asked for an F3 toggle, but DO27 uses the F-keys, so the owner changed it: the overlay is a setting
that the game's settings menu shows, DO27's alpha ships with it on, and the player's choice wins.
The runtime UI compiled its pipeline on the first frame that had quads. Any UI that appeared later
(this overlay, or a HUD toggled on) therefore compiled a pipeline mid-game. Those creates also
went uncounted, because `ferrite_ui` called the raw `wgpu::Device`.
Decision: `ferrite_framework::perf_overlay` (in `DefaultPlugins` with `ui`).
- The mode is `GameSettings.performance_overlay: Option<Off|Compact|Detailed>` (`#[serde(default)]`,
  older files load). `None` follows `PerformanceOverlay::default_mode` (engine default Off; DO27 sets
  Compact). An agent override (`perf_overlay.toggle`) sits above the setting and is not saved.
- There is no default key. The optional `"PerformanceOverlay"` input action has no binding.
- Hosts get `spawn_settings_entry` (a label and dropdown row) and the `settings_menu_entry()` descriptor.
- Every value comes from an existing source: `RealTime` delta, `Diagnostics`, the renderer's
  `cpu_timings`/`GpuTimings` (new `GpuTimings::passes()` list), `HitchReport` over a 5 s window,
  the frame-path counters, and `memory_report`. Texture totals come from the report the renderer
  already builds every 60 frames, cached as `FrameRenderer::texture_memory_summary()`.
- `ferrite_ui` gains `UiCanvas` (unit-square rects; changing it re-walks only its subtree and
  never re-runs layout). The frame graph uses it.
- `UiRenderer::draw` now creates its pipeline for the target format even when there is nothing to
  draw, so a window's UI pipeline exists from its first frame. `UiRenderer::warm` is the explicit form.
- The UI renderer's pipeline and bind-group creates go through `TrackedDevice`, so the hitch
  counters see them.
- The window path's boot tier warms every overlay layer on a warm worker
  (`OverlayDraw::warm`, job "overlay layers"). It covers the window format and both display-stage
  intermediates, so the UI pipeline is built inside the boot warm and never on a game frame.
- The resolution line reads `FrameRenderer::last_extent()` (output size, internal size and
  upscaler of the last view drawn).
- Hosts that drive their own `FrameRenderer` feed the overlay with `PerfOverlayRendererSample`.
- "CPU" is labelled "Render CPU": it is the renderer's encode, submit and present time, not the
  whole game frame.
Consequences: Showing the overlay creates no pipelines or bind groups (tested). Visible cost is
≤ 0.1 ms CPU (release) and ≤ 0.1 ms GPU (tested). Apps with `UiPlugin` but no UI compile one small
pipeline at boot. UI creates now appear in `play.hitch_report`'s device calls, which is the honest
number. Spec 18 gains `UiCanvas` (§ 1 visual components).

## ADR-161: Shipped pipeline caches, deferred forward variants, parallel compiles
Date: 2026-10-09   Status: accepted
Context: DO27's first launch on a tester's machine compiled the game frame's pipelines behind the splash for
5.6–6.8 s (RTX 5080), 7.6 s (RTX 3080 Ti), 8.5 s (GTX 1080), 13.6 s (RTX 5090 on the loaded farm host). A Vulkan
pipeline cache only applies to the GPU + driver that wrote it. `warm_site_costs` showed where the time went: 9
forward uber-shader variants per pipeline set (only 1–2 drawn by a typical frame), the GPU-driven forward
variants, and compute pipelines built one after another; 20 creation sites passed no pipeline cache at all.
Decision: (1) `ferrite package --pipeline-caches DIR` (default `<project>/pipeline-caches`) validates `.fpc`
files and ships them in `content/pipelines/` under `PipelineCacheKey::shipped_file_name` (stem + hash of the
whole key); at runtime a missing or unusable local cache is seeded from a shipped file whose whole key matches
(`CacheLoad::Seeded`, `ShippedLoad`), else the launch compiles as before. (2) The forward set's blend/premul/
additive and glass transmission pipelines are `pipeline_warm::DeferredPipeline`s. A warm (`warm_scene`/
`warm_extracted`, worker or loading screen) builds every variant a material of its frame can draw, visible or
not; the variants no loaded material uses build on warm workers after the first game frame
(`release_deferred`). Mid-play, a draw whose variant is not built (a material spawned later) is skipped until
the background has it (`try_get`, queued first): no compile on the frame path. Without warm workers they are
built eagerly as before. (3) Independent compiles run side by side
(`pipeline_warm::join`/`join_all`, carrying the warm tier and frame counters). (4) Every engine pipeline passes
`pipeline_cache::cache_for`. Fossilize-style replay (record per-site pipeline keys, prebuild them all in parallel
at boot) is the next step for GPUs outside the shipped set; not done here.
Consequences: a matching GPU/driver starts close to a second launch; others compile ~2× faster. Pixels are
unchanged (same pipelines, created at another time or thread). Pipeline counts now include the 20 formerly
uncounted sites. Android ships no caches (no test GPUs; APK assets are not a directory). Book: instant-load,
DO27 host checklist.

Addendum (integration, wave Q, 2026-10-10): `ferrite package` compares each shipped cache's wgpu version and shader hash with the engine it packages; a mismatch ships but prints a loud warning and is recorded as `pipeline_caches[].matches_engine = false` in `build_info.json` (a stale cache never seeds a player's cache, so it is dead weight). A game that sets a content salt sees the warning too (the packager cannot know the salt). `build_info.json`'s `engine` field is the engine crate version (0.1.0), no longer the literal "0.1".

Addendum (v0.1.0 validation, lane v010-minor, 2026-10-10): the key's engine shader hash covered only the core shader library (11 files), so a cache built on 10-09 still "matched" after later WGSL changes (hull-look, depth-shade) and `ferrite package` printed no warning (harmless: driver misses, but the warning was defeated). `engine_shader_hash` now folds a hash baked at build time by `ferrite_render/build.rs` (`src/shader_sources.rs`) over every engine shader source that can reach a pipeline: every `.wgsl` under the `src/` and `shaders/` trees of ferrite_render, ferrite_terrain, ferrite_vfx, ferrite_ui, ferrite_2d, ferrite_pt and ferrite_matgraph, plus every Rust source there that carries WGSL text (WGSL markers such as `@compute`, `var<`, `vec4<f32>`: the `shader_lib` composer, inline shaders, the DDGI / impostor / VFX / surface-graph / material-graph generators), each hashed whole with CR stripped. A Rust-only edit to such a file also moves the hash (one extra cache rebuild, never a stale match). Tests: the baked hash equals the tree's, every engine `.wgsl` in `crates/` (editor and test fixtures excepted) is covered, and an edit to any one source or a new WGSL file changes it. Gaps: values injected from Rust files without WGSL text (e.g. a `#define` chosen in pipeline setup) are not hashed, and an incremental build notices a newly marked Rust file in an unwatched directory only on its next rebuild of ferrite_render (clean and CI builds always do); both only cost driver misses. Material-graph shaders built from game content are not engine sources: the game's `set_content_salt` covers them, and `ferrite package` warns on salted caches as before. Consequence: every existing local and shipped cache is invalidated once (rebuilt behind the splash); re-generate shipped caches with this build. Specs/13 § Cache updated.

## ADR-164: Near sun tile — a high-resolution sun shadow over the first 4 m of the view
Date: 2026-10-10   Status: accepted
Status note: accepted 2026-10-21, shipped in v0.1.0. near_sun_tile in RenderProfile/FrameQuality shipped in v0.1.0 (commit 2945e1dd, lane hull-look).
Context: DO27's X-11 in game showed hull self-shadows that read as "garbled letters" on panels 1–5 m from the camera (Switchbacks, side view around the intakes), and the alpha look snapshot found the same saw-tooth under canopies on kraken / foundry_*_a52. The A/B there had ruled out translucent shadows, the filter, contact shadows and reflection occlusion; a 4096² cascade halved the teeth. Isolation on hero_ref x11 (sun-only aux pass, GI off, against the path tracer): the raster shadow has the PT's shape, with no missing caster, no peter-panning and no acne. Only its edge differs: cascade 0 spans 0–16 m on the ADR-061 / ADR-140 ladder, so a 2048² map has 1.5–2 cm texels. A hull flank the sun grazes stretches each texel by 1/cos to 4–10 cm steps. `HERO_SHADOW_FILTER=hard` shows the same steps, so no filter removes them. Every X-11 material is double-sided, so front- and back-face casting play no part. Four cascades on a 16 m – 4 km ladder cannot reach millimetre texels at 1–5 m, and Ultra's 4096² cascade only halves the steps.
Decision: `RenderProfile::near_sun_tile` / `FrameQuality::near_sun_tile` (tile edge in texels, 0 = off): Desktop High 2048, Ultra 4096, off elsewhere and in `FrameQuality::LAB` / reflection captures.
- **Placement.** An orthographic sun view fitted to the bounding sphere of the first `NEAR_SUN_RANGE_M` = 4 m of the view frustum (`frustum_slice_sphere`, the cascades' fit), snapped to its own texel grid. Its light eye sits as far up-sun as the cascades' (`cascade_back`). With paged shadows the tile covers a sphere 1.25× the slice's and keeps its centre while the slice's sphere stays inside it (`NEAR_TILE_SLACK`), so a strafing or orbiting camera moves and redraws it every meter or two rather than every frame.
- **Atlas.** The tile is the first square of the local-light shadow atlas (`layout_shadow_tiles_reserved`). The local tiles pack after it, and the atlas is just that square when no local light casts. It is the last entry of the tile list, so local tile indices do not change. It draws through the atlas tile jobs (instanced, per-draw and visibility-buffer paths), with the sun casters whose footprint touches it and whose cascade mask includes cascade 0.
- **Skipped entirely** (no draw, no lookup, `csm.count.w` = 0) when no mesh draw's bounds lie within 4 m of the eye. `ShadowCacheReport::near_sun_tile` / `near_sun_tile_drawn` say which.
- **When it redraws.** When its matrix moves, when cascade 0 has a dirty page or a full redraw, or when its last draw is invalid.
- **Lookup.** `lab_forward.wgsl` `sample_csm`: a mesh receiver closer than the range takes `sample_near_sun`, which uses the cascades' receiver-plane PCSS / PCF, normal offset and bias in metres. Over the range's last fifth it blends into the cascades. A receiver whose filter could leave the tile (12-texel margin) takes the cascades.
- **Terrain.** The heightfield is not drawn into the atlas. Its shadow comes from cascade 0 through `sample_cascade_above`, a 3×3 receiver-plane lookup that counts only blockers higher than the tile's topmost surface over the receiver plus 0.25 m. That height is read from the tile's depth at the receiver. A caster held by both maps is therefore never counted twice, with no fixed hand-off distance and no coarse fringe from cascade 0.
- Agent: `render.set_near_sun_shadow {tile}` (guide: `book/agents/near-sun-shadow.md`).
Consequences: hull close-ups at 1–4 m get ~5 mm sun-shadow texels on High (2.5 mm on Ultra) instead of 1.5–2 cm, so the stretched steps under intakes, ledges and canopy frames are gone. Mesh shadows on the ground within 4 m are sharper too (the vehicle's own shadow next to its skids).
- Terrain receivers are unchanged: they do not run this lookup.
- Translucent casters do not get a near translucency square. Glass tint within 4 m still comes from the cascades' translucency maps.
- Memory: a 2048² Depth32 square on High (16 MB, 64 MB at 4096² on Ultra) when no local light casts; otherwise a square of the existing 8192² atlas, with the local tiles packed around it.
- Frames without a mesh within 4 m (the default `do27_bench` chase at 9 m) are bit-identical and cost nothing; the measured near-range cost is in the lane report.
- Tests: `tests/near_sun_tile.rs` (sharper edge with the same umbra, bit-identical skip, far up-sun caster), `shadow.rs` layout / texel / WGSL-mirror tests.

## ADR-165: Glass reflects what is on screen, and the space under glass gets the glass's share of the ambient
Date: 2026-10-10   Status: accepted
Status note: accepted 2026-10-21, shipped in v0.1.0. Glass screen-space reflection (pane_reflection_visibility) and glass_enclosure ambient shipped in v0.1.0 (lane hull-look).
Context: DO27's X-11 canopy read milky on Mars and as a black void on Bore Twelve. Studio A/B against the path tracer found two engine faults.
- **The cockpit was lit by indirect light that neither the canopy nor the hull blocks.**
  - With the sun off the interior stayed bright; with the indirect light off it went black, as the PT shows.
  - Under a black sky the pilot and seat were still near-white from the IBL's ground half.
  - Translucent sun shadows already blocked the direct sun; the ambient under the glass was not attenuated at all.
- **Glass reflected only the environment map** (the outdoor IBL is a 64×32 equirect).
  - `pane_reflection_visibility` zeroed the reflection wherever the mirror ray hit on-screen geometry, so glass never reflected the hull or terrain beside it, and lost the ground at grazing angles.
  - Over Europa's black sky that left the canopy black. Over Mars it left a featureless sky gradient over a lit cockpit.
- The SSAO at a pane's pixel (the cockpit's AO behind the glass) also darkened the pane's own reflection.
Decision:
- **Glass screen-space reflection** (`pane_reflection_trace`, run by `fs_transmit_add` on the nearest transmissive pane when reflection occlusion is on and the refraction copy binds the opaque HDR and depth; panes behind it keep the old blocked-or-open test, since they show through the nearest at its transmittance).
  - The pane marches its mirror ray: 16 quadratic steps to 24 m, then a 3-step bisection.
  - A hit within a thickness of 10 cm + 2 % of depth + a quarter step takes the copy's colour (÷ pre-exposure) in place of the environment. It fades to the environment over the outer 6 % of the screen, and rough smudges keep half of the environment.
  - A ray that goes deeper behind a nearby surface is blocked as before (the old test's reach).
  - A miss keeps the environment.
- **Glass enclosure ambient** (`glass_enclosure`).
  - A receiver whose sun ray meets a translucent caster 0.25–1.2 m above it (the translucency map's nearest depth, at cascade 0's texel) multiplies its indirect diffuse and specular by that caster's transmittance. The weight falls to 0 over that gap.
  - The ground in a canopy's coloured shadow metres away keeps its sky.
  - Frames without translucent casters are unchanged.
- **No SSAO on blended or transmissive surfaces**: the AO at their pixel belongs to what is behind them.
Consequences:
- **X-11 studio.** The cockpit under DO27's ~2 % canopy now goes dark like the PT's. The pane mirrors the hull beside it and the cockpit under the far pane.
- **Europa.** A canopy seen at grazing angles mirrors the ice it faces. Seen from above it still mirrors black space, which is physically right for a smooth canopy under an airless sky.
- **Mars.** The milky veil, which was the lit cockpit under a featureless sky reflection, is gone.
- **Cost** is confined to transmissive pane pixels. Measured numbers are in the lane report.
- **Limits.**
  - The heuristic is keyed to the sun ray: a receiver under glass that the sun reaches from the side through open air keeps more ambient than the PT gives.
  - Reflections of what is off screen still come from the IBL.
- **DO27 content (not changed here).**
  - The X-11 glass base colour is sRGB ≈ 0.14 (linear ≈ 0.017). Base colour tints transmission (glTF), so one pass transmits about 1.7 %. Raising it to sRGB ≈ 0.55–0.60 gives the concept's visible pilot.
  - The roughness (ORM G) is 0.14 with grime up to 0.78; the grime reads as whitish smudges.

## ADR-168: A dormant stochastic SSR pass keeps its targets; only memory pressure frees them
Date: 2026-10-10   Status: accepted
Context: the sssr-budget lane made the stochastic SSR pass go dormant after 30 counter readbacks with no
glossy tile (only a quarter-resolution probe runs then), and going dormant freed all of its targets: the
pyramid, normals, history, variance, the ray/tile lists, the SPD chain, every bind group, plus the shared
"ssr color" output. The next glossy readback woke the pass and allocated all of it again. The rc1
rehearsal's 30-minute soaks (rig RTX 5080, 2560×1440, main e44dd12d) found the DO27 chase camera
crossing gloss-free views every 19–27 s: 67 (switchbacks) and 93 (bore_twelve) sleep/wake cycles. Each one
created 16 bind groups, 6 buffers and 17 textures (~70 MB), which made up 1072 of switchbacks' 1073 and 1488
of bore_twelve's 1489 bind-group creations after warm-up. `specs/27` § 2.4 allows zero.
Decision: going dormant keeps the targets and their bind groups and drops only the history. The first awake
frame zeroes every kept texture and buffer (`CommandEncoder::clear_texture` / `clear_buffer`), so it sees
exactly what a fresh, zero-initialised set would give it, and the pixels match the old path bit for bit
(test `a_wake_on_kept_targets_matches_fresh_targets`). The device now asks for `Features::CLEAR_TEXTURE`
wherever the adapter has it, and the Pascal min-spec mask includes it. Without that feature, a wake frees
and re-allocates as before. Targets are freed only by a resize or quality change, by a scene with no
possibly-glossy material for 60 frames (unchanged), or under memory pressure: `FrameRenderer::trim_memory()`,
which frees them only while the pass is dormant, and `ferrite_render::signal_memory_pressure()`, which the
render plugin calls on `LifecycleEvent::LowMemory` and which makes every renderer trim at its next frame.
The streaming texture budget is a fixed cap on material textures, separate from render targets, so freeing
reflection targets does not relieve it and it does not trigger a trim.
Consequences: on Desktop High and Ultra with a glossy material in the scene, the reflection targets stay
resident while the pass is dormant: ~185 MiB of stochastic SSR targets at 2560×1440 (~416 MiB at
3840×2160; they scale with the internal resolution, so DO27's 0.67 render scale holds ~83 MiB at 1440p),
plus the 28 MiB (63 MiB at 4K) "ssr color" output. The sssr-budget lane had saved that memory on gloss-free
views. Desktop Low, the Deck and mobile do not run the pass and allocate none of it (test
`tiers_without_the_pass_allocate_nothing`). The wake costs one clear of the set, about the same GPU work as
wgpu's lazy zero-init of a new set, without the allocation. `specs/27` § 2.4 unchanged. Agent guide:
`book/agents/hitches.md`.

## ADR-167: Game-frame warm speed: budgeted graph settle, concurrent pipeline variants, more graph workers
Date: 2026-10-10   Status: accepted
Context: DO27's Bore Twelve game-frame warm (`GameFrameWarm` → `warm_extracted` on a `PipelineWarmQueue` worker)
took 50 s cold and 10.8 s with a warmer cache, against about 2 s for the frame path (lane warm-speed). Probe:
`do27_chase` with `CHASE_WARM_WORKER=busy|idle` runs the same `warm_scene` on a worker while the main thread
submits a clear every 16 ms, and `CHASE_WARM_SPANS=1` sums spans over threads. Result: the worker costs what
the inline warm costs. Rig 5080, cold: 9.7 / 11.6 s inline against 6.8 / 11.6 s on the worker. the build server 5090,
cold: 20.2 s against 20.0 s. There is no lock contention, upload trickle or poll stall. About 85 % of the time
is driver compiles of six forward uber-shader pipelines, built one after another at 2.2-2.8 s each
(`FERRITE_PIPELINE_TIMING=1`). On top of that, `warm_extracted` ended with a full `settle_material_graphs()`.
DO27's scene has 6 graph sets of about 9-12 pipelines each, built on 2 matgraph threads (11.8 s per set
inline when cold on the 5090). The frame path never waits for those. They also run on the matgraph threads,
so the warm's "49 pipelines" did not count them.
Decision: (1) `warm_extracted` waits for graph builds only until `warm_graph_budget()`: 2 s from the warm's
start, `FERRITE_WARM_GRAPH_BUDGET_MS` overrides it. New `FrameRenderer::settle_material_graphs_for(budget)`.
The rest land on later frames exactly as on the frame path, drawing the standard surface until then;
`warm_scene` keeps its full settle. (2) `parallel_create::join` creates independent pipelines of one set on
scoped threads: the nine lab forward/blend/transmission variants, and the GPU-driven forward alpha pair,
which the first request now builds together. Helper threads keep the caller's warm tier, job count and
frame-path counters. (3) Material-graph workers are a quarter of the hardware threads, 2..=8
(`FERRITE_MATGRAPH_WORKERS`). 16 sets dropped from 69.6 s to 25.2 s on the 5090. (4) Each thread keeps a
naga_oil composer over the embedded library (`FERRITE_COMPOSER_CACHE=0` turns it off). Its output is the
fresh composer's, which a unit test checks. Compose was under 0.5 s of a warm, so this is a small win.
Consequences: Bore Twelve warm on the 5090 (shared card 3): cold 20 s → 11-12 s, warm driver cache 1.4 s on
the worker. Frames are unchanged once graphs land. The pipelines are the same objects; only their creation
order and threads differ. The first frames after a game warm can show the standard surface on graph materials
that missed the budget, as the frame path always did. An extra GPU-driven alpha variant is built when a
level has no alpha-tested material: a parallel compile, so no wall time. Specs: `13-renderer.md` § 2c.

Addendum (integration, wave Q2, 2026-10-10): the lane was built on e44dd12d, before ADR-161 (shipped-shader-cache) landed. ADR-161 already defers the blend/transmission variants and compiles a set's pipelines concurrently through `pipeline_warm::join` / `join_all` (helper creations counted as the caller's), including the GPU-driven variants a frame needs. Decision (2) and its `parallel_create` module (and `FERRITE_PARALLEL_CREATE`) were therefore dropped at integration in favour of ADR-161's mechanism; the GPU-driven alpha sibling is no longer built speculatively. Decisions (1), (3) and (4) are kept as written.

## ADR-169: GI Depth: probe light on terrain skips the relief AO; thin plates are probe proxies at any length
Date: 2026-10-10   Status: accepted
Status note: accepted 2026-10-21, shipped in v0.1.0. Thin-plate probe proxies and the terrain relief-AO skip under probe light shipped in v0.1.0 (merge 09fc29e5, commit 36acc23d).
Context: Under GI Depth (the Desktop High/Ultra default), the alpha look snapshot found shaded DO27 hero surfaces at 1.2–2.0× Cycles, against 0.93–1.0 for the engine's own path tracer. Mars canyon walls in shade on switchbacks_mid were too dark: p50 87 against the PT's 112. The A/B used absolute units against the engine PT. Hero comparisons used a fresh 256 spp PT of the current DO27 drop, because the turret mesh has changed since the snapshot. Terrain was measured surface-only: no media in the PT, and the raster's aerial perspective and froxel fog skipped by a temporary switch, at 960×540, 64 spp, 12 bounces.
- **Heroes: the studio ground was never traced.** `ddgi::proxy_candidate` drops a mesh whose 40-voxel brick would be coarser than `max_proxy_voxel` (8 m). hero_ref's 800 × 0.1 × 800 m ground box fell under that rule. Probe rays that went down missed it and read the sky map's lower hemisphere, which is a fully sunlit ground. Every probe under a hull or overhang therefore saw sunlit ground. Rejecting such meshes was meant for kilometre ground meshes with relief. For a plate the brick is exact: its thin axis resolves the surface (anisotropic voxels, `ddgi_bake`), and the coarse axes run along a flat surface.
- **Terrain: the probe light took the relief AO a second time.** Under the probes, the terrain multiplied the probe irradiance by min(heightfield cavity, baked macro AO). Both stand for occlusion by the relief, which the probes trace themselves (`ddgi_trace` hits the heightfield). A mesh under the probes takes only its own AO and the SSAO.
  - Shaded walls, raster/PT surface light: 150–300 m 0.74, 300–600 m 0.65.
  - Debug-view decomposition: macro AO 0.65–0.85 and cavity 0.8–0.97 on those walls.
- **Not changed, measured:**
  - **Sub-cell leaks.** Cascade-0 probes are 2 m apart, so a receiver inside a shadow smaller than a cell takes light from probes that see the sunlit ground beyond it.
    - A rock in a slab's 3.8 m airless shadow: 2.5× the PT (Balanced 2.4×). A rock under a 6 m roof: 1.7× (Balanced 1.45×).
    - The probes in the patch are right, and the probe trace was checked: sun shadow rays, back faces, relocation. The error is interpolation from the 2 m layer.
    - View/normal bias variants move it by at most 6 %.
  - **Walls farther than ~450 m from the eye** lie outside the cascades and keep the analytic terrain ambient: 0.59–0.63 of the PT in Balanced and Depth alike. Its wall bounce taps end at 270 m, so a canyon's opposite sunlit wall is mostly missed.
  - **SSGI adds its screen-space bounce on top of the probes' bounce** (a double count). Turning it off moves Depth by ~3 % here.
Decision:
- `proxy_candidate`: a mesh whose thinnest world extent is at most `max_proxy_voxel / 8` (1 m) is traced whatever its length. The voxel limit applies only to thicker meshes.
- `terrain.wgsl`: where the probes cover a pixel (`probe_gi.a`), its ambient (and the sky reflection built from it) takes `min(multi_bounce(ORM_rel), SSAO · ORM_rel)` in place of the relief-AO product. The bounce and planet-shine fill, which the probes do not replace, keep the full visibility.
- Balanced is untouched: no probes, so `probe_gi.a = 0`.
Consequences:
- hero_ref under Depth, 8 heroes against a fresh PT: shade raster/PT median 1.34 → 1.18; sunlit 1.00 → 1.00. Balanced is 1.22. Examples:
  - kraken front34 dark 2.25 → 1.82
  - reactor_a52 front34 dark 1.65 → 1.17
  - foundry_mobile_a52 side 9.3 → 5.2
  - before/after/PT sheets are in `docs/evidence/depth-shade/`.
- In game, flat set pieces, pads and floors longer than 320 m now occlude and bounce probe light. switchbacks traces 3 more meshes; bore_twelve and set_piece_borehole are unchanged.
- switchbacks_mid shaded walls, raster/PT surface light: 150–300 m 0.74 → 0.84, 300–600 m 0.65 → 0.68. Flats 150–300 m 0.73 → 0.81. Sunlit 0.92 → 0.95.
- Europa:
  - bore_twelve_close's trench walls 0.44 → 0.53.
  - Shaded flats, already over the PT under Depth (the sub-cell leak at cascade 1–2), rise 1–9 % (bore_twelve_wide 150–300 m 1.32 → 1.43). The macro AO had been partly hiding that leak.
  - Morning sheet p10 on the trench shots goes up 1–6 levels.
- Balanced frames are byte-identical (all seven morning shots).
- **Known issues, left for a later batch:**
  1. **Europa shaded flats.** Already over the PT under Depth, they rise a further 1–9 % (this ADR's one step the wrong way, small by eye and accepted).
  2. **The sub-cell leak.** Small shaded pockets and trench floors read brighter than the PT. Fixing it needs denser near probes (a 1 m near cascade over ±10 m), or a screen-space near field that replaces, rather than adds to, the probes' near part.
  3. **The SSGI double count under Depth.** About 3 % here.
  4. **The Mars far-wall bounce.** The analytic wall-bounce taps end at 270 m, and the probes cover only to ~450 m, so far canyon walls stay at ~0.6 of the PT in both modes.
- Cost (rig RTX 5080, do27_bench flyover, High 1440p, 120 + 600 continuous frames, interleaved A/B against main 12ab8661): GPU frame p50 +0.00–0.04 ms (switchbacks 8.629/8.631 → 8.633/8.651, bore_twelve 6.203/6.217 → 6.205/6.253); the probe pass ±0.01 ms.
- No golden moved (the Depth goldens pass unblessed). `tests/ddgi.rs`: the kilometre-ground test now uses a 4 m-thick ground (relief, still not traced); a new test traces a kilometre plate and checks that the probes over it stay active.

## ADR-170: Pipeline warm shutdown cancels between compiles; an exit hook joins what is left
Date: 2026-10-10   Status: accepted. Amended by ADR-276 (v0.1.24): the shutdown wait is 30 s (was 2 s) and the `atexit` join 30 s in all (was 5 s); after a device loss both wait at most 250 ms. The 2 s / 5 s figures below are the original values.
Context: `PipelineWarmQueue::shutdown` (on `WillTerminate`) stopped workers only between jobs and waited 2 s. A
warm job (a whole frame configuration) can compile for many seconds on a cold driver (first launch, no cache),
so on quit a worker could still be compiling, holding a `wgpu::Device` clone, while `main` returned and the
driver's exit handlers ran: the same crash class as the v0.1.0 telemetry quit segfault (80093b3b). A runner that
never sends `WillTerminate` never shut the queue down at all.
Decision: (1) Each queue has a cancel flag, set by `shutdown`. Warm worker threads (and their `join` helpers)
check it at `note_pipeline`, which `cache_for` calls at every pipeline creation site just before the compile;
once set, the job unwinds with `std::panic::resume_unwind(WarmCancelled)` (no panic hook runs, so no log
spam or crash bundle), `run_job`/`run_deferred` catch it, and the worker exits after the compile in flight.
Only warm worker threads carry the flag, so the frame thread and inline warms are never unwound. The unwind
is compiled only under `cfg(panic = "unwind")`: the shipping profile is `panic = "abort"`, where
`resume_unwind` would abort the process at every quit during a warm. There the running job continues, and
shutdown falls back to its 2 s wait and then the exit hook's join (3). (2) Workers
do not save the pipeline cache once the queue is shutting down (the exit path saves on its own thread).
(3) On Linux and Android, the first `start` registers an `atexit` hook (through the `platform/` seam). The GPU
driver registered its handlers when it loaded, earlier, and handlers run in reverse order, so the hook runs
first: it shuts down every queue still running and joins workers a shutdown left compiling, within 5 s in all.
The hook touches no thread-local and logs nothing. On glibc the exiting thread's thread-locals are destroyed
before `atexit` handlers run, and a panic there would abort a `panic = "abort"` build.
Consequences: in unwinding builds (dev, release), a quit during a cold warm stops after one compile instead of
the whole job. In shipping (abort) builds the job keeps compiling for up to 2 s + 5 s before the process exits.
Either way no warm worker is inside the driver when it tears down, unless the job outlasts 2 s + 5 s. A cancelled job is a failed job
("canceled at shutdown") and leaves no partial state anyone uses afterwards. Unwinding from a creation site
can poison a mutex the job held; engine code locks poison-tolerantly, and this happens only at shutdown. The
hook adds up to 5 s to process exit only when a worker is mid-compile (a test process leaving a stuck job).
Windows has no hook yet (the crash was NVIDIA Linux). Specs: `specs/13` § 2 (Teardown bullet).
Tests: `pipeline_warm::tests::shutdown_stops_a_long_job_between_compiles_and_joins_the_worker`,
`crates/ferrite_render/tests/warm_exit_hook.rs`, and `crates/ferrite_render/tests/warm_quit_abort.rs`. The last
builds `examples/warm_quit.rs` with `panic = "abort"` and requires exit 0 for a plain quit, a quit during a
warm, and a never-shut-down queue. It fails (SIGABRT) with an unconditional unwind.

Addendum (v0.1.2, lane v012-warm-cancel, 2026-10-11): shipping builds now stop a warm early too, through
ordinary control flow. Under `panic = "abort"` the job used to run on; a quit in the first seconds of a cold
first launch (the warm continues behind the lobby since ADR-173) exited 2.3–2.5 s after the quit on the 5080
and up to 2 s + 5 s on slower GPUs. On lavapipe, a warm still compiling when the exit hook's 5 s ran out
crashed the process at exit (SIGSEGV, reproduced by the new test with the checks disabled).
Decision: (1) `pipeline_warm::warm_cancelled()` (public) is true on a warm worker thread, or its `join`
helper, once its queue shuts down; it is always false elsewhere (frame thread, inline warms). (2) The engine's
warms check it between their compiles and return an ordinary error: `FrameRenderer::render_into` at every
phase and pass boundary (26 points) and before each inline material-graph set build; `warm_scene` /
`warm_extracted_at` before the GPU wait, and they settle the graph builds in 20 ms slices; `prewarm` and
`prewarm_material_graphs` between their phases and graphs; the engine's overlay-layer job between layers and
formats. Background `DeferredPipeline` builds were already one variant per worker iteration, and the worker
checks `shutdown` between them. `join` / `join_all` run their closures side by side, so a batch is one
"compile in flight"; their callers check after. The error is `RenderError::Encode("canceled at shutdown")`:
`RenderError` is not `#[non_exhaustive]`, so a new variant would break hosts that match on it in a patch
release. `run_job` reports any failed job of a cancelled queue as "canceled at shutdown". (3) The
renderer is left mid-frame, the state an existing `?` in `render_into` leaves. Command-buffer segments
the frame had already handed to its encode workers (`parallel_finish`) are not left behind: the frame's
`Segments` finish what no worker has started on the warm thread when they drop, and wait for the ones in
progress. So when the cancelled job returns, no encoder of it (each holds a device reference) is still
being finished on an encode thread. (Before this, a dropped frame left them to the detached workers, a
millisecond window for a device reference to outlive shutdown; the review of this lane found it.) The
renderer itself then drops normally. A cancelled game-frame warm hands its renderer back with the error,
as any failed warm does.
Shutdown is only called on exit, so nothing renders with it again. (4) The unwind is kept where panics
unwind (dev, test, release). There it stops a warm at the very next pipeline creation, including custom
host jobs that never check `warm_cancelled`. Removing it would make those slower to stop in dev builds and
gain nothing in shipping. A per-queue switch turns it off in the unit test of the control-flow path, so
that path is tested in process as well as in the `panic = "abort"` child.
Consequences: in a `panic = "abort"` build, a quit during a frame warm returns from `main` about one compile
batch after the quit. Measured on lavapipe: 0.57 s quit → `main` returns, 0.58 s to exit; never shut down
(the exit hook): exit 0.46 s after `main`. Unit test, six quit points: 1–9 pipelines compiled after the
cancel, shutdown 14–454 ms on an idle CPU. RTX 5080, real `--profile shipping`, driver shader cache off:
quit → `main` 11–53 ms at most quit points, 0.96–1.45 s when the quit lands on the forward uber-shader
compile (one compile, ~1–1.5 s cold; shutdown returns 2–3 ms after it); exit 40–60 ms after `main`. The
exit-hook path exits about 1.1 s after the quit. Host warm jobs that loop over
their own pipeline builds should check `warm_cancelled()`; jobs that do not are joined as before (2 s + exit
hook). One thread-local read per check on the frame path (26 per frame). Tests:
`pipeline_warm::tests::shutdown_stops_a_frame_warm_between_passes_without_unwinding` and
`warm_cancelled_is_false_off_the_workers`; `parallel_finish::tests::dropped_segments_finish_before_the_frame_returns`;
`tests/warm_quit_abort.rs`
`a_quit_during_a_frame_warm_returns_promptly_in_a_panic_abort_build` (child modes `frame-warm` and
`frame-warm-no-shutdown`). Without the checks, the child's quit waits the full 2 s and the process dies of
SIGSEGV at exit on lavapipe. Specs: `specs/13` Teardown bullet; the host checklist's warm section.

Addendum (v0.1.5, lane v015-races, 2026-10-12): `shutdown` returning left two kinds of holder of the queue's
shared state, found when `shutdown_joins_the_workers_and_releases_the_device` saw a strong count of 2 under
a loaded gate. (a) The process-wide registry of started queues held `Weak<Shared>` handles. Every frame
(`may_block` → `background_available`) and every deferred pipeline (`notify_queues`) upgraded them on its
own thread, so for a moment any thread could hold any queue, also one that `shutdown` was releasing. (b)
`shutdown` joined only the workers that finished within its 2 s wait. An idle worker that a loaded scheduler
kept off the CPU for longer went to the exit hook with its queue handle, although it was not compiling. (c) In
the unit-test binary, a test queue's workers also built other tests' deferred pipelines, and one lavapipe
compile under load outlasted the 2 s wait (seen in 2 of 3 full-suite runs of the new stress test). That
worker is inside a compile, which is the bounded path ADR-170 intends, so it is a test-isolation problem.
Decision: the registry holds a small `Hub` per queue (the workers' condvar, an `available` flag, and a
`Weak` used only by the exit hook), so asking about or waking queues never touches a queue. `shutdown`
clears the flag, removes the hub, and joins workers without a time bound once none is inside a job. The
per-queue `busy` count is raised under the state lock, so no worker starts a job after the shutdown flag.
Only a worker still inside a job at the deadline is left to the exit hook, as before. The frame path's
`background_available` is now one lock and a flag per queue, with no per-queue state lock (audit item 20).
The tests that require idle workers at `shutdown` use a test-only isolated queue: it builds no process-wide
deferred pipelines and does not count as available to other renderers.
Consequences: when `shutdown` returns, the only other holders are workers still inside a job (a stuck
driver compile, bounded as before). Tests: `pipeline_warm::tests::shutdown_leaves_no_other_holder_under_contention`
(200 start/shutdown cycles while 4 threads ask and wake and every core spins; it failed at round 8 before)
and `shutdown_joins_an_idle_worker_that_is_slow_to_exit` (a test-only exit delay of 300 ms against a 20 ms
wait).

## ADR-174: An abandoned game warm's stand-in keeps the map's installs
Date: 2026-10-10   Status: accepted
Context: ADR-166's watchdog abandons a game warm still running after 15 s; the stand-in renderer takes over
and the job's late result was dropped. The stand-in had only the translucent layers, so the map lost the
terrain shared draw, the GI field and the reflection probes installed before the warm (warm-guard follow-up,
perf/stability audit #17). On lavapipe-class devices the warm takes 18–50 s, so this path is real there.
Decision: `GameFrameWarm::start` gives the stand-in copies of the GI field (with its interior scene and bake
key) and the reflection probes besides the translucent layers (`FrameRenderer::share_installs_with`). The
shared pass draw is a `Box<dyn SharedPassDraw>`, cannot be copied and must go with the warm (the warm compiles
the terrain pipelines), so on abandon the handle is kept: when the job returns, the window path's `poll` moves
its shared draw to the renderer that took over (`salvage_shared_draw`) unless that renderer has one or the host
called `set_shared_draw` on it meanwhile (a `None` stands). Starting a new warm forgets an older abandoned one,
because that warm's terrain belongs to the old map. The rest of the late renderer is dropped and the report
stays `timed_out`. A warm that comes back normally is unchanged (the warmed renderer keeps its own
installs; the stand-in's copies are dropped).
Consequences: after a timeout the map is lit and reflected as before at once, and the terrain returns when the
slow warm finishes instead of never. If the job never returns (a hung driver) the terrain stays missing, as
before. The late renderer's GPU resources are dropped on the frame thread (one frame). Docs: the host
checklist's warm section. Tests: `pipeline_warm::tests::an_abandoned_warm_*`,
`a_game_warm_stand_in_starts_with_the_installs_and_the_warm_returns_them`.

## ADR-172: IO never blocks the frame: lossy console, off-thread crash context, background pak integrity
Date: 2026-10-10   Status: accepted
Status note: accepted 2026-10-21, shipped in v0.1.1. NonBlockingConsole, off-thread crash context publishing and the background pak integrity check (pak_verify.rs) shipped in v0.1.1.
Context: The v0.1.0 stability audit found three ways IO could stall or silently corrupt a player's session. (1) The console log layer wrote to stderr synchronously from whichever thread logged. Under a launcher that pipes stderr and never reads it, the 64 KiB pipe fills and the next `info!` blocks the frame thread forever. (2) `publish_context` did blocking `sendmsg` calls to the native crash monitor from the frame thread, so a stopped monitor eventually freezes a frame. (3) Paks carry a blake3 `content_hash` that nothing checked. A pak corrupted or half-patched on disk only showed up as odd assets or a SIGBUS. The owner's priority is the fastest possible load, so a check on the load path was not acceptable.
Decision: (1) When stderr is not a terminal, `ferrite_core::log::init` writes the console through `NonBlockingConsole`: a bounded queue of 1024 lines feeding a detached writer thread. A full queue drops the line and counts it, and the writer reports the count once stderr drains. `LogGuard::flush` waits at most 250 ms for the queue. Terminals, the file sink (a buffered regular file), `RingLayer`, Android logcat and telemetry's `json_layer` are unchanged. (2) `publish_context` only flips a flag. After arming, the monitor's connect thread becomes the publisher and does the blocking sends. Requests that arrive while it is busy coalesce into one, and `feedback::native::context_updates_dropped` counts the superseded ones. `minidumper::Client` does not expose its socket, so a per-send `MSG_DONTWAIT` would have meant re-implementing its framing, or making the fd non-blocking under the signal handler's `request_dump` (which must block for the ack). A crash on another thread cannot tear an in-flight context message: minidumper 0.11 sends each message as one `sendmsg(MSG_EOR)` packet on a SOCK_SEQPACKET socket, and the monitor replaces its context only on END. (3) `AssetServer` hands the mounted paks to `pak_verify::spawn_pak_verify`. This is a detached low-priority thread reading with plain `read` (no mapping, so no SIGBUS), capped at 64 MiB/s on every platform and starting 60 s after the mount. The priority is per platform: on Linux it is nice 19 plus the idle IO class, which only the BFQ scheduler honours (NVMe's default `none` and mq-deadline ignore it, hence the rate cap); on Android nice 19; on Windows `THREAD_MODE_BACKGROUND_BEGIN` (low CPU, IO and memory priority). There is no `tracing` span around a pak: `FrameProfiler` books spans from every thread into one frame, and a seconds-long span would read as that frame's top CPU cost. A pak is skipped when `cache://pak-verified.txt` already lists (build stamp, size, mtime, header hash, path). The build stamp is the engine version plus the executable's size and mtime. A mismatch logs an error telling the player to verify or reinstall, plus a `pak_corrupt` telemetry note. It is never recorded, so the next launch checks again. An all-zero hash means "not hashed" and is skipped. With no record location (Android today) the check does not run, because it would re-hash every pak on every launch. `FERRITE_PAK_VERIFY=0|force`; `ferrite doctor --verify-paks DIR` runs the same check synchronously. Settings `persist` now fsyncs the temp file before the rename and the directory after it, like `save_game::write_atomic`. Because that runs on the frame thread, settings writes are rate-limited (`SettingsPersistence`: a change is written at once if the last write is at least 0.5 s old, otherwise only the newest value is written once 0.5 s has passed; a pending value is also written on `AppExit` and when the world drops). A slider that changes `GameSettings` every frame costs one write and fsync per 0.5 s.
Consequences: Under a stuck stderr, `tracing` output loses console lines instead of hanging the logging thread. The file log, ring and telemetry keep every record. This covers `tracing` output only: `eprintln!`, direct stderr writes and the default panic hook (which `install_panic_hook` chains to) still block on a stuck pipe, and the writer thread then holds std's stderr lock while it is blocked. A panic under an unread pipe can still hang (as before this change). Console output is now asynchronous, so it can interleave differently with direct `eprintln!` output.
