gets `on_missing` and keeps the latch for the first tick that is sent, so the server sees the press too. (4) **Late inputs
merge (spec 120 § 6.3).** New provided method `NetInput::merge_late(late, next)`; its default keeps `late` when only it
carries a one-shot (`late != on_missing(late)`) and otherwise `next`, so a type with no `on_missing` override (no one-shots)
keeps the newest input; a type with one-shot fields overrides it field by field. On the server, a command for a tick already
consumed with a repeat (`repeated`, counted `late` as before) is merged into a per-player late slot in tick order, and the
next consumed tick takes `merge_late(late, value)`; a duplicate merges nothing (the tick leaves `repeated` on the first
copy). On the `TickDriver` path, `TickDriver::set_late_merge(Some(fn(late, next) -> I))` keeps the ticks each peer missed
(the last `LATE_MERGE_TICKS`, 256: a one-second stall on a 300 ms path fits; the first test run with 64 lost two presses
there); a late input for one of them returns true once and merges into the next tick (the late input
alone when that tick has none of its own; `TickDriver::late_merged` counts them). `NetServer` sets
`NetCodec::merge_late`, a new provided method whose default keeps `next` (the codec cannot see fields; a type with presses
overrides it). (5) **The packet limit is a token bucket** refilled with `max_input_packets_per_tick` tokens per server tick
and holding `INPUT_BURST_TICKS` (16) ticks' worth: a good peer's flushed burst (up to 64 packets at the default) is kept, a
peer that sends more than the limit every tick is cut to it after the bucket drains. No settings field, format or wire
change. (6) Agent surface: `net.prediction` gains `dilated` and `dilation_lag`.
Spec differences: spec 120 § 9.3 says the client runs at `1 +- 2 %`; the existing `max_dilation` default (5 %) is kept (no
default changed). The § 6.3 default "merge" can only be field-exact for a type that overrides `merge_late`: the `NetInput`
default keeps a lone press (its analog values are one frame older), the `NetCodec` default keeps `next`; both are written in
the trait docs. Spec 120 says input is captured "every rendered frame": the prediction path's frame is its fixed step (the
game writes `InputCommand` in `FixedUpdate`), so the latch is per fixed step; a game that samples devices per rendered frame
folds its presses into the value it writes (as before). The lockstep host (§ 6.3's third path) is not on this base.
Evidence: lane net-time-harness (N206, ADR-8185) was to be merged first, but its branch carries the v0.5.0 release line (112
commits, 14 conflicting files including `regia_asset` code) that the v0.6 integration line has not taken; the tests here use
`regia_net`'s own `LoopbackHub` with the spec 120 § 15.1 bad-wifi shape (Gilbert-Elliott bursts, jitter, reorder, duplicates
through `up_filter`/`down_filter`) and the clock-drift shape (new `LoopbackHub::client_frames` hook: frames per hub step per
client). Tests: `tests/dilation_input_capture.rs` (over 1,000 dilation events, every one-step press once on client and
server; per-frame displacement within 0.5-1.5x of a tick's step; an 8-packet burst kept; a late press merged once),
`tests/late_input_merge.rs` (the DO27 scenario on the prediction path: 0-300 ms per-peer latency, bursts, a one-second
blackout, duplicates; presses inside a blackout all kept), `tick.rs` unit tests (the DO27 scenario on the `TickDriver`
path, merge once, no merge without a merge function), `predict.rs` unit tests (the fractional clock, the default merge, the
latch). The old unit assertion "6 packets in one tick drop 2" now reads "6 in one tick from a quiet peer are kept; 6 every
tick are cut to 4" (the behavior the row asks for).
Consequences: no 0- or 2-tick hitch of the own pawn; no lost or doubled one-step press from dilation, late arrival, a
burst or a backward resync's hold. New public items: `NetInput::merge_late`, `NetCodec::merge_late` (provided methods, not
breaking), `TickDriver::{set_late_merge, late_merged}`, `tick::LATE_MERGE_TICKS`, `ClientPrediction::dilation_lag`,
`predict::INPUT_BURST_TICKS`,
`testing::{LoopbackHub::client_frames, ClientFramesFn}` (a new pub field of a struct with private fields: not breaking).
Behavior changes a host can see: `InputCommand` on the client holds the delivered value after the step (a second tick in a
frame shows `on_missing`); `NetServer` games get a late input in the next tick's `TickInputs` (previously dropped); a
player's late command now changes the next consumed command. Specs updated: 120 § 6.3 and § 9.3 ("Built" notes).

## ADR-8315: Per-shooter lag-compensation windows and checked view ticks (spec 120 § 9.6, N210)
Date: 2026-11-17   Status: proposed
Context: Audit row P5: `lag_compensation.max_rewind_ms` defaulted to 250 ms while an honest shot needs about RTT +
input lead + interpolation delay, so shots were clamped from about 130-180 ms RTT (`net_acceptance.rs` n03 said so),
and every claim inside the window was believed: the view tick a command carried was never compared with the
shooter's measured round trip, never required to move forward, and the hit-claim check compared it with a view the
same client reported. A 5 ms client could claim the oldest tick of the window and get a free 250 ms backtrack. Spec
120 § 9.6 asks for a per-shooter window `RTT + lead + interpolation delay + 1 tick` capped by `max_rewind_ms`
(default 400 ms, settable to 1,000); its § 1.1 promises exact lag compensation to 650 ms RTT and § 16 P5 accepts
"450 ms RTT shots exact" with the defaults. Those disagree: a 450 ms shooter's honest view is about 550-600 ms old.
Decision: (1) `regia_net::lagcomp::window::check_view_tick`, called from `interp::set_view_tick` when a server
consumes a command, computes the shooter's expected age from what the server measured: the round trip and its
variation for the peer (the server endpoint's `PeerRow` in `NetAgentState`, or `lagcomp::set_shooter_rtt` for hosts
whose transport publishes none), the averaged arrival margin of its commands (at most `margin_max_ticks`), the
reported interpolation delay bounded by the server's model of the client's interpolation clock (the target delay at
the server's send rate with 4 × the variation as jitter, inside `min_delay_ms..max_delay_ms`, never falling faster
than `lower_rate` from where it was, starting at `max_delay_ms`), plus one tick. The window is that age plus an
allowance (`VIEW_SLACK_MS` 50 + `VIEW_JITTER_FACTOR` 2 × the variation), at most `max_rewind_ms`. (2) The carried
tick must lie in `[now − window, now]` and may not be more than the allowance behind the shooter's previous checked
view; violations are clamped to the nearest allowed tick and counted per shooter (`LagCompWindows`,
`ShooterWindow`, `lagcomp.stats` `windows`). The clamped tick is what `NetViewTick` keeps, so rewound queries,
projectile view lag and the hit-claim check all use it (a claim at a stale tick is refused `view_tick_out_of_range`).
(3) A peer with no measurement gets `max_rewind_ms` (the future and backward checks still apply). (4)
`max_rewind_ms` defaults to **1,000 ms** and is clamped to `MAX_REWIND_CEILING_MS` (1,000): with per-shooter windows a
short link cannot use the cap, so the cap only decides how far long links reach, and 1,000 meets § 1.1 and § 16 at
the defaults; 400 would clamp the high-rtt profile's honest shots. Owner question Q5 stays open; a game that favors
targets sets 400 in `config/net.ron`. (5) No settings field is added (the slack constants are `pub const`), so
`config/net.ron` keeps its shape and version; only a default value changes.
Consequences: Shots at 450 and 650 ms RTT (high-rtt), on transatlantic and on mobile-4g are judged exactly at their
carried view with the defaults (`regia_net_soak/tests/lagcomp_window.rs`); a 5 ms client forcing a 250 ms-old view is
posed under 200 ms back, and forged, future and backward view ticks are clamped and counted
(`regia_net/tests/lagcomp_window.rs`). The history keeps 62 ticks at 60 Hz instead of 17 (more memory per
lag-compensated entity; recording cost per tick unchanged). Trust that remains: the interpolation delay a client
reports is believed up to the server's model of it, and the model starts at `max_delay_ms` for a new peer (about 10 s
at the defaults); a client can also inflate its measured RTT by holding acknowledgements, which lengthens its own
window as it lengthens its own lag. No Rust API break: `lagcomp.stats` adds `windows` from the new `LagCompWindows`
resource, `LagCompStats` is unchanged.
Specs updated: spec 120 § 9.6 (Built note), book/agents/net-lag-compensation.md, book/user-guide/networking.md.

## ADR-8219: Prediction at high RTT: RTT-scaled rollback depth, re-run over the cap, a measured start (spec 120 § 9.4, § 9.2)
Date: 2026-11-17   Status: proposed
Context: net-sota-audit row P3 and the time harness (ADR-8185): at about 400 ms RTT and above, prediction switched off
for the rest of the session. A rollback needing more than `max_resim_ticks` (32) ticks re-ran nothing, cleared every
predicted entity's history and snapped; the next server state was older than anything held, so it reset again, on
every state (650 ms RTT: 3,501 resets in 7,080 predicted ticks). `start_clock` skipped the catch-up over the cap, so a
high-RTT session started in that loop. The clock started on a guess (`margin target + 8`) at the first state frame,
before the transport's first round-trip sample, and the transport's first jitter value was RFC 6298's `RTTVAR = R/2`,
which put the margin target at its 8-tick clamp (a 100 ms link started up to 6 ticks over-led). The send-time map that
turns input acks into round trips was pruned only on an ack.
Decision: (1) The rollback depth scales with the measured round trip: `ClientPrediction::resim_depth` = RTT in ticks +
margin target + 2 + one state send interval, at least `max_resim_ticks`, at most the history
(`prediction.history_ticks`, default 64, clamped to `predict::MAX_HISTORY_TICKS` = 128). (2) Over the depth the client
does not clear: it writes the server's state at S into every predicted entity and re-runs S+1 ..= client tick from its
input history, exactly like a correction, and counts a reset. A rollback whose S left the ring (a lead resync, a lead
past the history) does the same. Only a rollback deeper than the client's input history (`INPUT_HISTORY_TICKS`, 128),
or a server state ahead of the client tick, still clears and snaps. We chose "re-run from S" over "rebase onto the
newest held tick" because S is the one state the client knows is right, the inputs since S are all held (the input
history is 128 ticks, the ring 64), and a re-run refills the ring, which is what ends the loop. (3) The rendered pose of
an over-depth rollback smooths through `NetVisualOffset` like any correction; only a teleport, an offset over
`snap_distance_m` (or a quarter turn) or a cleared history snaps. New counters `PredictionStats::snaps` (rendered pose
jumped) and `last_correction_m` (the pose change of the last rollback). (4) The start catches up from S to the client
tick whenever the input history covers it (it was capped at 32). (5) A connected `NetLink` marks the transport as
expected (`predict::expect_transport_rtt`); the clock then waits for the transport's first round-trip sample before it
starts, at most `START_WAIT_FOR_RTT_STEPS` (120) fixed steps after the first server state, then starts on the old
fallback. A process without a transport (the lockstep hub, a host that never calls it) starts as before. (6) The
transport's reported jitter (`LinkStats::jitter_ms`) is RFC 6298's `RTTVAR` filter seeded from the samples: 0 at the
first sample, then the same 1/4-gain mean deviation; the retransmission timeout keeps RFC 6298's own `RTTVAR` with its
`R/2` start. (7) The send-time map is pruned to the input history on every send. Not built: spreading one rollback's
re-run over several frames. The brief asked for "the cap becomes a per-frame CPU budget (spread resim over frames)";
spec 120 § 9.4 (which wins) asks for the RTT-scaled depth and "snap and continue". A partial re-run would leave the
predicted entities at an older tick for the gameplay, input capture and send that run between frames; the cost is
already bounded (at most `INPUT_HISTORY_TICKS` re-run ticks, one rollback per frame: only the newest state reconciles).
Consequences: `PredictionStats` gains `snaps` and `last_correction_m`, `PredictionReport` gains `resim_depth`, `TimeReport`
gains `correction_m` and `snaps` (struct literals need them; all derive `Default`). `net.prediction` returns
`resim_depth`, `snaps` and `last_correction_m`. `LinkStats::jitter_ms` reads 0 instead of `RTT/2` until the second
sample; the RTO is unchanged. Spec 73 § 13 test 9 ("a 40-tick lead resets instead of re-running") is superseded:
`tests/prediction.rs` `resim_cap_resets` now asserts the 40-tick lead re-runs as one correction and prediction stays
on. A high-RTT client re-runs up to RTT + lead ticks per correction (about 45 at 650 ms); corrections are rare (inputs
are resent 16 times). No settings field or format changed (`history_ticks` and `max_resim_ticks` keep their names
and defaults; their meaning is documented in `settings.rs`), no wire change. Specs updated: spec 120 § 9.4 Built note,
book/agents/net-prediction.md, book/user-guide/networking.md, book/agents/net-soak.md.

## ADR-8180: Session resume fixes: live-token takeover, flow control, resume transport (N102)
Date: 2026-11-17   Status: proposed
Context: Spec 120 § 10.3 and audit rows S2, S3, S7 (adversarial rows 7-9, soak F6). The session
layer turned four recoverable hiccups into lost players: a reconnect token worked only once the
old peer was already in `Grace`, so a client that came back before the server's own timeout
joined twice or was refused `server_full` by its own ghost; any reliable send refusal, backpressure
included, ended the link as `reliable_overflow` without grace while streams kept filling the
window; `NetSession::resume` always bound UDP, so a Steam lobby client resumed toward a synthetic
Steam address over UDP and timed out; the session core kept the pre-rebind address, so an address
ban after a NAT rebind banned the old IP. The transport also reported a same-address replacement of
a quiet sealed peer as `Left` (`client_quit`, no grace) and refreshed liveness only for payloads, not
for an authentic `Join` resend.
Decision: (1) A valid token matching a peer in `Grace`, `Loading`, `Joining` or `InGame`
(interrupted or not) resumes it; a live peer's old link is detached first (no goodbye: the driver
drops it with `NetServer::drop_quietly`; its streams fail `link_replaced`), with no allocation and
no capacity check. A token that matches nothing raises `ServerSessionEvent::TokenRefused { link }`
and the join goes on. (2) `NetServer::admit` drops a quiet sealed peer replaced from its own
address as `Timeout`; `on_peer_record` touches the peer for every authentic record, and the
same-nonce accept resend touches it too. (3) The session driver treats `SendError::Backpressure`
and `RateLimited` on the reliable channel as flow control: it holds the messages per link in order
and retries each flush; only a held backlog past `MAX_DEFERRED_RELIABLE_BYTES` (8 MiB) or another
refusal is fatal. The driver tells the core when a link's window is half full or held
(`set_link_backpressure` / `SessionClient::set_backpressure`); streams pause then and while the peer
is interrupted; `try_send_game` hands bytes back. A `reliable_overflow` while the peer is
interrupted enters grace. (4) `NetSession` keeps a `SocketOpener` (`connect_via`, `set_socket_opener`;
`connect` installs a UDP one) and `resume` opens its socket with it; the lobby connects through
`connect_via` with its transport. A `connect_on` without an opener keeps the old UDP resume.
(5) The driver passes the transport's peer address to `SessionServer::set_link_addr` every receive.
Consequences: No wire change and no format change. Additive API: `TokenRefused`, `SocketOpener`,
`udp_socket_opener`, `connect_via`, `set_socket_opener`, `has_socket_opener`,
`MAX_DEFERRED_RELIABLE_BYTES`, `SessionServer::{set_link_addr, set_link_backpressure,
is_backpressured, try_send_game, take_quiet_closes}`, `SessionClient::{set_backpressure,
is_backpressured}`, `NetServer::drop_quietly`. The one break is the `TokenRefused` variant
(exhaustive matches on `ServerSessionEvent` update; `api-snapshot --update --breaking`). Behavior changes a host can see: a live token now
replaces the old link (a captured current token, on a plain link only, can take a live slot as it
could take a grace slot before; sealed links keep the token secret); `session.state` peer rows add
`backpressured`. Refinement of the brief: its stream acceptance (5 s, 3 streams, 4x
`client_rate_bytes`, default 25 % `stream_share`) passes on the base, because that load queues about
215 of the 1024 window fragments in 5 s; the lane keeps it and adds DO27's 8 s stall edge with
`stream_share` 1.0 and 1 MiB streams, which overflows the window on the base. Slot reclaim is built
on the session layer (token); the soak harness's F6 runs `NetServer` without a session and has no
token, so F6's transport-only number waits for the transport resume ticket of spec 120 § 10.3
(NetLink/lockstep Noise payload). Specs 77 § 4 and § 7.4, 120 § 10.3 (Built note), the agent and user
guides were updated.

## ADR-8299: Validated address changes: path validation without a wire change, per-candidate budgets, CGNAT moves, O(1) lookups (N103)
Date: 2026-11-17   Status: proposed
Context: Spec 120 § 10.4, audit rows S3 (PARTIAL), H2 (WRONG), H5 (part), soak finding F1 and adversarial rows 11-13. A sealed
peer moved to a new address on its first authentic, newest record, so an on-path observer that raced a copy of a fresh record
from its own address took the peer's downstream (F1: 28 hijacks in one soak run), and the one-second spacing between moves then
kept the real client cut off. Eight forged records a second from anywhere spent the per-peer trial budget and pinned a peer whose
NAT really moved (row 12). Plain links and the client never followed an address change (row 13: `client.rs` dropped every
datagram not from the server's first address). A move into an address block already holding `max_peers_per_ip` peers was
refused, stranding a phone that moved onto a full carrier-grade NAT. Each datagram scanned every peer for its address, and each
rebind scanned every connection for its token.
Decision: (1) A record from a new address that passes the cheap checks (trial budget of that (peer, address), no other peer
there, not banned, newer than the peer's newest record) and authenticates makes the address a candidate (`regia_net::path`). Its
content is delivered; the endpoint keeps sending to its validated address and sends the candidate alone an acknowledgment-only
packet with the next sequence number (`Connection::path_probe`, never counted lost). A record from the candidate whose
acknowledgment fields name that number (`connection::packet_acknowledges`) validates it, and only then does the peer move
(`Session::set_peer_addr`). This is RFC 9000 § 8.2 / § 9.3 with an ack of a candidate-only packet number in place of
PATH_CHALLENGE, so no wire change. (2) Bytes to an unvalidated candidate are capped at 3x the bytes received from it (§ 8.1);
an unanswered probe is resent at most every 100 ms; at most four candidates per link. (3) Trial opens are budgeted per (session
token, address) in a fixed 4,096-slot table under a secret hash (`CandidateLimiter`), `REBIND_ATTEMPTS_PER_S` (8) per slot per
second; refusals are counted on the peer (`PeerRow::rebinds_refused`) as well as process-wide. (4) The one-second spacing between
moves is removed (`REBIND_MIN_INTERVAL_MS` kept for source compatibility, unused): validation makes flapping require real
reachability. (5) `max_peers_per_ip` limits joins only; a peer that moves keeps its slot. (6) A genuine duplicate of one of the
peer's last 64 records from a new address also makes it a candidate (`SecureLink::open_duplicate`, no window commit, nothing
delivered twice): otherwise a real move while an observer races every record leaves the peer on its dead address. A never-seen
record older than the newest from a non-primary address is delivered on the validated path without making a candidate
(reordering across a move). (7) Plain links do the same with the token and a packet sequence newer than any received. (8) The
client follows a server address change the same way (`NetClient::on_candidate_datagram`). (9) On a validated move the RTT
estimate and the loss window restart (§ 9.4); v0.5.x has no rate controller to reset, and outage-recovery pacing carries on.
(10) The address -> peer lookup (`Session`) and token -> peer lookup (`NetServer`) are hash maps; `Session::addr_probes` counts
one probe per datagram. (11) Merge note: this lane merged net-session-resume-fixes (ADR-8180) onto integ-v06m, whose
`NetSession` already refused `resume` after a `connect_on` on a caller-owned socket (`resume_on`). The resolution keeps that
refusal for a `connect_on` with no `SocketOpener`; `set_socket_opener(Some(..))` and `connect_via` make `resume` work, so ADR-8180
(4)'s "`connect_on` without an opener keeps the old UDP resume" does not hold on this line.
Consequences: No wire or format change. Host-visible API: new `regia_net::path` module (constants), `Session::{set_peer_addr,
addr_probes}`, `Connection::{path_probe, path_changed, remote_seq}`, `connection::{packet_acknowledges, packet_seq}`,
`SecureLink::open_duplicate`; new fields `PeerRow::{rebinds, rebinds_refused, path_candidate, path_probes}` and
`EndpointTotals::path_probes` (struct literals must add them; serde defaults keep old JSON readable); `Peer::addr` edits must go
through `Session::set_peer_addr` or `peer_by_addr` misses the peer. Behavior: a real NAT move now takes one round trip (plus
the client's next send) before downstream follows, and the records sent meanwhile are delivered. `tests/transport_trust.rs`
`rebinds_are_rate_limited` asserted the removed interval; its second half now asserts the move is not held. A full relay (an
attacker that forwards both ways) can still carry the probe and become the path, as any NAT can; it cannot read sealed traffic.
Specs updated: 120 § 10.4 (Built note), 70 (Built note); guides `book/agents/net-trust.md`, `net-crypto.md`,
`book/user-guide/networking.md`. Tests: `crates/regia_net/tests/path_validation.rs` (12), `path` unit tests (4).

## ADR-8298: Resume for replication games: dormant NetLink peers, resume ticket, grace hook (N216)
Date: 2026-11-17   Status: proposed
Context: Spec 120 § 10.3 (S2) and § 8.5. Replication games host through `HostedLink`, whose session has no socket; players join
over `NetLink` -> `ServerBridge`, which deleted the replication peer on the transport's `PeerLeft`: a phone that lost signal past
the timeout, or came back from a new address, returned as a new `PeerId` with its owned entities gone (the game despawns them on
`Left`). Spec 77 § 7.4 "owns its entities again" held only for session-only games. ADR-8180 (N102) built the session layer's
takeover; the transport had no token.
Decision: (1) Transport resume ticket: `JoinToken::resume: Option<[u8; 16]>` (flag byte + 16 bytes, after the join data; inside
the sealed `Join` record when encrypted) and `Accept::resume_ticket: [u8; 16]`, minted per accept as a keyed BLAKE3 of the server
secret, the peer and a counter (`CookieMinter::derive_ticket`); single use (a resume replaces the ticket, a spent one matches
nothing). Shape after RFC 8446 § 2.2 (an opaque server-minted ticket). Wire 5, the v0.6 line's bump (spec 120 § 12.1; any other v0.6
framing lane reuses it); a wire-3 build is refused with `protocol_mismatch`. (2) `ServerConfig::resume_grace_ms` (default 0, so
`NetServer` users and the session's own transport are unchanged; `LinkOptions::resume_grace_ms` default 60 s, the session's
`reconnect_grace_s`): a player's `Timeout` drop becomes `ServerEvent::PeerDormant`; its id is reserved in the transport `Session`
(counts toward capacity, never reissued) until the grace ends (`PeerLeft { Timeout }`) or a join presents its ticket
(`ServerEvent::PeerResumed`, same `PeerId`). A ticket of a still-connected peer is a live-token takeover (old connection dropped
silently, `resume_takeovers`), checked before the same-address refusal and with no capacity check (slot reclaim). Counters in
`EndpointTotals`. (3) Runtime dormancy (`regia_net::resume`): the node keeps the peer's link (no frames written; unreliable
messages dropped; reliable ones held with their queue tick, bounded at the reliable queue limits by dropping the oldest, never a
kick), its entities, `NetOwner` and interest; `ServerReplication::make_dormant` drops the connection state (copies, baselines, acks,
state link) and remembers the ids the client held. On resume a fresh connection state makes the next gather a join gather (full
state), the ids the server despawned meanwhile are written as despawns in that frame, held messages older than the grace are
dropped, inbound sequence state is forgotten, and `NetInterrupted` goes. During dormancy the owner's entities carry
`NetInterrupted`, so other clients see the pawn frozen. (4) `NetGraceHook { on_grace_expired: fn(&mut World, PeerId) ->
GraceVerdict }`: runs once per grace end, before the node forgets the peer; `Despawn` despawns its owned and player entities, `Keep`
hands them to the server (removes `NetOwner` and the marker); without a hook nothing changes and the game sees `Left` as before.
(5) Client: `NetLink::resume()` (fresh UDP socket) / `resume_on(socket)`, `resume_ticket()`; the endpoint is replaced without a
goodbye and the link's clock continues; `NetClient::resume_ticket`, `ClientConfig::resume`. (6) `LinkEvent::Dormant`/`Resumed`,
agent method `net.resume`.
Consequences: Wire 5 (old builds refused). Breaking API (listed in the release fragment's Upgrade): new pub fields on `JoinToken`,
`Accept`, `ClientConfig`, `ServerConfig`, `LinkOptions`, `EndpointTotals`; new variants `ServerEvent::{PeerDormant, PeerResumed}`
and `LinkEvent::{Dormant, Resumed}`. Behavior change for `NetLink` servers: a timed-out player is reported `Dormant` and `Left` only
60 s later (set `resume_grace_ms: 0` for the old behavior); `link::tests::a_silent_client_is_reported_left_and_dropped_from_the_node`
now checks both. Not built: automatic client reconnect with backoff (the game calls `NetLink::resume`); copies that only left the
client's relevance while it was dormant are not removed by the resume (despawned entities are); the host does not map
`session.reconnect_grace_s` onto `HostedLink` (the game's `LinkOptions` value applies); lockstep's ticket (N225). Specs 120 § 8.5
and § 10.3 (Built notes) and 77 § 7.4 (Replication games bullet, addendum Built line) were updated; book networking guide,
`agents/net-link.md`, COVERAGE row, provenance rows.

## ADR-7985: Version refusals name the older side; the frozen version probe; a content check on NetLink
Date: 2026-11-16   Status: proposed
Context: spec 120 row S6 (plan N109). A `protocol_mismatch` deny could not say which side is older, so a player could not tell
"update the game" from "the server is older"; `NetLink` games had no content check at all (no `Hello`, no manifest), so a client
with other replicated components or other game data joined whenever the game left `NetGame::content_hash` at 0. Spec 120
§ 12.2 asks for a plaintext version probe (the owner's DO27 design, re-derived with our own bytes) that every later build
answers, so even a build that predates every change here is named.
Decision: (1) `regia_net::version_probe`: request `RGVP | probe_version u8 | nonce u64 | zero padding to 64 B`, answer
`RGVR | probe_version | nonce | wire u32 | game_version str_u8 <= 32 | protocol u32 | content_hash u64` (<= 64 B, never larger than
the request, RFC 9000 § 8's anti-amplification rule), frozen forever (format `version-probe` v1 in format-hashes, every byte
pinned by a test; a later layout is a probe version 2 that still answers version 1). Answered by `NetServer`, the relay (outside
a flow; inside one it is forwarded to the host) and routed by the shared-port reader to a half that answers. Rate limited per
source prefix (IPv4 /24, IPv6 /56; 4/s, burst 8; a keyed fixed table so forged sources cannot grow it) and by the server's
global pre-proof answer cap. (2) Refinement of the spec, so new builds need no extra round trip: a **version stamp** (`RGVS |
wire | protocol | content_hash | game_version`) rides in the zero padding of every `ConnectRequest`, and a stamped request gets
the server's stamp after the detail of its `protocol_mismatch` deny. Old servers ignore the padding (they read only their own
fields); old clients are never sent the trailer (strict decoders refuse trailing bytes), but their deny detail now names both
versions and the side (`... : update the game (client_older)`). No wire-version bump: both changes stay inside bytes old builds
ignore, and the spec's § 12.1 bumps stay with their lanes. (3) The client: a stamped deny resolves at once; a bare deny (a
server that predates stamps) starts the probe, resent every 250 ms for 1.5 s; an answer names the server, no answer after a valid
deny means the server predates the probe, so it is older. `ClientEvent::VersionMismatch { server_game_version, ours,
server_is_older, side, message }` follows the `Ended` of the refusal; `LinkEvent::VersionMismatch` carries it to `NetLink` games;
`net.status` shows the last one as `version_mismatch` on both ends. (4) Order: dotted game versions (`NetGame::GAME_VERSION`,
new, default empty) first, then the wire version, then the protocol version; same versions and another content hash is
`content_differs`; anything else `unordered`. (5) Content on `NetLink`: `NetServer::set_content_hash` / `NetClient::set_content_hash`
put a run-time content hash into the version stamp, and a server that set one refuses a stamped request whose content differs
(`protocol_mismatch`, `content_differs`). The protocol id is left alone: the shared-port reader routes requests by it, and
folding a run-time value in broke that routing (the three `shared_port` tests caught it). A `NetLink` endpoint always declares
the app's replicated schema (`runtime::protocol_hash`: messages, replicated components, predictors, the hash `NetSession`
already requires) combined with the new `LinkOptions::content_hash`, so another schema or other content is refused. A client
that predates stamps sends no content and is not checked (it predates the check too).
(6) `NetSession`: the session `Hello` refusals append the side (`version_mismatch`, `protocol_mismatch`, `content_mismatch`
details), the session transport announces the manifest's game version in its stamp, and a transport `protocol_mismatch` keeps its
detail (`DisconnectReason::ProtocolMismatch(detail)`, was `TransportError("protocol_mismatch")`).
Alternatives rejected: a new `DenyReason` (an old client cannot decode an unknown reason byte, so it would see a malformed deny);
the probe alone (one more round trip and a 1.5 s wait for every new-vs-new mismatch); a wire bump for the stamp (refuses
every older build for bytes they can ignore); porting DO27's probe code (spec 120 § 2.3: the design is re-derived, no DO27
file was opened).
Consequences: additive API, but `ClientEvent` and `LinkEvent` gain a variant, `NetStatus` and `LinkOptions` gain a field
(release fragment, Upgrade). `NetLink` builds of this version still join older builds of the same game and content (no
protocol-id change); matched builds are the rule anyway (spec 120 § 12.1). Session `content_mismatch` details keep their item
list and gain one side line only when the releases differ. Spec 120 § 12.2 has a "Built" note.
New format `version-probe` (format-hashes, a corpus exception: a datagram, not a file), fuzz target `net.version_probe`.

## ADR-8184: Transport v2 part 1: packet numbers, acknowledgment frames and RFC 9002 loss detection (wire 5)
Date: 2026-11-17   Status: proposed
Context: Spec 120 § 4.1 (plan row N201, lane net-v2-acks-loss). The v1 header (16-bit sequence, one 16-bit
acknowledgment and a 32-bit mask) names 33 packets per reply, so ADR-7995 had to send header-only acknowledgment trains
for bursts (four packets for a 64-packet burst); per-fragment retransmission timers resent a fragment five times in an
8 s outage; an acknowledgment of a resent fragment was ambiguous. The base for this lane is ADR-7995's unified loop
(net-transport-unify), merged with net-version-probe (ADR-7985) and net-input-feedback (ADR-8077, wire 4).
Decision: wire 5. (1) Every packet carries the next 62-bit packet number, never reused; a retransmission is a new packet
carrying the old fragment. The number is sent in 2 or 4 bytes (RFC 9000 § 17.1, Appendix A decoding) with four times
the distance to the largest acknowledged number, not the RFC's two: a QUIC receiver's packet protection rejects a
misdecoded number, an unsealed Regia link has nothing that would, and a 1-byte number that arrived after 200 newer
packets decoded as another packet and acknowledged it (found by the seeded-links unit test: 149 messages never
delivered). (2) Acknowledgment frames (RFC 9000 § 19.3): largest, ack delay (us >> 3), up to 32 ranges; optional receive
timestamps for 16 packets, asked for in band by a flag (`LinkConfig::receive_timestamps`, off by default, read with
`Connection::take_receive_timestamps`) for the rate controller of § 4.2. Every packet with room carries the current
frame. Received ranges older than the 32 one frame names and not reported yet leave first, in frames of their own
flagged "older" (no round-trip sample from them), so a delivered packet is never left unnamed (the ADR-7995 train idea
on ranges). (3) Ack-eliciting packets are those with records, a new ping record included; acknowledgment-only packets are
not acknowledged for their own sake. A receiver acknowledges every second ack-eliciting packet, at most 10 ms
(`MAX_ACK_DELAY_MS`) after the first, and at once on reordering, a gap or a lone ping (a keepalive or probe: nothing
would share its packet, and holding it would stretch the round trip the peer measures; RFC 9000 § 13.2.1 allows it).
(4) Loss: packet threshold 3, time threshold 9/8 max(srtt, latest), floor 1 ms, both widened by observed reordering
(kept from ADR-7995); a packet acknowledged after its verdict undoes it and counts in `LinkStats::spurious_losses` (DO27
rule A7). (5) Probe timeout replaces the per-fragment timers: `srtt + max(4 rttvar, 1 ms) + max_ack_delay`, clamped to
`resend_min_ms..=resend_max_ms` and never under 9/8 of the round trip, doubled per consecutive expiry up to
`resend_backoff_max_ms`, reset by any acknowledgment, armed from the last ack-eliciting packet while reliable data is in
flight; one or two probe packets carry the least probed, oldest fragments. Keepalives are ack-eliciting pings, so during
an outage the path is probed by pings and data is repaired from the first acknowledgment after it (1 data resend, the
first probe, in an 8 s outage, against 5 on the base). Two consecutive expiries on a measured path enter outage recovery (ADR-7995). (6)
Round-trip samples only from the largest newly acknowledged packet when it is ack-eliciting and was neither declared lost
nor carried a resent fragment, minus the peer's ack delay clamped to 10 ms when the rest stays at or above the minimum;
`min_rtt` over 10 s (`LinkStats::min_rtt_ms`). The sealed record layer, session token and counter and the rebind path are
untouched: everything above lives inside the record.
Consequences: one reply acknowledges a burst of any size; resends per fragment in an 8 s outage drop from 5 to 1; a wire-4
peer is refused with `protocol_mismatch` and its version probe is answered. Header cost: 3 bytes plus the frame (about 6
bytes on a clean path) against 9; `PACKET_HEADER_BYTES` stays 9 as the fixed reserve, so `max_unreliable_bytes` is
unchanged. Host-visible: `REGIA_NET_WIRE_VERSION` 5; new `regia_net::ack` module; `LinkConfig::receive_timestamps`;
`LinkStats::{min_rtt_ms, spurious_losses, probe_timeouts, ack_only_sent}`; `ReceiveTimestamp`;
`Connection::{probe_deadline_ms, take_receive_timestamps, next_packet_number}`; constants `MAX_ACK_DELAY_MS`,
`ACK_ELICITING_THRESHOLD`, `MIN_RTT_WINDOW_MS`, `MAX_PROBE_PACKETS`, `MAX_RECEIVE_TIMESTAMPS`; `MAX_FORWARD_JUMP` is now
`u64`; `MAX_ACK_RANGES` is now 32 (ranges per frame, was 33-packet ranges per poll); `resend_timeout_ms` returns the probe
timeout. Not done here: the rate controller and pacing of § 4.2 (the receive timestamps are its input), DPLPMTUD (§ 4.3),
streams (§ 5, N203). (7) Redundant copies, beyond § 4.1, because the E2 bar (small reliable p95 <= 1.5x one-way at 5 %
loss) cannot be met by loss detection alone: about 5 % of first transmissions are lost, and any repair needs a round trip
plus the one-way delay (3.3x here), so p95 sat on the repair for two of three seeds (131 ms with items 1-6 alone, 110-124
ms on the base). A reliable fragment of at most 256 bytes (`REDUNDANT_COPY_MAX_BYTES`) rides once more in the next packet
that leaves anyway, with room, 1 to 20 ms (`REDUNDANT_COPY_WINDOW_MS`) after its first transmission (the redundancy idea
of RFC 2198; spec 120 § 6.1 does the same for inputs): no extra datagram (A6 holds), not a resend
(`LinkStats::redundant_copies`), and the copy becomes the fragment's latest transmission, so a verdict on the first
packet alone does not requeue it. E2 then measures p95 40-44 ms (1.1x) on all three seeds. Bulk data (larger fragments)
is never copied. (8) An outage is also entered when reliable data has waited as long as two consecutive timeouts would
take (`rto + min(2 max(rto, 250 ms), backoff cap)`) with nothing acknowledged since it left, on a measured path: with
keepalives as pings the probe timeout rarely expires twice, and ADR-7950's paced backlog after an outage must not depend
on it. (9) An acknowledgment that is due anyway serves as this side's keepalive (no ping added), so two idle peers
exchange one ping and one acknowledgment per keepalive interval. Spec 120 § 4.1 gets a Built note.

## ADR-8300: Path MTU discovery (DPLPMTUD) on transport v2 (net-v2-pmtud, N205)
Date: 2026-11-17   Status: proposed
Context: Spec 120 § 4.3 and audit row T2: every packet is 1,200 bytes including the sealed header, safe on IPv6's 1,280
minimum, but the transport never learns a larger path, and nothing tests a path that stops carrying large datagrams
(they vanish silently: no IP fragmentation with DF, often no ICMP). Owner goal 2026-11-15: netcode that does not lag out
or drop players.
Decision: (1) Datagram packetization layer path MTU discovery after RFC 8899, opt-in per endpoint
(`LinkConfig::mtu_probing`, `LinkOptions::mtu_probing`, server.toml `[net] mtu_probing = true`, an optional key of the
unreleased format version 4). A
pure state machine (`regia_net::pmtud::PathMtu`: base, searching, search complete, error) drives one probe at a time.
(2) Probes are a ping record plus padding to 1,280, 1,400 and 1,452 bytes (whole datagram, every header and the seal
included; probe sizes `MTU_PROBE_SIZES`). They carry no data and no acknowledgment frame, are acknowledged at once by
the receiver (a lone ping), are never loss samples, never move the probe timeout of reliable data, and are not sent
while the connection paces an outage backlog or probes an interruption. Only an acknowledgment raises the size; three
consecutive lost probes of one size (`MAX_MTU_PROBES`) complete the search at the size already confirmed, and the next
size is tried again after `MTU_RAISE_INTERVAL_MS` (600 s, RFC 8899 `PMTU_RAISE_TIMER`). (3) A probe counts as lost only
when a packet sent after it was acknowledged (packet threshold or its own probe-timeout deadline): during an outage,
when nothing gets through, an unanswered probe is inconclusive and leaves again after a probe timeout, so an outage is
never read as a black hole. (4) Black holes: the first lost packet above the base size puts the size in doubt, and data
goes at the base size from the next packet while a confirmation probe of the current size leaves at once; its
acknowledgment ends the doubt (random loss costs one probe and one round trip at 1,200 bytes), three lost confirmations
drop to the base (`LinkStats::mtu_black_holes`, search again after `MTU_BLACK_HOLE_RETRY_MS`, 60 s). Three large
packets lost in a row while a smaller packet sent after the first was acknowledged are a black hole at once
(`BLACK_HOLE_LOSS_BURST`). With nothing acknowledged at the size for 5 s a confirmation probe checks it
(`MTU_CONFIRM_INTERVAL_MS`, RFC 8899 `CONFIRMATION_TIMER`). (5) Reliable fragments stay cut for the base size: after a
fall back every unacknowledged fragment still fits one packet, so a black hole never strands reliable data (0 lost
reliable messages in mtu-blackhole). The probed size is used for packing (more records per packet) and for unreliable
messages: `Connection::max_unreliable_bytes` reads it live, the server bridge refreshes the replication state-frame
budget every frame (only on change), and client input bundles already read it per send. A larger state frame also
needs `replication.mtu_bytes` raised (the transport only caps it). (6) Wire: a new record tag `0x00` (padding to the end
of the packet, all zeros) inside wire 5, the open bump of the v0.6 line (spec 120 § 12.1 gives wire 5 to
net-v2-acks-loss; this lane reuses it, nothing is released on wire 5 yet). With probing off no padding is ever sent and
the wire is byte-identical to the base (a hashed test). (7) Observability: `LinkStats::{path_mtu, mtu_search,
mtu_probes_sent, mtu_probes_lost, mtu_black_holes}`, `Connection::{path_mtu, mtu_search}`; `net.status` and `net.peers`
carry them in `link`. `PeerQuality` (spec 120 § 13.1) is not built yet; when it lands it takes `path_mtu` from
`LinkStats`.
Consequences: an opted-in server uses up to 1,452-byte datagrams where the path carries them and falls back within three
probe losses where it stops; default behavior and the default wire do not change. Real UDP sockets do not set
`IP_MTU_DISCOVER`/`IP_DONTFRAG` yet, so an IPv4 path may deliver a probe as IP fragments (the probe then succeeds and the
size is used fragmented); setting DF per platform is a follow-up (`socket.rs`, needs a `socket2`/`libc` call per OS).
server.toml: the brief asked for a format bump, but ADR-7724 (a release moves a format at most one version step) folds it
into the unreleased v4 (v0.5.0 shipped v3) as an optional key, absent = false; v1-v3 migrate as before. Specs updated: 120
§ 4.3 Built note; `docs/formats/server-toml.md` (version 4 addition).

## ADR-7982: Relay protocol 2: one allocation per relayed client, permissions, version byte
Date: 2026-11-16   Status: proposed
Context: spec 120 § 10.6 (plan N112, DO27 need "net-relay-many-clients"): the relay kept one flow per host address and
answered a second client `Busy` (`relay.rs` Bind handler; test `a_flow_in_use_is_not_displaced`), and a flow was bound only
to the source address, so a forger who learned it could spend its 4 MiB/s and keep the real client's re-`Bind` busy
(audit H2). DO27 needs 16 relayed clients per player host behind strict NAT and 32 (later 40) per community dedicated
server, with no paid servers.
Decision: relay protocol 2 (`RELAY_PROTOCOL_VERSION` 2). Every protocol 2 control datagram is `RGNR | 0 | version | tag |
body` (no protocol 1 tag is 0, so the framings never overlap; `relay_version`, `versioned`); each answer uses its request's
framing. A client's `Allocate` (`encode_allocate`: the host, the bind key from `Lookup`, the client's own random 16-byte
allocation key, a cookie) reserves one port of the relay's pool (`RelayConfig::allocation_ports`, default 4,096) for that
client alone, the TURN shape of RFC 8656 § 5: the host sees each relayed client as its own source address
`relay_ip:port`, so the record layer, the peer table and rebinding above the socket do not change and no game-path wire
version moves. The relay answers `Allocated { port, peer }` to the client and `ClientJoined { port, client, host_key }` to
the host's registered address. An allocation forwards only between its two permitted addresses (RFC 8656 § 9); anything
else to the port is dropped and counted (`RelayStatus::permission_dropped`) before it touches any budget. A side whose
address changed sends `Refresh` (`encode_refresh`) to the port with its own key (the client's allocation key, or the
host's `host_key`), compared in constant time; a new source proves itself with a cookie round trip (`Challenge`), and a
`Refresh` from the address already permitted is answered `Allocated` (confirms the path and opens the sender's NAT).
`Allocate` also needs a cookie, so a forged source cannot reserve ports or fill another IP's cap. Caps answer
`Full { cap }` with the cap reached: per host `max_clients_per_host` (40), per source IP or IPv6 /64
`max_allocations_per_ip` (8), the pool; bandwidth per allocation per direction 4 MiB/s (kept), per host
`host_bytes_per_second` (64 MiB/s), relay-wide `relay_bytes_per_second` (0 = none). The same client key from a new address
takes its allocation back, on the same port, only after 5 s without the client's own traffic; an active allocation is never
moved by an `Allocate`. Idle allocations (60 s, both sides) free their port to the back of the pool. Protocol 1 requests keep
their protocol 1 answers and semantics (one `Bind` flow per host address, still `Busy`); a protocol 1 request with an
allocation tag gets `VersionTooOld { min: 2 }` in protocol 1 framing, a request from a newer protocol `VersionTooNew
{ max: 2 }`: never silence. Every anti-amplification rule is kept: `Allocate` is padded to 128 bytes (its two answers are at
most 70), `Refresh` to 64, refusals no larger than their request, control traffic limited per source IP (allocation ports
included for `Refresh`). `RelayServer::bind` opens the pool's sockets (system-chosen ports, or a range from
`allocation_port_base`) and reads only ports with a live allocation; `RelayCore::handle_allocation` is the sans-IO entry.
`--relay local` opens 64 allocation ports (`LOCAL_RELAY_ALLOCATION_PORTS`); the console command `relay` and
`ServerHost::relay_status` show `RelayStatus`.
Refinements of spec 120 § 10.6: (1) the allocation operation is a new `Allocate` request rather than a versioned `Bind`, so a
protocol 2 `Bind` keeps the protocol 1 single-flow meaning and the two never mix; (2) a rebinding client refreshes with its
own allocation key, not the lobby's bind key: every client of a lobby knows the bind key, so a bind-key refresh would let one
client move another's permission; possession of the bind key is proved once, at `Allocate`; (3) every relayed client shares
the relay's IP, so a host behind a relay needs `ServerConfig::max_peers_per_ip` at or above its relayed client count (0 = no
limit) and `handshakes_per_ip_per_s` to match: the client side and host wiring (lane 2 of 2, N113) sets this for relay
addresses; (4) `net.relay_status` as an agent method is left to N113, which puts the relay in a process the agent protocol
reaches; this lane ships the `relay` console command, `ServerHost::relay_status` and `RelayServer::status`.
Rejected: a client-id header on relayed datagrams (changes the framing every layer above sees and makes old hosts
unrelayable; spec 120 § 10.6); polling every pool socket each update (4,096 receive calls per update for nothing).
Consequences: new public API in `regia_net::relay` (`RelayConfig`, `RelayStatus`, `RelayCore::{with_config,
add_allocation_ports, handle_allocation, status, allocation_count, clients_of, live_allocation_ports, relay_config}`,
`RelayServer::{bind, with_allocation_sockets, from_core, status, local_addr}`, `encode_allocate`, `encode_refresh`,
`relay_version`, `versioned`, constants) and in `server_host` (`LOCAL_RELAY_ALLOCATION_PORTS`, `LocalRelay::status`,
`ServerHost::relay_status`); new `RelayTag` and `RelayReply` variants break exhaustive matches (release fragment, Upgrade).
Directory pages now reserve two bytes for the versioned head (a page is still at most 1,200 bytes). No `REGIA_NET_WIRE_VERSION`
change (the game path is unchanged; spec 120 § 12.1), no settings format change (`RelayConfig` is code-level; a `server.toml`
or relay config file key is N113's, with its migrator). Fuzz targets `net.relay.allocate`, `net.relay.refresh` and
`net.relay_reply.{allocated, client_joined, challenge, full, version_too_old, version_too_new}`. Spec 120 § 10.6 has a
"Built" note.

## ADR-8183: Relay host and client flow: registration from the game socket, join by code with relay fallback, `net.relay_status`
Date: 2026-11-17   Status: proposed
Context: spec 120 § 10.6 and § 10.7 (plan N113, DO27 need "net-relay-many-clients", lane 2 of 2; lane 1 is ADR-7982). The
host registered with the relay from a socket of its own (`server_host/join.rs`), so the NAT mapping the relay recorded,
handed to clients and relayed to was not the game's: a host behind a NAT was unreachable by code. `NetSession::connect(JoinCode)`
returned an error, no production code sent `Allocate`/`Refresh`, and there was no agent view of the relay.
Decision: (1) `server_host::relay_split(socket, relay)` splits the game socket into a game half and a relay-control half: a
datagram from the relay's IP (any port: the control port and its allocation ports) that starts with `RGNR` goes to the control
half, everything else to the endpoint. Every endpoint datagram starts with `RGN1`, so the two never collide. The registrar
runs on the control half with `JoinTicket::from_game_socket` (unspecified IP and port 0: "the address the relay saw is the
game port"; the ticket layout and version are unchanged, an old ticket still means what it meant). It renews every 15 s
(`JOIN_KEEPALIVE_MS`, the RFC 8445 § 11 keepalive scale), which keeps the game socket's NAT mapping toward the relay open, and
answers each `ClientJoined` with a `Refresh` from the game socket to the allocation port (cookie round trip when the mapping
differs, as behind an address-dependent NAT), so the relay's host permission is the game socket's mapping toward that port.
The host does not refresh again after the relay confirms: a later refresh would keep a departed client's port alive (a
refresh counts as host traffic); the game's own traffic keeps the mapping open. (2) `NetServer::add_relay_ip` (and
`NetSession::add_relay_ip`, `NetLink::add_relay_ip`): every client a relay forwards shares its IP, each on its own port, so the
per-IP peer cap and the per-IP handshake limiters skip relay IPs (at most 16 kept); the server-wide handshake budgets and the
relay's own per-host and per-source caps still apply. The dedicated server does (1) and (2) for `--relay` for session games,
link games (`HostGame::host_game_port_relayed`, `add_game_port_relay_ip`) and `--shared-port`; a game that binds its own port
without a link protocol keeps the separate registrar socket (logged). (3) `server_host::JoinPath`, the client: `Lookup` in the
protocol 2 framing and, from the second attempt, also in the protocol 1 framing, so a protocol 1 relay (which drops the
versioned framing) answers and is recognized (a protocol 1 answer waits 500 ms for the protocol 2 one); then the endpoint
connects to the host's reflexive address while, from `RELAY_RACE_START_MS` (500 ms), the client takes its own allocation
(`Allocate`, its cookie, then a `Refresh` from the game socket to the allocation port, which confirms the path and opens the
client's NAT toward it). At `RELAY_FALLBACK_MS` (1.5 s) the relay path wins if nothing came from the direct address and the
allocation is confirmed; `JoinSocket` then rewrites the server address to the allocation port both ways, so the endpoint above
talks to one address and its handshake retries complete over the relay. A relayed client refreshes every 15 s
(`RELAY_REFRESH_INTERVAL_MS`), which also moves its permission after a NAT rebind. Failures are codes, never a hang:
`relay_too_old` (direct failed and the relay is protocol 1), `relay_full` (a cap answered `Full`), `relay_no_allocation`
(16 unanswered attempts), plus `join_timeout`, `join_refused`, `join_ticket_invalid`. (4) `NetSession::connect(ConnectTarget::
JoinCode)` runs `JoinPath` inside the session's client link (`CODE@HOST:PORT`, or a bare code with `NetSession::set_relay`);
`NetSession::connect_by_code_on` takes any socket; `NetSession::join_route` reports the path. The ticket's key is pinned unless
the caller gave one. (5) `net.relay_status` reads `NetAgentState` relay reports (`publish_relay`, `RelayReport`: role,
relay, join code, relayed and confirmed clients, and for a relay this process runs its `RelayStatus`, `RelayConfig` caps and
`RelayCore::allocations`, the bytes each allocation forwarded each way). The dedicated server publishes `server_host` once a
second through `HostGame::publish_relay` (an app game inserts it into its world).
Refinements of spec 120 § 10.6/10.7: (a) the spec says a v2 client facing a v1 relay "falls back to the v1 bind with a logged
reason"; this lane ends the join with `relay_too_old` instead (the brief's acceptance): a protocol 1 flow carries one client
per host, so the fallback would let the first player in and fail every other one in a way they cannot read, and a v0.5.0 host
never received protocol 1 flows on its game socket anyway (it registered from another socket). (b) The full candidate checks
(host, reflexive, mapped candidates, paced pair checks, nomination by the sealed handshake) are lane net-nat-candidates; this
lane's direct candidate is the host's reflexive address and "direct answered" means any datagram from it. (c) The per-IP
limits exempt relay addresses by IP instead of the operator raising `max_peers_per_ip` for every relayed host (ADR-7982 (3)
left this to N113).
Rejected: a second socket per relayed client on the host (the relay already gives each client its own address); relaying the
host's renewals through an allocation (a renewal must come from the registered address); a periodic host-side `Refresh`
(keeps departed clients' ports alive, above).
Consequences: new public API: `server_host::{relay_split, RelayGamePort, RelayControlPort, RelaySplitStats, JoinPath,
JoinRoute, JoinSocket, RELAY_RACE_START_MS, RELAY_FALLBACK_MS, RELAY_ALLOCATE_ATTEMPTS, RELAY_REFRESH_INTERVAL_MS,
RELAY_SPLIT_QUEUE, fresh_allocation_key}`, `JoinTicket::from_game_socket`, `JOIN_KEEPALIVE_MS`, `JOIN_MAX_PENDING_ALLOCATIONS`,
`JOIN_ALLOCATION_ATTEMPTS`, `RelayRegistrar::{relayed_clients, confirmed_allocations, report}`, `LocalRelay::report`,
`ServerHost::relay_report`, `HostGame::{host_game_port_relayed, add_game_port_relay_ip, publish_relay}` (defaulted),
`NetServer::{add_relay_ip, is_relay_ip}`, `NetLink::add_relay_ip`, `NetSession::{connect_by_code_on, set_relay, relay,
add_relay_ip, join_route}`, `relay::{RelayReport, RelayAllocationView}`, `RelayCore::allocations`, `RelayServer::report`,
`NetAgentState::{publish_relay, remove_relay, relays}`; agent method `net.relay_status` (errors `relay_bad_params`,
`relay_unknown`). Breaking for exhaustive matches: `JoinError::{RelayTooOld, RelayFull, RelayNoAllocation}`. Behavior: the
registrar renews every 15 s instead of every 300 s; it accepts datagrams from every port of the relay's IP. No
`REGIA_NET_WIRE_VERSION` or relay protocol change, no settings format change. Spec 120 § 10.7 has a "Built" note.

## ADR-8340: NAT traversal from the game socket: candidates, paced connectivity checks, nomination, relay protocol 3
Date: 2026-11-17   Status: proposed
Context: spec 120 § 10.7 (row S5, plan N228, lane net-nat-candidates): join by code across every NAT pair, from the game
socket, with the relay as the fallback. After N113 (ADR-8183) the host registered from its game socket and a client raced the
host's reflexive address against its own relay allocation, but nothing in production sent a punch introduction or a check:
the relay's protocol 1 `PunchIntro` was used by no caller, and hole punching existed only as `simulate_hole_punch`. So a host
behind an address-dependent mapping was reachable only through the relay, even where both NATs could be punched.
Decision: (1) New module `regia_net::nat` (core, no ECS): `Candidate` (`CandidateKind` host, mapped, srflx, prflx, relay) with
RFC 8445 § 5.1.2 priorities (mapped ranks 105, between peer- and server-reflexive), `pair_priority` (§ 6.1.2.3), the
`CandidateSource` trait (host addresses now: `HostCandidates`, the socket's bound address or the routed interface toward the
relay; port mapping is net-nat-hosting-flow's implementation of the same trait), `gather` (deduplicated, at most 8), and the
check datagram `RGNC | kind | session key [16] | txid u64 | nominate u8 | priority u32` (request padded to 64 bytes) /
`... | mapped addr` (response, smaller). `CheckAgent` runs one session: one pair per remote candidate (one base, the game socket:
RFC 8445 § 6.1.2.4 pruning), highest priority first, one check per Ta = 50 ms (§ 14.2), RTO max(500 ms, Ta × pairs) (§ 14.3),
4 attempts per pair, peer-reflexive candidates from unannounced sources with an immediate triggered check (§ 7.3.1.3-4), an
answer accepted only from the address the check went to with its txid. `CheckPacer`: all sessions of one process at least 5 ms
apart (§ 14.2). (2) Relay protocol 3 (`RELAY_PROTOCOL_VERSION` 2 -> 3; `REGIA_NET_WIRE_VERSION` unchanged: the game path is not
touched): a protocol 3 `PunchIntro` carries a join code and the client's candidates and is padded to 800 bytes; the relay
resolves the code and answers both sides at once with `RelayReply::Introduced` (`PunchPeer` in protocol 3 framing: the other
side's reflexive address, the client's ticket and bind key, a session key from the relay's secret and a counter, this side's
own reflexive address, the other side's candidates), and drops the request when both answers together would be larger than it.
A host's candidates ride its `Register` as an extension after the cookie (marker 0xCA) in the protocol 1 framing, where
protocol 1 and 2 relays read zero padding, so the registrar needs no version negotiation. (3) The host: `relay_split` routes
`RGNC` datagrams from any source to the control half; a `RelayRegistrar` on the game socket (`JoinTicket::from_game_socket`)
announces its candidates, starts a controlled `CheckAgent` per introduction (at most 64 sessions, 10 s each), answers checks
that carry a live session key and checks the client back (counts in `NatReport`, `RelayReport::nat`, `net.relay_status`
`nat`). (4) The client (`JoinPath`): first request the protocol 3 introduction; a `VersionTooNew` (protocol 2 relay) sends
`Lookup` at once, and from the second attempt `Lookup` goes in both older framings too (protocol 1 relays drop the versioned
framing). It runs the controlling agent; the best answered pair carries the endpoint's datagrams (`JoinSocket` rewrites the
server address to it, and its last pre-path datagram, the handshake, is sent there again at once); the first datagram back from
the host's address or that pair ends the race (`DirectChosen`) and one nominating check tells the host. The relay pair starts at
500 ms and wins at 1.5 s when nothing else completed, as in ADR-8183. (5) `SimNat` gains the address-dependent mapping and
filtering of RFC 4787 (`NatMapping::AddressDependent`, `NatFiltering::AddressDependent`, `ALL`), so the test covers nine NAT
behaviors plus none, 100 host × client pairs.
Refinements of spec 120 § 10.7: (a) "the first pair that completes the sealed handshake is nominated": the client runs one
handshake (its endpoint has one server address), on the best answered pair, and the pair it completes on is nominated (regular
nomination, RFC 8445 § 8.1.1), rather than racing a handshake on every pair (which would leave half-open peers on the host). (b)
Checks are authenticated by the relay-issued session key only; the path's authentication is the sealed handshake with the
ticket's pinned key, so a forged check can at worst make one pair look valid and then fail its handshake. (c) The 1.5 s
relay bar is measured from the introduction (the ticket's arrival), as N113 measured it from `Lookup`'s answer. (d) The
protocol 2 operations keep the protocol 2 framing whatever `RELAY_PROTOCOL_VERSION` says (`versioned`, `encode_allocate`,
`encode_refresh`), so a protocol 2 relay still answers a new client's `Lookup`, `Allocate` and `Refresh`; only the protocol 3
introduction uses version 3. (e) A client whose ticket arrived through `Lookup` while the introduction's answer was lost asks
for the introduction again (3 times, 100 ms apart, until the relay race starts at 500 ms). (f) ICE validates a pair only on an
answer from the address the check went to (RFC 8445 § 7.2.5.2.1); when both sides map per address and port, no pair is ever
symmetric, so those 9 of the 100 pairs (any filtering) take the relay, where `simulate_hole_punch`'s one-way model reports a
punch for 3 of them (permissive filtering on both sides); the test's predictor says so.
Rejected: a client-to-relay round trip per candidate (STUN binding per candidate; the relay already sees the one reflexive
address that matters); putting the host's candidates in the join ticket (old clients reject a new ticket layout); a separate
check socket (the mapping punched must be the game socket's); racing the relay from 0 ms (spends an allocation on every join).
Consequences: new public API `regia_net::nat` (all items), `relay::{Introduction, RelayReply::Introduced, encode_introduce,
encode_register_with_candidates, RELAY_INTRO_MIN_VERSION, RELAY_INTRO_REQUEST_BYTES, RELAY_CANDIDATES_EXT, RelayCore::
introductions}`, `SimNat::{mapping, filtering}`, `NatMapping::ALL`, `NatFiltering::ALL`, `RelayRegistrar::{add_candidate_source,
candidates, nat_report}`, `JoinPath::{add_candidate_source, candidates, checks, observed, direct_remote}`, `RelayReport::nat`.
Breaking for exhaustive matches: `RelayReply::Introduced`, `NatMapping::AddressDependent`, `NatFiltering::AddressDependent`;
for struct literals: `RelayReport::nat`. `RELAY_PROTOCOL_VERSION` is 3 (a protocol 2 relay answers a protocol 3 request
`VersionTooNew { max: 2 }`; tests now probe `RELAY_PROTOCOL_VERSION + 1`). Two N113 relay-path tests put their clients behind
symmetric NATs, because an open client now reaches a symmetric host on a checked pair (their subject is the relay path).
Spec 120 § 10.7 has a "Built" note.

## ADR-8351: The Steam mock takes the soak harness's seeded impairment (N219, net-impaired-steam-mock)
Date: 2026-11-17   Status: proposed
Context: Spec 120 § 10.8 and audit rows S7/H7: the Steam transport was only tested lossless and in order.
`MockSteamNet` delivered every message at once and in send order; `set_online` only blackholed a peer;
`tests/lobby_sockets.rs` and `tests/net_link_steam.rs` ran clean. The soak harness's impairment network
(`regia_net_soak::impair`, ADR-7899) works at the `DatagramSocket` seam, but `regia_net_soak` is a test-only crate
that `regia_steam`'s library cannot depend on, it is not on the v0.6 line yet, and a lobby-launched session uses
the mock's own `P2pMessages`, not a socket the test can swap.
Decision: `MockSteamNet` gets per-user access links (`MockLink`, `MockDirection`, `MockBurst`): the harness's
direction model (outage windows, random loss, Gilbert-Elliott burst loss stepped once per message, a drop-tail
bottleneck counting a 28 B header, latency plus order-keeping jitter, an overtaking reorder hold, duplication) and
its numbers for `clean`, `good-wifi`, `bad-wifi`, `mobile-4g`, `transatlantic`, `congested` and `flappy`
(`MockLink::profile`, `MOCK_LINK_PROFILES`). A message crosses the sender's up direction at send time and the
receiver's down direction when it reaches the receiver's side. Time is virtual (`advance_ms`, `now_ms`); every
draw comes from a SplitMix64 stream per user and direction seeded by `set_seed`. Sends on an impaired link always
succeed (loss is silent, like a datagram into the network). `link_stats()` counts drops by cause, reorders,
duplicates and messages in flight. A clean link, the default, keeps the old path: delivery at once, in order.
No agent method: the mock is a test fixture; `net.conditioner_set` keeps conditioning UDP and loopback endpoints.
Consequences: Additive API only (`regia_steam::{MockLink, MockDirection, MockBurst, MockNetStats,
MOCK_LINK_PROFILES, MOCK_HEADER_BYTES, MOCK_FLAP_*}`, `MockSteamNet::{set_seed, set_link, set_default_link, link,
advance_ms, now_ms, link_stats}`); no wire or format change. New test `regia_steam/tests/net_impaired_steam.rs`:
lobby-launched Steam sessions on good-wifi (60 s), bad-wifi (5 min with zero drops, leaves or disconnects and every
reliable message once and in order) and flappy (the player stays through 3 s outages, every interruption ends), and
a suspend/resume on bad-wifi over Steam with the same `PeerId`. Links are per user, so both ends of a lobby
session are impaired (harsher than the harness's clean dedicated-server side). `flappy`'s 12 s outage on every
fourth client and `mobile-4g`'s MTU and NAT rebinding are per-client harness extras a single link does not carry.
The mock's model is a second copy of the harness's until `regia_net_soak` lands on the line; then one may use the
other's types. The merge of net-session-resume-fixes into this lane kept its `SocketOpener` with the v0.6 line's
`resume_on`: `resume()` refuses a `connect_on` session only when no opener is set. Specs 120 § 10.8 (Built note)
and 89 (tests), the networking and Steam guides and the net lobbies agent page were updated.

## ADR-8387: Net integration P-net: one wire bump for transport v2 and resume, the marker stays opt-in, merge-doubled docs dropped (integ-v06p-net)
Date: 2026-11-17   Status: proposed
Context: integ-v06p-net merges fourteen netcode lanes onto integ-v06o (lockstep core, second pass, sessions,
steering golden, desync detection, clock filters, dilation and input capture, the lag-compensation window,
high-RTT prediction, path validation, dormant resume for `NetLink`, path MTU discovery, NAT candidates and the
impaired Steam mock). Every lane but one is based on the v0.5.0 tag line through net-soak-profiles-v2 and
net-next-design, and several carry other net lanes (net-time-harness, net-input-feedback, net-session-resume-fixes,
net-v2-acks-loss, net-version-probe, net-relay-host-flow). Three conflicts needed a decision rather than a union:
(1) net-v2-acks-loss (transport v2, ADR-8184) and net-link-resume-dormant (the resume ticket in the join token and
the accept, ADR-8298) each set `REGIA_NET_WIRE_VERSION` to 5; (2) net-session-resume-fixes, as merged by three
lanes, registers `NetInterrupted` as a replicated component in the default `NetPlugin`, while the v0.6 line made
that registration opt-in (`NetPlugin::replicate_interrupted_marker`) because a replicated component changes the
protocol hash and every game would refuse its v0.5.0 peers and replays; (3) net-v2-pmtud gated the
`replication.mtu_bytes` check of `NetSettings` behind the `ecs` feature, while the v0.6 line already moved
`MIN_STATE_MTU_BYTES` into `settings.rs` so the check builds without it. The recursive merges also appended the same
v0.5 ADRs (ADR-7688 to ADR-8077, up to six copies each), COVERAGE rows and provenance rows once per lane.
Decision: (1) Wire version 5 is the v0.6 line's one bump (spec 120 § 12.1) and carries both changes: neither has
shipped, so no build speaks a version 5 with only one of them. The constant's doc and the `crypto` and `input_mtu`
version pins name ADR-8184 and ADR-8298. (2) The v0.6 line's opt-in stays: `NetInterrupted` is set on the server's
authority copies always and replicated only when every process calls `replicate_interrupted_marker`; the user guide's
`NetLink` resume section says so. (3) The check stays on in every build (the v0.6 line's form). Identical copies of
an ADR, COVERAGE row or provenance row are dropped down to the most copies any merged source had; nothing that
differs is dropped. `docs/formats/server-toml.md` keeps the full text where net-clock-filters' base carried a
damaged one-character-per-line copy. Resolutions that keep both features are listed in each merge commit.
Consequences: a v0.6 build refuses v0.5.x peers at the handshake as before (`protocol_mismatch`, wire 4 or lower);
the version probe still names the mismatch. Games that relied on the marker reaching clients by default (none on
the line) call `replicate_interrupted_marker`. Spec 120 and the user guide carry the merged lanes' Built notes; the
release fragment `docs/releases/v0.1.28-integ-v06p-net.md` lists the merged lanes and the upgrade notes.

## ADR-8318: slot-ordered range and nearest queries
Date: 2026-11-17   Status: proposed
Context: DC-3.4a: collision pairs alone do not accelerate acquisition, perception
and other range scans. Their slot order, exact float expressions and immediate
movement visibility are simulation behavior. An arbitrary callback can return a
small score for a distant row; geometry cannot bound such scores. Similarly,
`first_k_within` without an exact predicate can only promise conservative candidates.
Decision:
- Add `spatial`, sharing grid geometry with the existing broadphase. Slot is the
  array index, never an entity id. Build once per tick; intrusive cell lists make
  updates allocation-free even when all rows move into a previously empty cell.
- `within` delivers conservative candidates in ascending slot order; the caller
  retains its exact radius/distance predicate. `within_mut` additionally permits
  immediate XZ updates through the index and regathers only unvisited slots.
  Radius, band, flags and group changes require a new build. Queries are not nested
  inside a mutable visitor. `first_k_within` returns the first k candidates;
  `first_k_within_by` accepts the caller's predicate for the first k exact hits.
- `nearest` evaluates a pure caller-supplied squared XZ distance, visits expanding
  cell rings, and breaks ties by the lowest slot. The finite max radius bounds the
  search, but no incumbent-distance early exit is taken: no claim about arbitrary
  scoring callbacks is made. Use ordered `within` for game-specific best scores.
- Extend ADR-8048's conservative bounds to query radius: replace the first body's
  radius by |query radius|. For an overlap predicate on squared XZ distance using
  f32 subtraction, multiplication and addition, the axis displacement of an
  accepted finite row is at most |r| + max|row radius| plus roundoff. The inherited
  pad reach/256 + |center|/262144 + 0.001 dominates f32 roundoff in subtraction,
  radius addition, squaring and endpoint formation (including underflow near zero).
  Monotone cell coordinates therefore include every accepted row; overflowed
  reach or reach squared, or non-finite query data, scans all cells. Non-finite
  row position, radius or band is wild and bypasses geometric pruning; the same
  mask and FloorRule still apply. An infinite squared threshold must scan all
  rows because a caller may use `!(distance > threshold)` and accept infinities.
- Reuse the crate's no-dependency instrumentation seam: SpatialStats is the host
  profiler's input; the host wraps build/query batches in its tracing tick span.
Consequences: APIs add no content format and change no pair-pass output. The
caller must retain its exact predicates and cannot treat candidates as exact
hits. New user and agent sections document this contract and the upgrade surface.

ADR-8318 boundary follow-up: a subnormal positive cell size can make its reciprocal
infinite. Converting a negative infinite scaled bound saturates to `i64::MIN`;
the inherited floor step then subtracted one and panicked in checked builds.
Use saturating subtraction before the existing clamp. This changes no finite
in-grid coordinate or successful collision output and makes the extreme case
conservative. `subnormal_cell_sizes_and_extreme_updates_are_conservative` failed
with that integer overflow before the fix and covers both finite extremes and NaN.

ADR-8318 ordering follow-up: range gathering marks a reusable slot bitset and
emits its set bits in ascending word/bit order instead of sorting candidates for
every query. The bitset costs one bit per slot and adds O(n/64) word traversal;
it removes repeated comparison sorting for the 900-row workload. This preserves
every visited sequence (including the new cross-target trace) and the allocation
contract. No nearest candidate or result order changes.

ADR-8318 coverage refinement: the book checker rejects non-schema names in the
runtime protocol-method table. This feature explicitly exposes host-owned Rust
stats rather than a protocol method. Its COVERAGE row therefore lives in an
adjacent Rust-method table, identifying the future profiler input without falsely
claiming `sim.tick_profile` is registered by this lane. No coverage guard is changed.

ADR-8318 ring traversal follow-up: enumerate the clipped top/bottom row segments
and only enumerate interior side columns when those columns exist in the query
rectangle. The old clipped square loop visited no new cells along those sides
but still scanned its interior rows, giving quadratic empty work on a 1-by-N
grid. The revised loop is O(cells + maximum grid dimension), preserves the exact
row-major perimeter sequence, and is checked against exhaustive cell enumeration
for square, rectangular, single-row and single-column grids. The numeric trace
is retained unchanged.

ADR-8318 numbering: commits before this note cited ADR-8251. The lead assigned
ADR-8318 for this lane. The decision text is unchanged; only the number moved.

## ADR-8195: `regia_nav::det::{search, layer}`: DO27's A* and tunnel layer copied as one unit; regia_nav depends on regia_world_geom (S-02)
Date: 2026-11-17   Status: proposed
Context: plan row S-02 (DO27 absorb plan § 2, under ADR-8012) asks for DO27's two-level deterministic A* (`ir-sim/src/pathing/
search.rs`) on S-01's grid (`regia_nav::det::grid`, ADR-8049). DO27's search calls its tunnel layer (`pathing/layer.rs`:
`TunnelLayer`, `octile_m`, `PORTAL_COST`, `TUNNEL_COST_PCT`) on six lines, and W-04's tunnel proofs need `plan_layered`, so the two
files are one unit. The layer reads DO27's tunnel description, which lives in `regia_world_geom::compat::state::MapTunnels` since
W-01/W-02. Source: tag regia-absorb-2 (e6c84ba6d); `search.rs` and `layer.rs` have no diff between regia-absorb-1 and
regia-absorb-2.
Decision:
- **Copy.** `search.rs` 1-882 becomes `regia_nav::det::search` and `layer.rs` 1-379 `regia_nav::det::layer`, Stage A: every cost,
  heuristic, tie-break `(f, h, index)`, neighbor order, corridor dilation (1 then 3 clusters), expansion cap
  (`MAX_FINE_EXPANSIONS`, `fine_expansions_for`), string pull (`MAX_SKIP`) and the layer's junction, portal, open-cut and shoulder
  rules are the source's. `PATH_TICK_BUDGET` and `path_tick_budget_for` (`pathing/mod.rs` 57-70) come with the search's test.
- **Seams (the only edits).** (1) The layer is an argument: `plan_layered(grid, layer: Option<&TunnelLayer>, scratch, profile,
  from, from_tunnel, goal, goal_tunnel, tunnel_pct)`; DO27 read it from its grid (`NavGrid::tunnel_for`), which S-01 does not carry.
  `layer::layer_for(grid, layer, profile, size_limit)` is that rule with the size class as a setting (`PRESET_TUNNEL_SIZE_LIMIT`
  = 1: the large class goes round, as in DO27). `plan` is `plan_layered` with no layer (DO27's `plan` on a grid without tunnels).
  Nine arguments trip `clippy::too_many_arguments`: the function carries a reasoned `#[expect]`, because a struct would change
  every call site of DO27's switch. (2) The pilot-only crawlway arms are dropped: S-01's grid has no crawlway graph, and with an
  empty one (every DO27 map ships none) DO27 runs none of them, so node ids, scratch lengths and neighbor order are unchanged.
  (3) Profile tables index through `GridSettings::profile_index`. (4) `crate::math::{sqrt, sqrt_f64}` -> `regia_detsim::math`
  (libm, DO27's bits; `sqrt_f64` already exists, so `MATH_BITS_VERSION` does not move); std float `min`/`max`/`clamp` in the layer
  -> `regia_detsim::float::det_*` (ADR-8085; no value they feed reaches a decision with a different bit: the zero-sign case only
  enters squares and differences with a nonzero term). (5) `stat.funnel` reads S-01's `NavStatic::lowered`.
- **Interior mutability kept.** `TunnelLayer::set_closed(&self, ..)` replaces the closed set behind a `Mutex`, as DO27 does, so a
  host can close nodes on a layer shared by grid clones. Documented on the type; Stage B row W-13 (blockers) replaces it with an
  explicit input.
- **Dependency.** `regia_nav` depends on `regia_world_geom` (Systems -> Foundation, a downward edge the layer check allows).
  `regia_world_geom` must never depend on `regia_nav` (DO27 sign-off Q1). The `det` module's import test allows
  `regia_world_geom::compat::` beside std, serde and the lockstep kit.
- **Pins.** `two_runs_give_the_same_hash` (256 seeded calls over S-01's fixtures, the tunnel world and a serpentine maze
  whose end-to-end plans exhaust the cell cap, twice; full, partial, coarse and underground plans all occur),
  `plan_layered_takes_the_tube_and_routes_round_when_closed`, and the determinism golden `crates/regia_nav/goldens/
  search_plans.detgold` (F-02 format, ADR-8046) through `search_plans_pinned_on_every_arch`: x86_64-linux and
  aarch64-macos record the same run hash.
Consequences: DO27 swaps `pathing/search.rs` and `pathing/layer.rs` for these modules: its `grid.tunnel_for(p)` call sites pass
`layer_for(&grid, grid_tunnel, p, PRESET_TUNNEL_SIZE_LIMIT)` to `plan_layered`, and its crawlway maps (none shipped) wait for the
row that ports `crawlways.rs`. W-04 ports the navmesh tunnel half and the tunnel proofs; S-03 the agents and budgets. Updated:
`docs/provenance.md`, `docs/ported-sources.toml`, `docs/03-workspace-and-dependencies.md`, `docs/ci/lockstep-closure.toml`
(the `det` module row covers the new files), book page `book/agents/det-grid.md`.

## ADR-8295: Deterministic grid at scale: cluster size, region-graph repair, path-request queue
Date: 2026-11-17   Status: proposed
Context: audit gap GR-4 (sprint-buildout-ai-nav): the det grid's hierarchy was fixed at 8 x 8 clusters with one-byte labels
and at most 64 regions per cluster; the coarse graph was read off the cluster borders on every expansion with no table
to repair; there was no request queue, so a tick where 1,000 units ask for paths ran 1,000 searches with nothing to bound
or spread the cost deterministically. DO27's 256 x 256 canvas is fine today; 4096 x 4096 RTS maps are not.
Decision:
- **Cluster size is a setting.** `GridSettings::cluster_cells` (serde default 8; `hover_ground_jet` sets 8): a power of two
  from 2 to 128 (`GridError::BadClusterSize`). A power of two keeps `cluster_of` a shift (8: `/ 8` and `>> 3` agree) and
  keeps a local coordinate inside a byte for the flood stack. Labels stay one byte while `cluster_cells^2 <= 254` (2, 4, 8)
  and are two bytes from 16 up (`LabelWidth`, `NavGrid::wide_labels`, `NO_REGION`), selected when the grid is built. The
  flood is one generic function over the label type; at one byte it runs the source's steps, so the labels, regions and
  `state_hash` are unchanged (two-byte labels hash their own bytes after the empty one-byte layers). The search reads
  `cluster_cells`/`max_regions` from the grid instead of the constants; at 8 every node id, scratch length and neighbor
  order is the source's. `CLUSTER` and `MAX_REGIONS` stay as the default's values.
