every 250 ms. Host-visible: new enum variants `ClientEvent::QualityChanged`, `ServerEvent::QualityChanged` and
`LinkEvent::QualityChanged` (exhaustive matches must add them); new fields `PeerRow::{grade, quality}`, `NetStatus::quality`,
`DiagnosticsOverlay::worst_grade`, `EndpointTotals::socket_dropped` (struct literals must add them); new trait method
`DatagramSocket::dropped_sends` with a default; new `NetClient::quality`, `NetServer::peer_quality`,
`NetSession::{peer_quality, link_quality, peer_stats_samples}`, `ServerHost::net_stats_mut`, modules `quality` and
`stats`. Specs: 120 § 13 (Built note). Tests: `crates/regia_net/tests/quality_signals.rs`, `quality`, `stats` and
`socket` unit tests, `regia_agent` `net::tests`.

## ADR-8889: Landing PeerQuality (N110, ADR-8182) on the v0.7 net base
Date: 2026-11-20   Status: proposed
Context: ADR-8182's connection quality was built on lane/sprint-net-quality-signals (65100c17b) over integ-v06m and never
merged; v0.7 needs it on the v0.6.1 roll-up (integ-v061a 92cd068dd), about 5,700 commits later. Since then the base gained
wire 5 (ADR-8184), its own socket drop counter (`EndpointTotals::socket_drops`, ADR-8407), the rate controller (ADR-8301),
resume with dormant peers (ADR-8298) and the `NetLink` client's own reconnect (ADR-8352). Wire 5 shipped in v0.6.0 and v0.7
opens exactly one wire step (6), made by v07-wire6-resume-ticket (ADR-8858), which is not on this base.
Decision: (1) The source diff is applied whole (generated files regenerated), its tests kept, with these changes.
(2) Clock stamps are additive inside wire 5's version number: the server appends `sent_ms u32` to each tick sync, which a
v0.6 client never reads (it does not require the record to end after the tick), and a client sends its `LANE_CLOCK` (5)
record only after a tick sync that carried a stamp, so a v0.6 server never sees the lane it would refuse as `unknown_lane`.
No version bump here: the stamps ship in v0.7 under wire 6, whichever branch merges first; nothing in this lane depends on
the version number. (3) The socket drop counter of ADR-8182 (6) is not landed: the base's `socket_drops` (an absorbed send is
an error, never counted in `datagrams_out`) is the same item; `DatagramSocket::dropped_sends` and
`EndpointTotals::socket_dropped` are dropped, and the integration test `socket_drops_are_not_counted_as_sent` asserts the
base's counter with the base's contract (its socket answers `WouldBlock` where the source's answered `Ok`). (4)
`PeerQuality::queue_delay_ms` and `send_allowance_bps` read `LinkStats` (the rate controller), not 0. (5) A resume starts a
fresh connection and so a fresh grade: the server keeps the grade last shown for a dormant or taken-over peer and, after
`PeerResumed`, reports `QualityChanged { from: that grade, to: the new one }` when they differ; `NetLink`'s client keeps the
grade it last forwarded and, after a reconnect's `PeerRestored`, reports the change back to `Good` (the new connection's
starting grade). Without it a HUD that follows the events stays on `Interrupted` after every resume. (6) A loss fraction
counts toward the grade from 67 resolved packets, not 32: 67 is the fewest at which one lost packet stays under the `Good`
band (1/67 < 0.75 x 2 %). With 32, one loss is 3.1 %; on this base the server resolves about 45 packets in the first 1.25 s
of a good-wifi link (wire 5 and the rate controller send fewer eliciting packets than wire 4), and one early loss showed
`Fair` for 2.5 s (seed 3: `[(2024, Good, Fair), (4524, Fair, Good)]`; flappy: the same 4 s after two of six restores).
Consequences: a v0.6 peer and a peer of this branch (both wire 5) send each other nothing the other refuses. The
bad-wifi acceptance (fair or poor within 3 s on eight seeds) depends on when the seeded path first loses a packet: on this
base seed 1 loses none in its first 2.7 s, with RTT p95 64-68 ms, so by the § 13.1 limits the link is `Good` until its
first losses (about 3.8 s). Only jitter (4-6 ms against good-wifi's 0.5-1) and RTTVAR tell it apart that early, and § 13.1
does not grade them; whether it should is the owner's to rule (the test is kept as it is). Two more acceptance checks of
`quality_signals` are red on this base for the same reason, a seeded path's losses falling where they do on wire 5's packet
timing (about 36 server packets a second): good-wifi seed 4 ends its 10 minutes with 4 of 363 upstream packets lost in the
last 10 s (1.1 % against the test's 1 %; the leg dropped 53 of 21,624, 0.25 %, and the grade stayed `Good` throughout on
all eight seeds), and flappy (seed 3) shows one `Fair` spell (82.0-87.3 s) after its fourth restore, where 2 of the first 94
packet numbers of the restarted window never arrived (2.1 %). Neither test, seed nor bar is changed. The `RateLimited` event of § 13.1 stays unbuilt (no API to declare the rate a game needs). Spec 120 § 13 has a
Built note; ADR-8182 stands for the design.

## ADR-8648: Packaged lobby hub process (NL-06)
Date: 2026-11-18   Status: proposed
Context: NL-06 asks for a `regia-lobby-hub` binary staged by `regia package --server`, with `hub.toml`, rate limits,
a health endpoint, the existing agent method `lobby.hub_status`, and an in-process soak of 1,000 presences. The hub
core and the join broker are NL-04 (ADR-8559) and NL-05 (ADR-8607). DO27's `ir-hub` `src/bin/ironreach_hub.rs` was
read as requirements (regia-absorb-4, c9513623fe278ce58a3df3bd707d6fe91796e50a; the absorb-1 copy of that file is
identical; nothing copied). `tests/server_cfg_limits.rs` already has an NL-04 requirements row. The brief is stricter
than that process: configuration is a file with named field errors, the server key is created on first run and refused
inside a project, and DO27's `--relay` flag is not a `hub.toml` field (the relay address rides the owner's
`ReachOffer`). Address and identity limits sit in front of the core, including its member-data limits when that layer
is present.
Decision: (1) **Process.** `regia-lobby-hub` (a `[[bin]]` of `regia_cli`) loads `hub.toml`, binds UDP, creates the
server key if the file is missing, and serves until SIGTERM or SIGINT. The first signal drains (peers are kicked with
`DisconnectReason::ServerShutdown`, new hellos are `hub_draining`); a second signal exits at once. SIGHUP is ignored
(restart to change the file). A missing config file uses the built-in defaults. Exit 2 is a named field error, exit 3
a bind failure, exit 0 a finished drain. (2) **`hub.toml` v1** (`hub-toml`). Fields: `format_version`, `bind`, `port`
(default 7810), `key_path` (empty means `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/regia/lobby-hub.key`, else `$HOME/.config/regia/lobby-hub.key`,
else `%APPDATA%\regia\lobby-hub.key`), `caps` (session, lobby, members, chat, handle, idle; defaults are the hub's
DO27 caps), `limits.per_address_per_sec` (30) and `limits.per_identity_per_sec` (20), and `status` (TCP `GET /health`,
default `127.0.0.1:7811`). Unknown keys and bad types are named field errors (`field: expected ...`), stricter than
`server.toml`. A key path whose ancestor contains `Regia.toml` is refused. (3) **Rate gate.** `AdmitGate` is a
one-second sliding window per address, then per identity, capped at 4,096 buckets and dropping buckets idle for two
seconds. `HubHost` admits a hello after the player proof and every later request before the core, so the gate is in
front of chat and of member-data limits. (4) **Health and agents.** `GET /health` reuses `server_host::health`
(200, or 503 while draining). No new agent method: `HubProcess::publish` writes the existing `lobby.hub_status`
report under the label `hub`. New refusal codes: `hub_address_rate_limited`, `hub_identity_rate_limited`,
`hub_draining`. (5) **Package.** `regia package --server --with-lobby-hub` copies the `regia-lobby-hub` binary that
sits next to `regia`, writes a default `hub.toml`, and appends a README section. It does not build the hub. The
`--json` result gains `lobby_hub`. (6) **Soak.** `run_hub_soak_1000` connects, registers, chats and drops 1,000
in-process presences for ten cycles of 1,000 simulated seconds (10,000 seconds on the caller's clock). `state_bytes()`
stays under 8 MiB and a counting allocator's rise under 32 MiB, and neither grows after the first cycle.
Consequences: new binary, frozen format `hub-toml` v1 (unmigrated; `regia upgrade-project` probes `/hub.toml`), fuzz
target `net.hub_toml`. Host-visible: `HubError` gains `AddressRateLimited`, `IdentityRateLimited` and `Draining`;
`package::PackageArgs` gains `with_lobby_hub` (struct literals must name it); the package JSON object gains
`lobby_hub`. No new crate (the soak's counting allocator is the existing `regia_test_utils` dev-dependency). The
workspace test build of `cargo xtask preflight --changed` is owed to the integration line because `Cargo.lock` records
that dev-dependency edge.
are new. No new dependency, no frozen content format. Spec 89 § 15 gains a join-brokering note.

## ADR-8891: Land the lobby-hub binary: the hub ships with every server package, units start packaged binaries, the flood test is split by layer, and the hub client's clock on wasm32
Date: 2026-11-20   Status: proposed
Context: lane/sprint-lobby-hub-binary (ADR-8648, NL-06) built `regia-lobby-hub` but was not in v0.6.0; the v0.7 net
line lands it on integ-v061a (92cd068dd). Four things were open when it landed:
1. KI-NT-043: `regia package --server` writes `deploy/regia-relay.service` (ExecStart `/opt/regia/relay --listen ...`)
   and `deploy/regia-hub.service` (ExecStart `/opt/regia/hub --listen ... --key ...`), but the package ships neither
   binary, and `regia-lobby-hub` takes neither flag. The hub was only staged behind the lane's `--with-lobby-hub`.
2. `lobby_hub_fixes` `a_create_and_list_flood_from_one_and_many_connections_stays_bounded` asserted 1,998 of 2,000
   rewound lists counted as `hub_list_rewind` and saw 117: the address gate (30 requests a second per address,
   ADR-8648) now refuses most of the flooder's requests before the core sees them. The lane loosened the assertion
   to `0 < rewinds < 1998` and `address > rewinds`, which no longer proves the core's bound.
3. `HubClock::default()` called `Instant::now()`, which panics on `wasm32-unknown-unknown`.
4. `format_corpus_upgrade` failed on four fixtures in the hub lane's own run.
Decision:
1. Every `regia package --server` stages `regia-lobby-hub` (`regia-lobby-hub.exe` for a Windows package) from beside
   `regia`, plus `hub.toml` and the README section; a missing binary stops the package with the build command. The
   unreleased `--with-lobby-hub` flag is removed (it never shipped). `deploy/regia-hub.service` starts
   `<prefix>/regia-lobby-hub --config <prefix>/hub.toml --key-file <prefix>/hub.key` (the port, caps and limits stay
   in `hub.toml`, one source; no environment line, the hub reads none). No relay unit is written: Regia has no
   standalone relay binary (`--relay local` runs one inside a server for development), and a unit that cannot start
   is the bug. The hub's command line moves to `regia_cli::lobby_hub_args::LobbyHubArgs` so the package test parses
   the unit's ExecStart with the parser the binary runs. On a Linux package with a glibc floor, the staged hub is
   checked against the floor and a newer requirement is a warning, not a failure (the hub is the build beside
   `regia`, not a build at the floor; see Consequences).
2. The test's intent is bounded work under a flood. The rewind counter did not lose its meaning; it moved behind a
   new layer, so each layer is asserted on its own with the same or a tighter limit:
   - Core layer: the same flood with the gate opened (`HubLimits` at `u32::MAX`) asserts exactly 1,998 rewinds again,
     the original limit. The per-address gate does not make this redundant: an attacker with many addresses and no
     player key passes it, so the core's rewind window must hold alone.
   - Gate layer: under the default gate, the flooder's requests that reach the core (sent minus
     `hub_address_rate_limited`; nobody else passes 30 a second) are at most `per_address_per_sec` times the number
     of started seconds in the run, every counted rewind is one of them, and the snapshot bound (at most 2) and the
     honest client's answers hold.
3. `HubClock::default()` is `Monotonic` where std has a monotonic clock and a manual clock at 0 on wasm32 (the host
   advances it with `set_ms` from the browser's frame clock); `Instant::now` is never called there.
4. Nothing to change: on this base plus the merge, `format_corpus_upgrade` passes 8 of 8 (hub-toml included); the
   four failures were on the hub lane's older base, which integ-v061a's corpus and migrator repairs supersede.
Consequences: A server package now always contains the hub and needs `regia-lobby-hub` beside `regia` (cargo
install and cargo build of regia_cli put it there); a cross package (Windows from Linux) needs a cross build of the
hub placed there. The hub in a Linux package is the host build, so it may need a newer glibc than the package floor
(warned): building the hub with the game's toolchain and floor is a follow-up. The relay still has no packaged binary
(new known issue). `PackageArgs` loses `with_lobby_hub` (never released). Specs updated: `docs/specs/89-lobbies.md`
(packaged hub process), `docs/formats/hub-toml.md`; book: `book/agents/net-lobby-hub-binary.md`,
`book/user-guide/networking.md`.

## ADR-8893: Per-OS default-gateway readers and don't-fragment on every UDP socket
Date: 2026-11-20   Status: proposed
Context: `port_map::default_gateway_v4` read `/proc/net/route` only, so Windows, macOS and Android hosts always reported
`port_map_unavailable` (ADR-8370). Real UDP sockets never set don't-fragment (KI-NT-028), so on IPv4 a path MTU probe
(ADR-8300) could arrive as fragments and be acknowledged: the probed size read high on paths that carry less. Linux's
default (`IP_PMTUDISC_WANT`) fragments locally above the cached path MTU; Windows and macOS clear DF by default. The QUIC
transport always ran its own discovery and ignored `mtu_probing`.
Decision:
1. Gateway readers behind `port_map/platform/<os>.rs` (`docs/04-conventions.md` § 8), no new dependency (`libc`, and an
   `iphlpapi` import declared like the existing `ws2_32` one): Linux and Android `/proc/net/route`, then an IPv4
   `RTM_GETROUTE` dump over `NETLINK_ROUTE` (all tables; main table first, then the lowest `RTA_PRIORITY`; Android keeps
   each network's default route in its own table and denies `/proc/net/route` to apps); Windows `GetIpForwardTable`
   (lowest `dwForwardMetric1`); macOS `sysctl {CTL_NET, PF_ROUTE, 0, AF_INET, NET_RT_FLAGS, RTF_GATEWAY}` (unscoped default
   before `RTF_IFSCOPE`, `rtm_version` 5 only). The parsers are public and pure; a denied table (`EACCES`) or no default is
   `Unsupported`, so the documented code stays `port_map_unavailable`.
2. `UdpTransport` sets don't-fragment on every socket through the socket platform seam: `IP_MTU_DISCOVER` =
   `IP_PMTUDISC_PROBE` (and `IPV6_MTU_DISCOVER`) on Linux and Android, `IP_DONTFRAGMENT` / `IPV6_DONTFRAG` on Windows,
   `IP_DONTFRAG` / `IPV6_DONTFRAG` on macOS; IPv6 sockets also set the IPv4 option for v4-mapped traffic, best effort.
   PROBE (not DO) because the endpoint probes for itself (RFC 8899) and must not be capped by ICMP-learned state. DF is
   always on, not tied to `mtu_probing`: data packets are at most 1,200 bytes unless probing confirmed more, and RFC 9000
   § 14 asks the same of QUIC. `SocketBufferReport` gains `dont_fragment` (read back), shown by `net.socket_buffers`.
3. A send refused as too large (`EMSGSIZE`, `WSAEMSGSIZE`) records the size per destination (at most 1,024
   destinations, then the memory starts over) and `max_datagram_size(dest)` drops below it, so `transmit_packet` returns
   `TxRefused::TooLarge` and a refused probe ends the search (`probe_refused`) instead of counting as a socket drop and
   being resent every poll.
4. QUIC: the UDP socket handed to quinn sets don't-fragment; `QuicListener::set_mtu_probing(false)` and
   `QuicDatagramSocket::connect_with_mtu_probing(.., false)` turn QUIC's own discovery off (1,200 pinned). `bind` /
   `connect` keep it on, as spec 120 § 4.3 says ("The QUIC option starts at 1,200 and enables its own discovery"). Regia's
   probing is not run inside QUIC: QUIC's datagram limit bounds it, and a larger Regia probe is refused as too large.
Consequences: Hosts on Windows, macOS and Android can map ports. On a path whose interface MTU is under 1,228 bytes a
1,200-byte datagram is now refused instead of fragmented (such a path breaks spec 120's 1,200-byte floor anyway).
`SocketBufferReport` literals need the new field (Upgrade). Tests: `regia_net/tests/gateway_readers.rs`,
`regia_net/tests/dont_fragment.rs` (harness-free: it enters an unprivileged user+net namespace with a 1,400-byte
loopback), socket and quic unit tests. Specs updated: 120 § 4.3 and § 10.7 Built notes; book networking guide,
net-socket-buffers and net-host-check pages.

## ADR-8853: Warm successors for replication games: the successor journal (spec 120 § 10.5, N302)
Date: 2026-11-20   Status: proposed
Context: Spec 120 § 10.5 gives replication games a host migration in two parts: the host streams a journal to one or
two warm successors (N302, this ADR), and on host loss the first successor becomes the server from it (N303). The
lockstep re-host (N301, ADR-8809) does not help a replication game: its clients do not hold the world. The spec's
paragraph fixes the outline (a full state every 5 s, the input and event log every tick, the bulk stream, the best
connected clients) and leaves open what "best connected" means for a star topology, how the journal is budgeted, how a
successor knows its shadow is right, what bounds its memory, and what happens when a successor leaves. The owner's
DO27 successor-journal design is the model [D27]; its requirements were re-derived from spec 120 and the DO27 study, and
no DO27 code was read or ported. Two things the dependency (the transport) does in practice shaped the build and were
measured before deciding: (a) the bulk stream is one ordered stream that the scheduler serves last and paces, so a
large message on it stands in front of everything behind it; (b) the rate controller's allowance is far below the
link's capacity (about 58 KiB/s on `good-wifi` for an app-limited game, and at or near its 4 KiB/s floor for much of a
`bad-wifi` run).
Decision:
1. **Shape.** `regia_net::migration`, sans-IO, in the ECS-free core. `JournalHost` (host), `JournalSuccessor<W>` (every
   client, idle until appointed), `ShadowWorld` (the game's server-shaped state: `load_full`, `apply`, `digest`). The
   game supplies the full state's bytes, a 32-byte world digest and two blobs per tick (inputs, events).
   `JournalHost::pump_server` drives a `NetServer`; payloads are game messages on `Channel::Stream(StreamId::BULK)`
   (first byte 0x40-0x45), so there is no transport framing change and no wire version bump.
2. **Successors.** Up to two. Rank: clients whose link can carry a journal, then starved ones (send allowance under
   16 KiB/s), then interrupted ones (never appointed); inside a group the lowest round trip + variation + 10 ms per
   percent of loss, ties by the lowest peer id. A host of a star topology knows only each client's link to itself, so
   that is "best connected" here (the lockstep election uses a round-trip matrix; a listen server has none). The
   score is smoothed with a 10 s time constant: on `bad-wifi`, where every link is statistically the same, the
   scores of the moment differed by the switch margin at almost every comparison (9 to 13 changes of successor in
   90 s before smoothing).
   Successors are sticky, because every change costs a full state: a sitting one is replaced when it leaves or goes
   silent (at once), when it fell out of the journal and is not warm again while a link that is not starved waits, or
   when another client's score is under half of its own and 20 ms better (both checked every 10 s). When the first
   goes, the second becomes the first and keeps its shadow.
3. **Budget.** Per successor a token bucket filled at `budget_share` (default 0.25) of
   `NetServer::send_allowance(peer)` (128 KiB/s assumed when the link has no rate controller); nothing borrows; an
   idle bucket holds two ticks of the rate. The transport's own scheduling of the bulk stream is unchanged.
4. **One fragment at a time.** One poll hands a successor one payload of at most `part_bytes` (900): the log and a
   part of the full state, bundled, so it is a single fragment of the bulk stream. `poll_links` (and `pump_server`,
   through the new `NetServer::stream_status`) hands out the next payload only while at most one fragment of the
   stream is unacknowledged, and none when the peer's allowance is under 32 KiB/s (stop-and-wait). Two measurements
   forced it. (a) On `good-wifi` with 8 KiB full-state parts the shadow's lag reached 17 ticks (p99 14), because
   each part took the paced stream many ticks and the log queued behind it; with small parts p99 is 1 tick. (b) On
   `bad-wifi` a journal that fed the bulk stream every tick cost 7 of 8 clients their connection within 70 s
   (`Disconnected(ProtocolError)` on the client: the stream's reassembly stall deadline, spec 120 § 5.2), and the
   same seeds without the journal lost nobody. At the rate floor the sender's pacer holds bulk repairs back (a
   repair of a background stream waits for the pacer like new data, except on a probe timeout) while new fragments
   keep arriving behind the gap, and after about 2 s of that the receiver fails the link. With one fragment in
   flight nothing is ever stored behind a gap, whatever the pacing does. The price is throughput: one payload per
   poll, 54 KB/s per successor at 60 Hz.
5. **Order.** The log goes before full-state data. A successor's first full state starts before its log; every later
   one starts after the log has reached its tick, so the shadow compares digests by replay first.
6. **Digest at every full state.** The record of a full-state tick carries the host's digest. Match: the full state
   that follows is adopted without loading (its bytes replace the base, the log is cut). No match, or no comparison:
   the full state is loaded, its digest checked again (`journal_digest_mismatch` makes the shadow stale and the host
   takes another full state, at most one extra per second), and the log held after it is replayed.
   `replay_divergences` tells a game its log leaves something out.
7. **Depth.** 600 ticks of log after the newest full state, on both sides. One past is refused
   (`journal_past_window`) and the shadow is stale. The host's log waits at the window for the next full state (the
   shadow stays promotable at its tick); a successor whose next record has left the host's ring is seeded again.
8. **Lean log.** A log payload is `kind, appointment low byte, first tick low 16 bits, count` and per tick one flags
   byte plus only the blobs that are not empty: an idle tick is six bytes. The ordered stream makes the low bits
   enough to detect a stale or skipped payload. At the allowance floor a quarter share is 1 KiB/s, and the first
   encoding (19 bytes per idle tick) used all of it.
9. **Acknowledgments.** Cumulative, 26 bytes, on any channel (the pump's users send them unreliable): appointment,
   state, applied tick, newest full state seen, digest counters. The host reads the journal lag from them.
10. **Full states on demand.** `full_wanted` is true on the 5 s cadence only while a successor is free to start one,
    and for a successor the newest cannot seed.
11. **Agent surface.** `net.migration {endpoint?}` over `NetAgentState::publish_migration`; one error code,
    `migration_unknown_endpoint`; refusal codes `journal_*` in `last_refusal`.
Consequences: Additive API (`regia_net::migration`, three `NetAgentState` methods, one agent method); no wire, format
or settings change. Where the build differs from the brief or the spec: the spec says the journal is "budgeted by the
rate controller" and the build makes that a quarter share of the peer's allowance; "best connected" is the client's
link to the host; full states are metered into small parts (item 4); the log's header is five bytes (item 8); a
starved link ranks last. What the measurements say about limits: on `good-wifi` a quarter share is about 14 KiB/s,
which carries a 50 KiB world every 5 s next to the sample game's log with the shadow one tick behind; on `bad-wifi`
the allowance sits at or near the 4 KiB/s floor for much of a run, a quarter share is then 1 KiB/s, and only a world
of a few KiB stays warm. Whether the rate controller should hold bursty-loss links that low is a question for its
owners (N202 line), not decided here. The stall in item 4 (b) is a transport defect any user of the bulk stream can
hit (ADR-8624 moved join snapshots off it for the same reason): an honest sender's bulk repairs can be starved by
its own pacer for longer than the receiver's stall deadline. The journal avoids it; the fix belongs to the stream
and scheduler lanes (N203/N204). Not built: the hand-off and telling the other clients who the successors are
(N303); an adapter from `NetLink` replication to a full state and a log; allowance-aware sizing of the full-state
period. Specs updated: spec 120 § 10.5 "Built (N302)" note; book `agents/net-migration.md` (new),
`user-guide/networking.md` (Warm successors), `COVERAGE.md`; `docs/provenance.md` row.

## ADR-8901: Host migration for replication games: the hand-off (spec 120 § 10.5, N303)
Date: 2026-11-20   Status: proposed
Context: ADR-8853 (N302) gave a listen server one or two warm successors: clients whose shadow world trails the host
by a tick or two. Nothing happened with them when the host was lost: the other clients did not know who the
successors were, a promoted shadow had no server to live in, and the transport's resume ticket (spec 120 § 10.3,
ADR-8298) is minted by the server a client was connected to, so it means nothing to a successor. Spec 120 § 10.5 asks
for: the first successor becomes the server, clients resume to it with their tokens and keep their `PeerId`s and
`NetId`s, the second successor takes over if the first does not answer within 3 s, and a 16-player listen match
continues within 5 s with every entity present.
Decision: a new sans-IO module `regia_net::handoff` in the ECS-free core, and three small calls on `NetServer`.
1. **Everything a client needs is distributed before the loss.** Each successor makes the key pair of the server it
   may become and announces the public half and a port to the host (`HandoffClient::set_appointed`, `poll_out`). The
   host (`HandoffHost`) sends every client a **roster** (the successors in the journal's order, each with the address
   it would serve on, its public key and this client's ticket for it, plus the two thresholds) and every successor a
   **grant** (a secret and the list of players). They are game messages on the reliable channel of the sealed link;
   there is no wire version bump and no settings change.
2. **Tickets a successor can check and cannot forge for another.** The host derives one secret per successor: a keyed
   BLAKE3 of its random master secret over the successor's id and announced key. A client's ticket for a successor is
   a keyed BLAKE3 of that secret over the client's id, 16 bytes, the size of the transport's resume ticket. The
   successor gets its own secret only. Alternatives rejected: handing a successor the host's cookie secret (it could
   then forge the host's cookies and every ticket); one match-wide secret as in the lockstep re-host (the second
   successor could then join the first successor's server as anybody).
3. **The promoted server holds every player dormant.** `NetServer::adopt_dormant(peer, ticket)` puts a player into
   the server's dormant table as if it had timed out there; the client presents the ticket as its resume ticket and
   the existing resume path of § 10.3 gives it the same `PeerId` (`PeerResumed`). `keep_peer_id` keeps the promoted
   successor's own id for its player; `start_at_tick` starts the tick driver at the shadow's tick, so the clients'
   tick sync carries on. `PromotionPlan::apply` does all three. No new join path and no change to the handshake.
4. **Path validation and server authentication come from the handshake that exists.** A resuming client pins the
   announced key (`ClientConfig::server_key`), so only the successor the host named can take the match over, and the
   successor's cookie exchange validates the client's address like any join.
5. **Loss, takeover, restore.** A client treats the host as lost after 1.5 s of silence (`host_lost_ms`, the
   transport's interruption threshold; lower would act on a burst, higher eats the 5 s) or when the connection ended.
   It then tries the roster's successors in order, each for `takeover_ms` (3 s). A client runs its attempt on a
   second socket and keeps the connection to the host; when it hears the host again first it stays
   (`HandoffAction::StayWithHost`), so a client's own outage costs it nothing. A resume attempt resends its
   handshake packets every 100 ms instead of the transport's 250 ms: the attempt lasts 3 s at most and each lost
   handshake packet is time the match stands still.
6. **A successor arms, then commits.** The first build promoted the successor at its turn. The acceptance run with
   an outage of the first successor's own link (2.5 s, host fine) showed what that costs: the successor promoted,
   gave up its connection to a host that was still there, and served nobody. Now a successor that announced a port
   (`HandoffClient::with_port`: a second socket) **arms** at its turn (`HandoffAction::Arm`): it opens its server,
   holds the players and counts ticks from the shadow's tick, and keeps its shadow and its connection to the host.
   It **commits** (`Commit`: promote the shadow, simulate on from the server's tick) when a majority of the lost
   host's clients, itself included, has resumed to it, or when its own connection to the host ended (a goodbye, or
   the transport's timeout); it **disarms** (`Disarm`) when it hears the host again first. A successor without a
   port has one socket and promotes at once (`Promote`), with the old weakness; one that took over without a
   majority reports `NoQuorum` after 10 s.
7. **The roster's order is the journal's and is not sorted by which shadow is warm.** A first draft listed warm
   successors first, which saves 3 s when the first successor is cold. It was dropped: every change of the order is
   a window (one reliable delivery) in which two clients hold different rosters, and two successors that each think
   the other is first both wait 3 s and then both promote. With the journal's order the roster changes only when the
   set of successors does.
8. **The lost host's own player** was owned by `PeerId::SERVER`. The promoted successor gives it the lowest `PeerId`
   above every player's (`PromotionPlan::host_seat`) and holds it dormant with a ticket of its own; the game moves
   the entities. A host that was only cut off notices that every client is silent (`HandoffHost::deposed`), stops
   hosting and comes back as a client with `HandoffHost::comeback`.
9. **Readout.** `HandoffClient::poll_event` (host lost, resuming, promoted, resumed, restored, and on the promoted
   server who resumed, quorum, no quorum) and the `handoff` object of the agent method `net.migration`.
Consequences: measured on the build server in seeded virtual time, on the real transport over the soak harness's impaired
links (`crates/regia_net_soak/tests/migration_handoff.rs`): 16 players (a host and 15 clients), 60 Hz, the host stops
at 20 s. After the hand-off every path is client to client, so a datagram crosses two impaired links. Times are from
the moment the host stopped.
- First successor (bar 5 s). `good-wifi`, seeds 1 to 3: the successor committed after 1.61 to 1.63 s and the last of
  the 14 other clients was accepted after 1.65 to 1.75 s. `bad-wifi`: committed after 1.83 to 1.86 s, last client
  after 2.14 to 2.32 s. Every client kept its `PeerId`, had a state frame of the new host by then, and its inputs
  moved its entity again. The promoted world was the lost host's world of the promoted tick (digest equal), 0 or 1
  tick before the host's last, and all 16 player entities were present at the end.
- A host that says goodbye (`good-wifi`): committed after 26 ms, last client after 228 ms.
- First successor dead too (bar 8 s): the second successor committed after 4.61 to 4.63 s on `good-wifi` (last
  client 4.65 to 4.75 s) and 4.83 to 4.85 s on `bad-wifi` (last client 5.02 to 6.08 s; the shadow was 0 to 15 ticks
  behind).
- A host cut off for 8 s: its clients moved as above; it saw itself replaced 1.5 s into the outage and was back as
  a client on the kept seat 68 to 85 ms after its link returned.
- An outage of one client's own link (2.5 s): the client started a resume, heard the host 17 ms after the link
  returned and stayed; the same outage on the first successor: it armed and disarmed. Nobody was promoted and
  nobody left in either run.
- Before the arm-then-commit step and the 100 ms handshake resend (promotion at the successor's turn, 250 ms): last
  client after 1.66 to 1.90 s on `good-wifi` and 2.18 to 3.11 s on `bad-wifi`; with the first successor dead 5.21 to
  7.36 s on `bad-wifi`.
- One step of the way there that failed: an armed server left at tick 0 and moved to the shadow's tick at the
  commit. The clients that had resumed before the commit never had an input applied afterwards. The armed server now
  starts at the shadow's tick and counts ticks; the cause inside the clients' tick clocks was not looked into
  further.
- Twenty more seeds per row (11 to 30), same bars, all passed: the slowest client was back after 1.75 s
  (`good-wifi`) and 2.70 s (`bad-wifi`) on the first successor, and after 4.82 s and 6.28 s with the first successor
  dead. The promoted shadow was at most 1 tick behind on `good-wifi`. On `bad-wifi` it was 238 ticks (about 4 s)
  behind in the worst of the 20 runs: the journal's lag on a link at the rate floor (ADR-8853), rolled back for
  everybody.
The 5 s is mostly the 1.5 s loss threshold; the 8 s is that plus the first successor's 3 s.
Not built, and why: (a) an agreement between the successors. Two clients that hold different rosters (the host was
lost inside the one reliable delivery after a successor was replaced) can end on two servers; `NoQuorum` on the
smaller one is the readout, and the lockstep election's claim exchange (ADR-8809) is the model for a fix. (b) A
client that resumed to an armed successor has left its host; if that successor never gets a majority and disarms
(the two shared an outage the others did not), that client is dropped and has to join again. A commit message from
the successor that the clients wait for before they let go of the host would close it. (c) Reaching a successor
behind address translation: the roster carries the address the host saw and the announced port; a port mapping
(§ 10.7) or the relay (§ 10.6) is the way through, and neither is wired to the hand-off. (d) The `NetLink` (ECS replication) adapter: the
game still writes its `ShadowWorld`, and moves the lost host's entities to the kept seat itself. (e) Ticks the journal
had not delivered are rolled back for everybody; on `bad-wifi` that is up to the journal's lag (ADR-8853 measured up
to 2.8 s). Specs updated: spec 120 § 10.5 "Built (N303)" note; book `agents/net-migration.md` (The hand-off),
`user-guide/networking.md` (Host migration: the hand-off), `COVERAGE.md`; `docs/provenance.md` row.

## ADR-8837: outliers and large bodies kept off the deterministic grid (DC-3.4c)
Date: 2026-11-19   Status: proposed
Context: Audit gap DC-3.4c (det-core-03, follow-up to ADR-8048 and ADR-8318). `DetBroadphase` sizes its grid to the
span of every finite body and doubles the cell until that span fits `max_cells`, so one body parked at 1e6 m (a
pooled or dead entity) put every other body in one cell and the pass went quadratic again. Its gather reach was
`|r_a| + max|r| + margin` over all bodies, so one 60 m body widened every row's gather. `DetSpatial` had the same two
gaps (span of all tame rows, `max_radius` of all rows). AI perception grid coarsening (plan I-02) waits on this.
Decision:
- `BroadphaseConfig` gains `world_bounds: Option<[f32; 4]>` (`[min_x, min_z, max_x, max_z]`, default `None`) and
  `large_radius: Option<f32>` (default `None` = `2 * cell_size`; `Some(inf)` turns the class off).
  `DetBroadphase::new` normalizes bounds with a NaN or `min > max` to `None`, a NaN large radius to infinity and a
  negative one to zero. Helpers `BroadphaseConfig::large_threshold` and `is_outside`.
- `DetBroadphase` files each body in one of four lists: wild (non-finite x, z or radius; unchanged), large (finite,
  `|r| > threshold`), outlier (finite, outside the bounds) or a grid cell. The grid spans the cell bodies only; the
  grid gather reach uses the largest radius of the bodies that can be in a cell (finite and not large, whatever their
  position, since an outlier may be pushed inside mid-pass). Each row adds an outlier or large body to its candidates
  only when the body lies inside the row's padded window `x +- (|r_a| + margin + |r_b|) +- query_pad` on both axes:
  the ADR-8048 argument with `|r_b|` in place of `max|r|` (a contact implies `|fl(dx)| < |fl(r_a + r_b)|`), and the
  window is the same one a grid gather turns into cells, compared directly instead of through the monotone cell
  index. A non-finite window keeps the body; a wild row gathers every list. Candidates stay one list sorted by slot,
  each body in exactly one list, so the `(a, b)` order and every bit are unchanged. A body the visitor moves is
  re-filed between lists as before. `BroadphaseStats` gains `outliers` and `large` (counted at the start of a pass).
- `BroadphaseConfig`'s `DetState` (`brodconf`) is version 2: after the floor rule, a `u8` tag (0 = `None`,
  1 = `Some`) plus values for each new field. Version 1 snapshots are refused with `bad_version` (the snapshot
  version rule; snapshots are not saved content, no migrator).
- `DetSpatial` reads the same config: the grid spans the tame rows inside the bounds that are not large; outlier rows
  file into clamped edge cells (cell indices are monotone and clamped, so every query shape stays conservative, as
  for rows moved outside the build bounds by `update`); large rows live in a second always-gathered list after the
  wild list (range, first-k, segment, sector, box, nearest and `any_within` all read it). `max_radius` excludes large
  rows. `SpatialStats` gains the gauges `outlier_rows` (at the last build) and `large_rows` (now).
- Measured on the acceptance scenes (candidate tests, a counter, 30 ticks): 900 bodies over 1 km^2 plus one parked at
  (1e6, 0, 1e6) with bounds: 2544 against 2544 without it (bar 1.1x; without bounds the first two ticks alone take
  809100 against 160). 899 bodies of radius 1 plus one fixed 60 m body: 1598 against 1165 (1.37x); of those, 1194
  are the other rows' pairs (1.025x, bar 1.2x) and 404 are pairs with the large body, 328 of them rows within its
  contact reach (the bodies it pushed out sit on its rim and must be tested each tick). The brief's 1.2x bar on the
  total cannot be met by an exact pass on this sparse scene (about 39 tests per tick without the body); the test
  checks the split, and the total is listed for an owner ruling. With the large class off: 190684.
  `broadphase_cost --spread` (900 bodies plus one parked and one 60 m body): 405450 candidate tests per pass with
  the old settings, 3884 with bounds and the large class, same contacts.
Consequences: Results are unchanged for every setting (pruning only); DO27's pins (`stress_210`, the crowd hashes)
and the det goldens do not move. A host with many bodies outside its bounds or above the large threshold pays one
window check per row per such body (no contact test): keep both lists short. New public struct fields break struct
literals without `..Default::default()` (release fragment, Upgrade). Specs: book/agents/det-ids-broadphase.md
"Outliers and large bodies", book/user-guide/deterministic-simulation.md "Choosing cell size, world bounds and large
radius".

## ADR-8875: nearest ring early-out and first-k gather early stop (D-02, R3)
Date: 2026-11-20   Status: proposed
Context: Plan v0.7 § 2.2 item B (D-02). `DetSpatial::nearest` (ADR-8318) walked every Chebyshev ring of the
`max_r` rectangle even after an incumbent closer than any later ring was found: the det-core-01 query mix
(900 nearest at 120 m, 40 m cells) read about 49 cells a query where 9 decide it, and the spatial index p99 was
1.646 ms on a loaded host against the 0.4 ms bar. `first_k_within_by` gathered every list of the rectangle before
visiting in slot order, so `k` did not bound its cost (det-soak-ai-on finding 3).
Decision:
- `nearest` stops before ring `k >= 2` when `floor = (k - 1) * cell - max_radius - query_pad((k - 1) * cell, big)`
  is positive and `floor * floor > best_d` (strict), `big` the largest of `|x|`, `|z|` of the point and of the grid
  origin. Proof: cell indices are floors and the clamp into edge cells is 1-Lipschitz, so a row filed `k` rings
  away lies more than `k - 1` cells away on one axis (clamped rows and points only look closer). The f32 rounding of
  `(v - origin) * inv_cell` (about 3 ulp relative, 12 ulp of `big` absolute) and of `1 / inv_cell` stay far inside the
  ADR-8048 pad (`gap / 256 + big / 262144 + 0.001`), as does the caller's rounding of its squared distance. Rows in
  cells have `|radius| <= max_radius`, so a score measured to the row's disc is covered. Every later ring has a
  larger floor, so the walk ends. Such rows score above `best_d` and can neither win nor tie (ties keep the lowest
  slot), so the result equals the linear scan's for any score that is never below the squared XZ distance to the
  row's disc (the documented contract: center distance, disc distance, penalties, NaN to reject). Wild and large
  rows are still always tested. A non-tame point or a grid without finite cells disables the cut.
- `first_k_within` and `first_k_within_by` read the rectangle's non-empty lists (plus the wild and large lists) in
  ascending order of their lowest slot (`list_min`, kept by `file`, and recomputed by `unfile` when the lowest slot
  leaves). After list `i`, every candidate below list `i + 1`'s lowest slot is marked, so those slots are visited
  (ascending, the same `matches`, counters and debug records as `within`) before list `i + 1` is read. The k-th hit
  ends the query with the remaining lists unread. Visit sequence, results and `candidates` equal the old path. The
  sort scratch is reserved to `max_cells + 2` at build (no query allocation).
- `SpatialStats` gains `nearest_rings` (rings walked) and `first_k_lists` (lists the first-k gather read).
- Callback-call sequences change: `dist_fn` is no longer called for rows past the early-out. The `spatial_queries`
  det golden hashes each `nearest` callback call (`nearest_candidate`), so its trace moves (cause: this ADR); the
  results it hashes (`nearest`, accepted range candidates, moves) do not. The AI soak pin, the crowd pins and every
  other det golden do not hash callback calls and do not move.
Consequences: Fixed-scene counters (tests/spatial_early_out.rs): 900 nearest queries at 120 m test about a fifth of
the candidates and walk 2 rings a query instead of 4 to 7; `first_k_within` with `k = 1` reads one list a query.
A score that can be below the geometric distance (an arbitrary priority) was already outside the `nearest` contract
and must use `within` plus a host reduction. Timing evidence: docs/evidence/det-spatial/README.md (quiet hosts named,
never a test assert). Release fragment docs/releases/v0.1.28-v07-det-spatial-nearest-p99.md (two new public
`SpatialStats` fields under Upgrade).

## ADR-8839: Flow fields get their agent method, debug arrows, and every cluster size
Date: 2026-11-19   Status: proposed
Context: Flow fields (`regia_nav::det::flow`, ADR-8294) shipped in v0.6.0 without the agent surface rule 8 asks for:
the `sim.grid_flow {goal, profile, window}` method and the debug arrows were owed to seams that had not landed
(ai-nav-05's det publish seam; det-core-14's debug sink). The sink has since landed as `regia_detsim::debug::DebugSink`
(ADR-8562); no det publish seam exists. The v06p-sim integration also found that `ClusterFlow` assumed the fixed
`CLUSTER` = 8 and one-byte `NavGrid::labels`, while ADR-8295 made `GridSettings::cluster_cells` configurable (2 to 128;
16 and up store two-byte `wide_labels`): at 4 its cluster rectangles were wrong, at 16 and up it indexed an empty label
row and panicked.
Decision: (1) `ClusterFlow` follows the grid's cluster size: `CellRect::cluster` uses `NavGrid::cluster_cells()`, labels
are read at either width (the stored value of `NavGrid::labels_ref`, blocked = 255 or 65535), and the public
`RegionKey` widens from `(u32, u8)` to `(u32, u16)`. At the default 8 every value, key order and eviction tie is the
same, so the flow golden does not move. (2) Debug arrows go through the existing sink: `DebugKind::Flow` ("flow") and
`DebugWhat::FLOW` ("flow", in `ALL`; the indexes ignore it; no capture), `FlowField::debug_emit(sink, rect, cap, y)`
(goal: a circle of 0.35 cells; other cells: a 0.8-cell shaft toward `FlowArrow::to` plus a two-line head; no
allocation), the `FlowDebug` `DebugSource` for `DetDebugDraw::record` and `FixedStepSim::det_debug`,
`ClusterFlow::debug_emit_cached`, and `DetDebugColors::flow`. (3) The agent method reads a grid the host publishes,
like `nav.det_agents` (ADR-8405): `regia_nav::det_view::DetFlowView { tick, grid: Option<Arc<NavGrid>>, settings,
full_max_cells }` with `publish(tick, &grid)` (copies only when the generation or size moved), `publish_shared` and
`clear`. `DetFlowView::query(profile, goals, rect, cap)` builds a full `FlowField` up to `FLOW_FULL_MAX_CELLS`
(1024 x 1024) grid cells and a `ClusterFlow` above (`ClusterFlow::view` answers the same window shape), keeps the last
field behind a mutex (same grid `Arc`, generation, profile, goals, settings and kind: no search), and caps the window
at `FLOW_WINDOW_MAX_CELLS` (4096). `sim.grid_flow { goal, profile?, window?, max_cells? }` is `read`, not mutating
(the kept field is the view's own and changes no state another call can observe except speed), `heavy` in the rate
limits; goals are world points `[x, z]` (1 to 64), the window defaults to 32 x 32 cells around the first goal. Codes:
`no_det_flow` (not found), `grid_flow_bad_goal`, `grid_flow_bad_profile`, `grid_flow_bad_window`,
`grid_flow_goal_blocked` (invalid params). Integration values that no goal reaches are JSON `null`.
Consequences: Agents can inspect any flow field a host's grid supports and see its arrows in `sim.det_debug_draw`.
Host-visible API changes (release fragment, Upgrade): `RegionKey`'s label is `u16`; `DebugKind` has a new variant
(`ALL` is `[_; 7]`), `DebugWhat::NAMED` is `[_; 6]` and `ALL` gains `FLOW` (an agent's `"all"` now lists `flow`);
`DetDebugDraw::kind_counts` returns `[_; 7]`; `DetDebugColors` has a new `flow` field. A host that publishes a large
grid pays one grid copy per changed generation (or shares an `Arc`), and the first `sim.grid_flow` call on a
4096 x 4096 grid builds the clustered route (about 1.7 s on the min-spec laptop, ADR-8294's numbers) on the agent's
call. The editor's Profiler ▸ Lockstep tab has no flow toggle yet (Show ▸ Lockstep draws flow arrows when a source
records them). Specs: book/agents/det-grid.md (cluster size, debug arrows, `sim.grid_flow`),
book/agents/det-ids-broadphase.md (`flow` part).

## ADR-8877: the deterministic navigation is its own crate, `regia_nav_det`
Date: 2026-11-20   Status: proposed
Context: `regia_nav::det` (grid, two-level search, tunnel layer, navmesh, tunnel bake, layered runtime, region graph,
path requests, flow fields, fog line of sight, agents, crowds, walls; ADR-8049, ADR-8174, ADR-8195, ADR-8295, ADR-8486,
ADR-8555) imports only std, serde, thiserror, tracing, `regia_detsim` and `regia_world_geom::compat`, but it lived in
`regia_nav`, which depends on `regia_ecs`, `regia_app` and `regia_scene`. A headless lockstep sim that wants the
deterministic navigation therefore linked bevy_ecs (ADR-8174's open question). The review sprint-v06-absorb-rev-b R3
adds that a `[[module]]` row of `cargo xtask det-scan` gets only the line rules: no `clippy.toml` (so typed float
`min`/`max`/`clamp` and trig calls without a float hint on the line, e.g. its R1 lines, are never denied) and no
dependency check. Options were a `no-ecs` feature on `regia_nav` (every ECS module behind a cfg, `regia_ecs`,
`regia_app` and `regia_scene` optional, a feature-matrix row; the det code would still sit in a crate whose
`clippy.toml` cannot carry the lockstep list without denying the ECS code's floats) or a new crate holding the files.
Decision: a new workspace crate `crates/regia_nav_det` (layer 0a Foundation, beside `regia_detsim` and
`regia_world_geom`) holds the former `crates/regia_nav/src/det` files unchanged in content except module paths
(`crate::det::x` -> `crate::x`, doc examples `regia_nav::det::x` -> `regia_nav_det::x`, the include path of the
det-navmesh page copy, and the import-scan test now scans the crate's `src/` and bans naming `regia_nav` instead of
`crate::agent`, which now is this crate's own deterministic agents). Its dependencies are `regia_detsim`,
`regia_world_geom`, serde, thiserror and tracing (ron and the world-geometry fixtures as dev-dependencies); no new
external dependency. `regia_nav` depends on it and re-exports it as `pub use regia_nav_det as det;`, so every
`regia_nav::det::*` path and type stays the same (one type, two paths). The three goldens the moved unit tests read
(`flow_fields`, `search_plans`, `navmesh_bake`) and the det-navmesh page copy move with them (bytes unchanged); the
`tunnel_plans` and `layered_plans` goldens stay with `regia_nav`'s integration tests, which keep using the
`regia_nav::det` paths. `docs/ci/lockstep-closure.toml` replaces the `[[module]]` row with a `[[crate]]` row, and the
crate carries the lockstep `clippy.toml` (a copy of `regia_detsim`'s). `regia_nav/src/layered/geom.rs` keeps its own
`[[module]]` row: it is glue between the ECS navmesh builder and the layered runtime. `cargo xtask api-snapshot`'s
source scanner now reads a public whole-crate re-export of a sibling workspace crate listed in the new
`api_snapshot::MOVED_MODULES` (`("regia_nav", "regia_nav_det")`; `pub use <crate> [as alias];` with
`crates/<crate>/src/lib.rs` beside the scanned crate) like the module it stands for, with `crate::` inside the
sibling naming the sibling (`scan::scan_crate_with`); every other outside re-export stays one line as written. The list
is explicit because the `regia` facade, also a stable crate, re-exports whole crates on purpose: reading those in place
changed 23 of its lines in a trial run. So `docs/api-snapshots/regia_nav.txt`
keeps its 997 `det::*` lines unchanged and the move needs no `--breaking` rows (unlike ADR-8239's rules move, which
predates this). `xtask/src/layers.rs` lists the crate and its two same-layer edges; the book-snippet manifest gains
it (det-navmesh.md's example names `regia_nav_det`). Tests first: `xtask` `regia_nav_det_depends_on_no_ecs_crate`
(walks the crate's resolved normal-dependency closure: no `bevy_*`, `regia_ecs`, `regia_app`, `regia_framework`,
`regia_physics`, `regia_platform`, `regia_render`, wgpu or winit), `det_scan_lists_regia_nav_det_as_a_closure_crate`,
and `xtask/tests/api_snapshot.rs` `a_crate_reexported_whole_lists_like_the_module_it_replaced`; all three fail on
the base.
The lockstep `clippy.toml` found six sites, all in test code, none on a tick: two test-harness reads of
`REGIA_DET_GOLDEN_DIR` (`flow_bits_match_the_pinned_hash`, `search_plans_pinned_on_every_arch`) and the std `clamp`
that `clamp_by_compare_matches_std_clamp` compares with take a reasoned `#[expect(clippy::disallowed_methods)]` (the
pattern of `regia_detsim::golden::engine_golden_dir`); two navmesh tests fold waypoint heights with `det_max` in
place of `f32::max` (asserts unchanged; noted on the S-06 `[[do27]]` row). The non-test code was already clean (the
review's R1 lines had become `det_min` on the line).
Consequences: A lockstep sim depends on `regia_nav_det` alone (no bevy_ecs in `cargo tree -p regia_nav_det -e normal`).
The deterministic navigation now gets the full closure checks: typed `clippy::disallowed_methods` for float
`min`/`max`/`clamp` and std trig, and `det-scan`'s workspace-dependency check. No bits move (same sources, same
arithmetic); every golden and pin holds with its bytes. Host-visible: none for code that names `regia_nav::det::*`;
`cargo test -p regia_nav --lib det::...` filters become `cargo test -p regia_nav_det --lib ...` (book pages updated).
A future `regia_nav::det` item must be added in `regia_nav_det`. Specs: docs/03 (crate row), docs/ci/lockstep-closure.toml,
book/agents/det-grid.md, det-navmesh.md, det-orca.md, docs/formats/nav-det-navmesh.md (golden path).

## ADR-8838: Every engine golden is required on every leg; the qemu leg is owed, not failed, under `--qemu-when-present`
Date: 2026-11-19   Status: proposed
Context: Plan v0.7 § 2.2 B (D-05, exit bar 4) asks for every det golden and pin on every leg: x86-64 Linux, qemu
aarch64, the TEST Pixel 9 Pro, the Steam Deck, Windows and macOS. Three gaps stood in the way. (1) The runners
(ADR-8081) required only four scenarios on every leg (`CLEAN_SCENARIOS`: steer, slope, collide, match rules). The
`det_golden` binary prints a line for all 15 committed engine goldens, but the other eleven, `math_rng_fixed_vectors`
among them (KI-GP-001: "not yet in `CLEAN_SCENARIOS`"), were held to the clean rules only where a leg happened to
report them, so a leg that lost one still passed. (2) The gate hosts (the build server, the test machine) have no `qemu-aarch64`,
so `cargo xtask det-golden gate` fails with `qemu_missing`. That kept the gate step from being wired in, and the qemu leg
cannot start on its own once the owner installs qemu-user. (3) The goldens and pins of `regia_nav` (5 goldens) and
`regia_world_geom` (the two-peer golden, the lattice and query-table pins, `mesh_bits`, the mover pins) are outside
the runner, which runs only `regia_detsim --test det_golden`.
Decision:
1. `CLEAN_SCENARIOS` lists every committed golden in `crates/regia_detsim/goldens` except the plant (15 names, in the
   registry's order, then `spatial_queries` and `match_rules_ctf_koth_3600`). The xtask test
   `every_committed_engine_golden_is_a_clean_scenario` reads the goldens directory and fails when a golden is
   committed without joining the list; `a_leg_without_math_rng_fixed_vectors_fails` pins the KI-GP-001 case.
2. `det-golden run` and `gate` gain `--qemu-when-present`. Where `qemu-aarch64` is missing (on `PATH`, or the file
   `$QEMU_AARCH64` names), the qemu leg is not staged; `logs/qemu.log` holds `regia-det-leg-owed qemu_missing: ...`.
   `verify` lists such a leg in `Verdict::owed` (code `leg_owed`) rather than in `problems`. When the owed leg was the
   only aarch64 leg, "no aarch64 leg reported" is an owed line too. The summary verdict is `OWED` (`summary.json`
   `status`, plus an `owed` array), and the exit code is 0 if nothing else failed. A log with any report line is
   judged by the normal rules even if it carries an owed line, and without the flag a missing qemu still fails with
   `leg_error`. A new `manual` job `det-golden-gate-qemu` in `docs/ci/nightly-jobs.toml` runs
   `cargo xtask det-golden gate --qemu-when-present` from the gate tree, so the leg starts the day qemu-user is there.
3. The nav and world-geometry goldens and pins run on the legs by hand from staged test binaries for now. Each crate's
   whole suite is built per target (`cargo ndk ... test --no-run`, `cargo test --no-run --target
   x86_64-pc-windows-gnu`, the host build for the Deck) and run with `REGIA_DET_GOLDEN_DIR` and
   `REGIA_WORLD_GEOM_FIXTURES` pointing to staged copies. A target line is recorded with `REGIA_BLESS=1` on that leg,
   and only after its check run reported `unrecorded_target` with `agrees_with_reference: true`. Every recorded line
   was diffed against the x86-64 Linux line before it was committed, and the plant is never recorded off its reference
   target. Folding these suites into `det-golden stage` (a test list per package) is follow-up work. Four pins
   could not run off the source tree, because they read a build-tree path. They now honor the same overrides or embed
   their table: nav `navmesh_bake_id_pinned_on_every_arch` (which also lacked the `regia-det-golden ` prefix), nav
   `default_cluster_keeps_the_search_pins`, world_geom `crater_profile_matches_the_integer_table` and world_geom
   `t3_vectors_match_the_compat_query`.
Consequences: A new engine golden now needs a `CLEAN_SCENARIOS` row, and every leg must report it. The fixture logs in
the xtask tests carry all 15. The gate step can be wired now and needs no change when qemu-user lands: the summary
turns from OWED to PASS or FAIL. An OWED gate is not cross-architecture proof, and the summary says so. No engine API,
format or agent method changes; `regia-det-leg-owed` and `leg_owed` are new runner protocol lines, documented on the
book page "Determinism goldens on every target". The leg results (golden lines per target, pins per leg) are in the
lane report and the release fragment `docs/releases/v0.1.28-v07-det-golden-legs.md`.

## ADR-8876: The canonical lockstep `atan2`: correctly rounded, signed zeros as `+0`, canonical NaN (`MATH_BITS_VERSION` 1)
Date: 2026-11-20   Status: proposed
Context: `regia_detsim::math::atan2` was the bare libm 0.2.16 `atan2f`. Its bits are the same on every host for
ordinary inputs (pure Rust, no FMA contraction), but three things about it were not canonical. (1) Signed zeros:
`atan2(-0, -1) = -π` and `atan2(-0, 1) = -0`, so a `-0` from `f32::max`, `0 * -x` or a subtraction decides the
heading's sign (sprint-wgeom-floor-compat report line 111; DO27's sim wraps its `atan2f` in `canon_zero` on both
inputs and `canonical` on the result; Regia had that wrapper only in `regia_world_geom::compat::source_math`,
ADR-8167, ADR-8579). (2) NaN: the result of a NaN input is `x + y`, whose sign and payload differ between x86-64
(first operand) and aarch64 (a signaling NaN first) when both are NaNs. (3) The function was defined only as "what
this libm build returns", up to one ulp from the true value, so another tool, language or libm cannot reproduce it
except by linking the same code. Plan v0.7 § 2.2 item B asks for a canonical `atan2` and a `MATH_BITS_VERSION` bump;
the constant itself (named in spec 121 § 14 and the world-geometry handshake docs) did not exist in code yet.
Decision:
- **Function.** `math::atan2(y, x) = canonical(cr_atan2f(canonical(y), canonical(x)))`. `cr_atan2f` is a Rust port
  of CORE-MATH's correctly rounded binary32 `atan2f` (Sibidanov and Zimmermann, MIT; `math/cr_atan2f.rs`, header,
  `docs/ported-sources.toml`, provenance row): a binary64 rational fast path, a rounding test, a double-double
  degree-63 accurate path and a tiny-ratio path. `__builtin_fma` is `libm::fma`, an exact IEEE operation (every
  correct implementation gives the same bits; no host FMA unit is assumed, so `f64::mul_add` and its host-libc
  fallback stay banned). Rust's round-to-nearest environment is the only one supported, as for every other
  `math` function.
- **Policy.** Signed-zero inputs count as `+0` (DO27's and ADR-8579's lockstep rule): `atan2(±0, x>0) = +0`,
  `atan2(±0, x<0) = +π`, `atan2(±0, ±0) = +0`. Any NaN input gives `0x7fc0_0000`. A zero result is `+0`
  (`atan2(-1, +inf)`, an underflowed negative ratio). Infinities take the IEEE 754-2019 § 9.2.1 values. Every other
  input pair gives the correctly rounded value, so the function is defined by the mathematics: any correctly rounded
  `atan2f` plus these three steps reproduces it.
- **Old bits.** The version-0 function stays as `math::atan2_libm` (bare `atan2f`), documented as not for new tick
  code. It is used where bytes must match a tool built on that libm: `compat::source_math::atan2` (Stage A, the
  source game's bits; its canonical steps around `atan2_libm`, so Stage A does not move) and the tunnel bake's
  `MouthPortal::yaw_mdeg` (KI-WD-029: the source baker's signed-zero `atan2`, format `do27-tunnels-v2/1`).
- **Version.** `regia_detsim::MATH_BITS_VERSION = 1` (new constant; `0` names the regia-absorb copy). Every change
  to a `math` function's bits bumps it; `tests/math_bits.rs` pins the version beside the per-function hashes
  (`math_bits_version_names_the_pinned_bits`) and pins `atan2_libm` to the version-0 `atan2` hash
  (`atan2_libm_keeps_the_version_0_bits`).
- **Vectors.** `tests/atan2_canon.rs` with two committed vector files (compiled in, so a leg runs the binary off the
  source tree): 690 edge pairs (every pair of 26 edge values and 14 hand-picked pairs) and the 4596 non-NaN published
  hard cases of CORE-MATH's `atan2f.wc`. Expected bits come from an original decimal-arithmetic oracle (80 digits,
  exact binary32 rounding), never from the function under test. A million-pair seeded sweep checks correct rounding
  against binary64 `atan2` wherever binary64 decides the rounding. Each vector test prints a
  `regia-atan2-vectors {json}` hash line per target.
Alternatives rejected: (a) keep libm `atan2f` and add only the zero and NaN steps (DO27's form): no golden outside the
signed-zero cases would move, but the function stays "whatever libm 0.2.16 computes", the brief's rule 2 excludes it,
and a future libm bump or a port to another language could not reproduce it from a definition; (b) an integer or
fixed-point `atan2` (CORDIC): exact and portable, but either coarser than binary32 or much slower, and every sim
heading would lose precision; (c) round binary64 `atan2` once: double rounding makes it wrong on a set of inputs
(a rounding test plus a fallback is what CORE-MATH does, with a proof); (d) change `compat::source_math` to the new
function: Stage A must keep the source game's bits until DO27 switches.
Consequences: every det golden and pin whose run calls `math::atan2` on an input where libm `atan2f` is not
correctly rounded, or on a signed zero or NaN, moves once; they are re-pinned in one commit naming this ADR (the
lane report lists them with the old and new hashes). Stage A (`stage_a_bit_table_is_pinned_on_every_arch`, the
compat goldens, `mesh_bits`, `t3_vectors`) and the tunnel bake's portal yaw do not move. DO27, when its sim moves
onto `regia_detsim`, adopts version 1: its `math::atan2` (libm plus the same zero and NaN steps) differs only on the
inputs where libm is not correctly rounded, by one ulp; its lockstep handshake should carry `MATH_BITS_VERSION`. The
accurate path costs more than libm on the rare inputs near a rounding boundary (about 1 in 2^24 of random pairs);
the common path is one division and a rational in binary64. Specs: spec 121 § 14 already names the constant; book
page `agents/lockstep-math.md` gains "The canonical `atan2`". Fragment `docs/releases/v0.1.28-v07-det-atan2-canon.md`.

## ADR-8840: The periodic FP-environment check in `regia_detsim` (`FpEnvWatch`), and `SimHarness` checks every step
Date: 2026-11-19   Status: proposed
Context: The det-core audit (sprint-buildout-det-core § 3.1) listed "periodic FP-env check" as open: a library on
the sim thread can set flush-to-zero mid-match and the guard only ran at sim-thread start. Since then the threaded
sim host checks on a cadence (`SimHostSettings::fp_check_every`, ADR-8526) and the lockstep host and seat check before
every frame they hand out, but `regia_detsim`'s own runner, `SimHarness` (the loop a DO27-shaped external sim and the
soak and profile tools drive), still guarded only at `new` and `resume`, and the kit had no reusable check a host
with its own loop could adopt. Measured on x86-64 before this change: with FTZ planted on the thread between steps 3
and 4, the probe scenario's steps 3..8 all flushed their subnormal product (`flushed = 5`) and the state hash differed
from a clean run's.
Decision: `regia_detsim::fpu` gains `FpEnvWatch` (cadence `every`, default every step; `0` never; the first step
always), with `before_step(tick)` and `after_step(tick)` as the two defined points and `check(tick, point)` for an
unconditional check. Each checked point calls `ensure_default_fp_env` (one MXCSR/FPCR read, a write only when it
differs; no new unsafe), counts `checks`, `corrections` and `during_step` (found after the step: the environment
changed inside it, so that step may already differ from a peer's), keeps the first and last `FpEnvChange { tick,
point, report }` and logs a `tracing::warn`. `FpCheckPoint::code` is `before_step` / `after_step`. `SimHarness`
owns one (every step) and brackets each `DetScenario::step` with it; `fp_env()` reads it and
`set_fp_check_every(n)` changes the cadence (and resets the counters). The counters are diagnostics, not state:
`save`/`resume` do not carry them and they never enter a hash. `set_flush_to_zero_for_tests` is also compiled for
the crate's own unit tests (`cfg(any(test, feature = "fp-test-hooks"))`); the feature and its public surface are
unchanged. The threaded sim host keeps its own guard (no change to `regia_framework`); a later lane may move it onto
`FpEnvWatch`.
Consequences: A foreign FTZ between two harness steps no longer reaches the sim (the hash matches a clean run), and
one inside a step is named with its tick. Cost: two control-register reads per step. No det golden or pin moves: on a
default thread both checks find the default and change nothing (the default environment is what every recorded hash
already assumed). Host-visible: new public types in `regia_detsim::fpu` and two new `SimHarness` methods; no field or
variant was added to an existing public type. Book: lockstep-math (the periodic check) and det-sim-harness;
COVERAGE row; provenance row; release fragment `docs/releases/v0.1.28-v07-det-fp-env-owed.md`.

## ADR-8856: Rules zone shrink multiplies before dividing
Date: 2026-11-20   Status: proposed
Context: The rules-pve-br-rts-fixes verification (finding 1) showed that the shrink interpolation's `i128`-overflow fallback in `regia_rules::zone` (`lerp`, called from `ZoneState::tick`) computed `delta / total * elapsed`, dividing first. On a restored circle at the `i64` edges with a phase near `u64::MAX` ticks the quotient is short by up to `total` centimeters: the committed proof reads center `[1, 0]` where the interpolation says `[9223372036854775805, 0]`, so a unit outside the true circle stays inside and takes no `ZoneDamage`; with a span under `shrink_ticks` the quotient is `0` and the circle parks on `from` for the whole phase, damaging a unit inside the true circle. This supersedes the last sentence of ADR-8802 decision (4) ("the shrink interpolation divides first when `delta * elapsed` would pass `i128`"), which specified that fallback.
Decision: `lerp` scales in `u128`: `moved = |delta| * elapsed / total` (both operands stay below `2^64`, so the product always fits), applies the sign after the divide, then adds to `from`. `moved` never exceeds `|delta|` because `elapsed < total`, so the result stays on the `a`..`b` segment and inside `i64`; the conversions' `min` and `unwrap_or` arms only keep a hostile restore panic-free. Deterministic integer math only, no float. A lane proof (`a_restored_shrink_shorter_than_total_ticks_still_moves`) locks the parked-on-`from` case beside the committed full-span proof.
Consequences: The committed proof passes unchanged and the lane proof passes; the rest of `cargo test -p regia_rules` is untouched (the known pre-existing `phases::all_phase_settings_off_keeps_s14_bits` hash failure stays with the lead). No host-visible API change, no serde shape change, no format bump, no book change (the book's "integer interpolation" wording already matches). The v0.1.28-rules-pve-br-rts-fixes fragment's "cannot overflow" sentence is amended to name the fallback it shipped with.

## ADR-8652: Finished-match records (`match-result` v1), sinks and the history folder
Date: 2026-11-18   Status: proposed
Context: Nothing recorded a finished match (audit gaps GR-10.1 to GR-10.4): no result record, no match history and no per-player match stats. The dedicated server persisted the world but not results, leaderboards took manual submits and platform stats were manual calls. The match session drained its `MatchOver` event to whoever stepped it, and the agent's input and objective paths drained events without the session seeing them, so a plugin watching the session could not tell who won or when a host ended the match. The board's serialized shape is pinned by the S-14 hash test (`tests/phases.rs`), so the winner could not go on the board.
Decision: `MatchSession` gains `launched_step` and `match_end: Option<MatchEnd { step, tick, winner, reason }>` (serde defaults); `drain_events` keeps the first `MatchOver` drained since the launch, `launch_row` clears it. The agent's session JSON leaves both keys out, so the published `rules.match_*` result objects are unchanged. `regia_framework::match_results` builds a `MatchResult` (new JSON format `match-result` v1, unknown fields refused) from the session, its per-seat ledgers (ADR-8500) and the end-of-match ledger (ADR-8406), and `MatchResultsPlugin` writes `<root>/<utc-date>/<match_id>.json` with `save_game::write_atomic` on the IO task pool, retries a failed write once, then rotates by `keep_days` and `keep_count`. Ordered `MatchResultSink`s run on the main thread: `LeaderboardSink` (framework) and `PlatformStatsSink` (`regia_steam`, so the framework gains no platform dependency); a web upload is a game's sink. Names are left out unless `include_names`; a `name:` key is written as a BLAKE3 hash; no IP address is recorded. Player keys come from `MatchPlayerKeys`, bound with the server persistence identity rule under `net`. The match id is `Random`, `Fixed` (sent by the host) or `Derived { seed }` (every lockstep peer derives it); the record holds no wall clock, so peers that share the id write identical bytes. Settings are a resource: `server.toml` v4 is frozen, so `[match_results]` keys join it only with its next version and a migrator. A dedicated server's root defaults to `<server dir>/matches` (a `HostEvent::Started` hook). Agent `rules.match_results` (newest first, `limit` 1..=200) and `rules.match_result`; CLI `regia server results`. The merge of buildout-rules-teams-scores into this line also fixes `MatchSession::step_with`, which ran the flag and hill rules twice per step after the integ-v06s-final merge (the phases branch and the drop-check tick were both kept); `step_phases` now takes the host's drop check.
Consequences: Match history, per-player stats, ranked play and dispute tooling read one format. New frozen format `match-result` v1 (format-hashes row, corpus `match-result/v1.json`, fuzz target `match_result_json`, `regia upgrade-project` probe and a migrator stub). Host-visible: two `MatchSession` fields and `session::MatchEnd` (struct literals of `MatchSession` need them or `..Default::default()`), a new `MatchResultsPlugin` in server builds. Specs: `docs/specs/12-assets.md` (format row), `docs/specs/76-dedicated-server-package.md` § 18. The record's ordering within a day uses file modification time; a folder copied without times orders same-day records by id.

## ADR-8880: Match results land on the v0.7 rules line; records hold player ids only (owner Q4 pending)
Date: 2026-11-20   Status: proposed (OWNER: rules Q4, player names in stored match results; built to the plan default "ids only")
Context: The match-results lane (6fdeb9622, ADR-8652) was built on a base without the teams-scores fixes (79b46546d, ADR-8657) and left reds (agent contract, format corpus) and no format-hashes row. Its records could carry a display name per player behind `MatchResultsSettings::include_names`. Whether a stored record may name players is the owner's rules question Q4; the v0.7 plan's default is "ids only". `match-result` v1 freezes in format batch 2 (Sat 2026-11-28), so whatever v1 allows is permanent until v2.
Decision: (1) Land 6fdeb9622 on the v0.7 rules line (integ-rules-v07b 97004e28a): each conflicted file takes the line's version and re-applies only the match-results delta, so ADR-8657's fixes (ledger row ids from generation and seat, pause and joins carried by a move, rebalance early stop, one hill credit per unit, reflected `MatchRules`/`FriendlyFire`/`SelfDamage`) and ADR-8652's records both hold. (2) Ids only: `PlayerResult` has no `name` field, so a v1 reader refuses a row with one (`match_result_malformed`, unknown fields are refused); `MatchResultsSettings::include_names` and `PlayerKey::name` are removed and `MatchPlayerKeys::bind(seat, key)` takes no name; `bind_net_player` drops the name the identity rule returns; a `name:<n>` key is always written as `name-hash:<32 hex>`. (3) `MatchSession::launched_step` and `match_end` are not serialized while unset (`0`, `None`), like the line's other late session fields, so a session that never ended keeps its serialized shape. (4) `match-result` v1 gets its format-hashes row in batch 2.
Consequences: If the owner answers Q4 "names allowed", that is `match-result` v2: an optional `name` on a player row, a number-only migrator from v1 (v1 files have none), an upgrade-project row, a v2 corpus fixture and an opt-in setting; v1 files keep loading. Host-visible against the unmerged lane: `MatchPlayerKeys::bind` lost its third argument, `MatchResultsSettings::include_names`, `ResultContext::include_names`, `PlayerKey::name` and `PlayerResult::name` are gone. Updated: book/agents/match-results.md, book/user-guide/game-modes.md, docs/formats/match-result.md, docs/specs/76-dedicated-server-package.md § 18, book/COVERAGE.md rows, the agent schema and guide text.

## ADR-8881: rules session items (R-04): session version, vacated credits, in-order ballot guard, `row_skipped` on the wire, hosted rule sets, option binds
Date: 2026-11-20   Status: proposed
Context: plan row R-04 (plan-v07-to-v10 § 2.2, item C) collected seven open items from the rules reviews before the
v0.7 format freeze (batch 2 freezes 11-28): (1) `MatchSession`'s serde shape had no version and dropped unknown keys
(teams-scores review); (2) a credit to a coordinate nobody holds still opened a ledger row, so a departed player's
pawn that kept killing or dying put that player back on the score sheet (v06 teams-scores fixes, adapter report);
(3) an in-order map ballot walked from the index with no repeat guard, so its first option could differ from the row
the next launch plays (rules-review-fixes-b); (4) `RulesEvent::RowSkipped` had no logic-graph kind and no wire byte
(same report); (5) the dedicated host's rotation did not resolve rule sets or call `NetSession::set_rules_hash`
(ruleset-format report); (6) rule-set options did not bind to session fields, a game had to read them (same);
(7) `SessionPatch` could not set the genre sections (integ-rules-v07a).
Decision:
1. `MatchSession` gains `version` (first key, `MATCH_SESSION_VERSION` = 1) and `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]`. A
   session without the key (v0.6) reads as version 1; 0 or a newer version is refused with a message that starts
   `match_session_version`. Every shape change of the session or a type it holds bumps the constant from now on.
2. `MatchSession::vacated` (sorted, not serialized while empty) lists coordinates a player left or moved off
   (`Leave`, `assign_team` moves, the launch rebalance) that nobody holds since. `credit_kill` and `note_hit` give a
   vacated coordinate nothing and open no row there; the seated side of the same kill is still booked, and assists go
   to credited contributors only (`LedgerBook::credit_kill_where`). A coordinate nobody ever held (a game's unseated
   bots, S-14) is credited as before, so `damage_with_ledger_slots_credits_the_match_session` keeps its meaning.
   Seating the coordinate again takes it off the list. `MatchSession::credits_seat` answers the rule.
3. In order, `Playlist::vote_candidates_for` keeps its wrap-once walk but puts rows the repeat guard holds back
   (`no_repeat_last`) after the other eligible rows, each part in walk order, as a launch passes them. With no guard
   the ballot is unchanged.
4. `row_skipped` joins `MATCH_EVENT_KINDS` (38 kinds); `MatchEvent::fields` gives the launch step as `tick`, the row's
   playlist index as `round` and the skip code as `reason`. Wire kind byte 38 carries step (varint), index (varint),
   map id (string) and a reason byte (0 too_few_players, 1 too_many_players, 2 missing_content, 3 recent). The match
   event format byte stays 1: kinds are additive, and an older client counts kind 38 as malformed, as it already does
   for any kind it does not know.
5. `HostGame::rule_sets` (default `None`) hands the dedicated host the game's rule sets; `AppHostGame` reads them
   through `HostGameHooks::set_rule_sets`, which `regia_framework`'s session bridge points at `RuleSetRegistry`. At
   start the host computes `RuleSetLibrary::playlist_rules`; a starting row whose rule set does not resolve stops the
   start (exit code 4, content). The host calls `NetSession::set_rules_hash` with the playlist's hash before it hosts
   only when the game opts in (`HostGame::rules_in_manifest`, `HostGameHooks::set_manifest_rules(true)`, default
   off): the handshake refuses any manifest difference and no client sets a rules hash yet, so on by default every
   client would be refused (`pack:@rules`) by any host whose playlist names a rule set, the shipped `tdm` and `ctf`
   included. A game turns it on once its clients call `set_rules_hash` with `playlist_rules` over the same playlist. On a travel a row whose rule set does not resolve with its options is passed over with its
   `ruleset_*` code as the skip reason. Only rows whose `mode` names a rule set of the library are resolved
   (`RuleSetLibrary::resolve_hosted_row`): an empty mode, a game's registered rules name and a bare skeleton id with
   no rule set run as before and add nothing to the hash. A row key the rule set does not declare is left to the game
   (S-14 rows carry game-read options) and does not enter the hash; a declared option with a bad value is refused.
   `server.rotation_get` gains `rules_hash` (16 hex digits or null) and `rules_in_manifest`. A reload recomputes the
   hash for the next session start; a running session keeps the manifest it started with.
6. `OptionDef` gains `bind`, one of `OPTION_BINDS` (19 session fields: flow start delay, the phase timers, the
   objective limits, touch radius and home-flag rule, team rebalance and assist window, the respawn seed, the zone
   score limit, race laps, the surrender window), of the option's kind. The value (the row's, else the default)
   replaces the rule set's own value before the settings are checked; on an optional field 0 is off. A bind outside
   the table, of the wrong kind or bound twice is `ruleset_invalid` at `options[n].bind`; a value the field cannot
   hold (negative, too large) is `ruleset_option_range` at `options.<key>`. `rules-ron` v1 is unreleased, so under
   the ADR-8619 rule the version grows instead of taking v2 (as ADR-8748 did): `bind` is optional and not written
   while absent, every existing v1 file reads unchanged, and a third corpus fixture (`rules-ron/v1-binds.ron`) uses
