server reads up to one client send interval (16.7 ms) after the packet arrived, on top of the path's 0-10 ms of
jitter. A thin sender's round holds one to three samples, and the smallest of so few is over the 25 ms threshold
often: 866 of 2,208 client rounds per seed read over 25 ms on round trips. The return path's packet sizes (ADR-8692)
are a second term of the same sum, visible only in the round trip.
(2) The detector's noise is load-bearing. Every variant that reads the queue more exactly cuts later on the server's
side, and the congested rows have no margin for that (growth stops at 97 % of the bottleneck; a cut a few hundred
milliseconds late is a second over the link):

| Variant (all with the stamp on the wire) | rpc bar, seeds 1-104 over | congested/4 1-200, seeds with a second over (worst) | listen-uplink/64 1-40, seeds over (worst) | Client delay cuts per seed (rpc run / listen) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| round trips alone (the base's rule) | 0 | 0 (99.9 %) | 9 (106.9 %) | 84.9 / 38.0 |
| candidate (b): 5th percentile of 10 s of round minima as the minimum | 0 | 3 (102.1 %) | 30 (130.7 %), 12 ends, `no_wedged_client` 26 | 39.9 / 43.6 |
| candidate (a) as a reading: every queue reading is min(one-way, round trip) | 3 | 86 (107.0 %) | 6 (101.6 %) | 124.9 / 667.7 |
| one-way readings alone | 4 | 71 (105.4 %) | 4 (101.6 %) | 172.2 / 878.3 |
| round trips, every reading over at least 4 samples | 3 | 46 (109.1 %) | 11 (102.6 %) | 36.3 / 8.1 |
| min(one-way, round trip) over at least 4 samples | 6 | 102 (108.9 %) | 4 (136.5 %) | 33.2 / 249.8 |
| the same over at least 8 samples | 8 | 144 (133.0 %) | 22 (139.7 %), 54 ends | 0.8 / 0.6 |
| round trips decide; a verdict needs the one-way floor (2 rounds) at 5 ms / 12 ms | 0 / 1 | 0 / 0 | 5 (100.6 %) / 11 (100.8 %) | 82.4 / 83.4 |
| the same with the one-way floor over 6 samples, 12 ms, every sender | 2 | 1 (102.0 %) | 6 (101.0 %) | 58.9 / 29.2 |
| the same, app-limited senders only; an unconfirmed verdict stays pending | 0 | 0 (99.9 %) | 7 (100.5 %) | 57.6 / 27.6 |
| app-limited only, pending: 8 samples and 8 ms / 6 and 16 ms / 4 and 12 ms | 0 / 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 / 0 | 6 / 10 / 9 (100.5 / 100.5 / 100.6 %) | 61.2 / 55.2 / 69.4 |
| app-limited only; an unconfirmed verdict is dropped (the rising count restarts) | 0 | 0 (99.9 %) | 8 (100.5 %); seeds 41-200: 30 (127.9 %), one involuntary end (seed 90) against 26 (107.5 %), none | 46.4 / 20.3 |
| dropped, not for the peers of a shared uplink | 0 | 0 (99.9 %) | 8 (106.9 %); seeds 1-200: 35 (107.5 %), as the base | 46.4 / 20.8 |
| dropped, over 8 samples (shared-uplink peers checked) | 0 | 0 (99.9 %) | 8 (100.5 %) | 38.6 / 16.0 |

**Taken: row 10 (app-limited senders only, six samples, 12 ms, the verdict pending) with the shared-uplink scope of
row 13.** Rows 12-14 remove more of the client's cuts, but they move the server: on a dedicated server the peers'
controllers are app-limited at times too, and with their unconfirmed verdicts dropped the server's loss cuts rise 5 %
(congested/8, 60 s, seeds 1-100: 30.2 -> 31.6 a seed; congested/4: 13.7 -> 14.4) and the smallest snapshot budget
of a run falls under the base's 24 entities on 13 of 100 seeds (to 8 on two). With the verdict pending the server's
counts do not move at all (65.0 against 65.2 delay cuts, 30.2 loss cuts and no seed under 24 in both).

The one-way readings cut more, not less, where the sender is thin (rows 3-4). Not traced to the end: the readings
are exact to 2 ms where the round trips move in whole ticks, and the noise-adaptive threshold reads less noise from
them, so it would sit lower. bufferbloat+bulk
(0 of 100 over, worst 66.7 %) and lossy-fat-pipe (seed 69 `random_loss_kept`, as before) are the same in every row.
Decision:
1. **Wire 6: the acknowledgment frame carries `arrival`, a `u16` after the ack delay**: the low 16 bits of the
   receiver's millisecond clock when the frame's largest packet arrived (`AckFrame::arrival_ms`; 0 in a frame of
   older ranges, which gives no sample). Two bytes a frame, in every frame, not negotiated. It is the one-way delay
   measurement of RFC 6817 § 3.1 (the receiver's clock at arrival, returned to the sender; no synchronized clocks).
   It rides the one wire step of v0.7 (ADR-8858's wire 6); a wire 5 peer is refused at the handshake as for every
   other wire 6 change.
2. **`cc::OneWayDelay`** turns the stamps into samples: the stamp is unwrapped against the peer's clock as estimated
   from the previous stamp (half the 65.5 s span is the limit; 20 s without a stamp restarts the measurement), the
   send time comes off, and the first sample fixes the scale's origin, so a sample minus the 10 s windowed minimum is
   the queueing delay on the way out. A sample is taken where a round-trip sample is (the newest packet of a frame,
   first acknowledgment, ack-eliciting, never declared lost). `RoundSample` carries the round's smallest sample, the
   windowed minimum and the round's sample count.
3. **Round trips decide, exactly as before. An overuse verdict (threshold or gradient) of an app-limited sender
   stands only if its own packets confirm it**: the smallest one-way sample of the latest rounds that hold at least
   `ONE_WAY_CONFIRM_SAMPLES` (6) samples (at least two rounds, at most eight) must sit `ONE_WAY_CONFIRM_MS` (12 ms,
   half the threshold) over the minimum. App-limited is the controller's existing definition (nothing held back and
   less than half the target sent in the round). An unconfirmed verdict is counted
   (`RateController::unconfirmed_overuse`) and waits: the rising count stays, so the cut follows in the round the
   one-way delay confirms it. A sender that fills its target, a peer that sends no stamp, the trendline's verdict
   (one-way already) and the peers of a sender that splits a shared uplink (`set_shared_uplink`, ADR-8859) are
   untouched. The reasons for the scope are rows 9 and 12 of the table: checking every sender's verdicts costs the
   congested row its margin, and a listen host's peers are each app-limited against their own targets while together
   they fill the uplink (with them checked and dropped, listen-uplink/64 seed 90 lost a client).
4. Nothing else reads the one-way delay yet: the background window (the bulk scavenger), the shared uplink's host
   queue and the loss bound's queue evidence still read round trips.
Rejected, with the numbers above: candidate (b) (it blinds the detector where the queue is real: listen-uplink/64 over
on 30 of 40 seeds, 12 involuntary ends); the one-way delay as the reading, alone or as a minimum with the round trip,
with or without a sample span (the congested row goes from 0 to 46-144 seeds of 200 with a second over; the rpc bar
fails 3-8 of 104); a sample span on round trips with no wire change (46 of 200); the confirmation for every sender
(1 of 200, rpc 2 of 104); dropping an unconfirmed verdict, over six or eight samples (11 to 19 fewer client cuts a
seed, but the server's loss cuts move, above: a candidate once the rule can tell a client from a server that is
app-limited on its own bottleneck). Also rejected: the stamp only in frames that give a sample (a flag bit or a second frame
shape for two bytes); a wider or microsecond stamp (the connection's clock is milliseconds, and the read phase is
tens of milliseconds); reusing the negotiated receive timestamps (16 per frame, up to 80 bytes, off by default, and
relative to the frame's largest packet, so two frames share no clock); a lower threshold for one-way readings (a
retune of the server's loop against rows with no margin: its own lane).
Consequences, same binary (a scratch switch withholds the one-way samples), rule on against off; measured before
the shared-uplink scope was added, which no dedicated run has: `rpc_p95_with_bulk` 0 of seeds 1-1000 over in both
(mean ratio 1.027 / 1.025; control p95 138.7 / 138.8 ms, transfer p95 141.8 / 141.7 ms); a client's delay cuts on
congested+bulk 86.5 -> 58.7 per seed (4 clients, 60 s) and its mean target 43.6 -> 49.8 kB/s; the server's cuts
unchanged (36.8 delay, 13.6 loss). congested/4 seeds 1-200: 0 with a second over in both (worst 99.9 %), client cuts
17.6 -> 13.8, client target 83.7 -> 95.0 kB/s, server cuts 14.9 delay and 13.7 loss in both. At 8 clients, 60 s:
congested seeds 1-100: 25 with a second over against 26 (worst 105.6 %); congested+bulk: 37 against 38 (worst
106.9 %); `rpc_p95_with_bulk` 0 of seeds 1-200 over in both, client cuts 174.4 -> 115.4. 23 more profiles, seeds
1-20: clean, good-wifi, hostile, high-rtt, rtt-step, nat-rebind, cgnat, long-outage, flappy, bufferbloat,
downstream-loss, asym-bufferbloat, wifi-to-cell, listen-uplink, lossy-fat-pipe, rtt-extreme, mtu-1280, mtu-blackhole
and transatlantic keep every bar and every failing-bar count; bad-wifi client cuts 272 -> 246, mobile-4g 172 -> 143
and mixed 90 -> 80 with the same bars (mixed's wall-clock `tick_p99` fails 11 against 15 of 20); clock-drift
16.6 -> 12.8 with the same bars (a peer clock that runs fast only loses the check; one that runs slow reads 0 for a
queue that grows slower than the drift, 5 ms/s at the profile's 0.5 %). Listen servers, the committed code (rule
and scope) with the rule on against off: listen-uplink/64 seeds 1-200 keep every count (35 seeds with a second over
the host's uplink, worst 107.5 %, `no_wedged_client` 10, `staleness_p99` 2, no involuntary end; host delay cuts
160.9 against 161.0), client cuts 36.3 -> 26.3; congested/8 on a listen server, seeds 1-40: 3 over in both.
The stamp itself, same binary with the two bytes left out of the frame and the rule off: listen-uplink/64 seeds
1-200: 32 seeds over (worst 109.3 %, `staleness_p99` 5) against 35 (107.5 %, 2) with it; the suite's pinned seed 3
reads 96.1 % without the stamp and 100.1 % with it; congested/8 on a listen server: 5 over against 3; congested/4
seeds 1-200: 0 over in both (99.7 % against 99.9 %).
Host-visible API (release fragment v0.1.28-v07-net-delay-detector, Upgrade): `ack::AckFrame::arrival_ms` and
`cc::RoundSample::{delay_samples, round_min_one_way_ms, min_one_way_ms}` (new public fields: struct literals);
new `ack::ARRIVAL_STAMP_BYTES`, `cc::{OneWayDelay, ONE_WAY_WINDOW_MS, ONE_WAY_RESTART_MS, ONE_WAY_CONFIRM_MS,
ONE_WAY_CONFIRM_SAMPLES}`, `cc::RateController::unconfirmed_overuse`. Wire: every acknowledgment frame is two bytes
longer (wire 6). Spec 120 § 4.1 item 2 and § 4.2 items 1-2 Built notes; book/user-guide/networking.md; provenance row.
Known issues: (i) two thirds of the client's cuts remain (58.7 per seed). They were not traced one by one; the rule
leaves a verdict standing in a round the client was not app-limited in (a command or a re-bundled input burst) and
when six one-way samples in a row sat 12 ms over the minimum (a few percent of readings at this path's read phase
and jitter, and a pending verdict is checked again every round). Removing them needs the detector to read over
enough samples, which the congested rows do not survive today (table, rows 5-7), or a dropped verdict, which the
server's loss cuts do not (rows 12-14): the controller needs headroom that does not lean on early noise cuts first.
(ii) A peer that stamps wrong arrivals can keep its own sender's app-limited verdicts unconfirmed; the loss bound
and every saturating round are not affected, and the traffic it shapes is the traffic toward itself.
(iii) The stamp's two bytes cost three existing tests something. The lockstep shape's acknowledgment frame
(`a_lockstep_link_carries_a_small_ack_frame_for_the_whole_run`) goes from a mean of 7.51 to 9.51 bytes; its bound of
9.0 now reads "9.0 plus the stamp" (the lead rules on it; sending the ack delay in whole milliseconds would give one
byte back). The default wire's pin (`pmtud::probing_off_by_default_leaves_the_clean_wire_byte_identical`) is retaken:
the same 1,388 + 1,282 datagrams. Two seeded tests are red at this lane's head and were left untouched for a ruling:
`pmtud_robust::random_loss_never_drops_the_size` seed 21 (its last instant now falls while one lost large packet has
the size in doubt, when `path_mtu` reports the base size: search complete, no black hole, full-size data in every
second) and `rate_control::listen_uplink_at_64_clients_drops_nobody_and_stays_fresh` (the pinned seed 3 of
KI-NT-031's row: one second at 100.07 % of the host's uplink, with the rule on or off).
(iv) Not done in this lane: the listen-uplink overshoot (KI-NT-031, plan N-20) and wire-byte accounting
(KI-NT-032). Measured for N-20 on this base, listen-uplink/64, 20 s, seeds 1-200, with or without this change: 35
seeds have a second over the host's uplink; the worst second is at most 100.5 % on 21 of them, 100.5-101.0 % on 11,
and over 101 % on 3 (seed 177: 107.5 %, seed 36: 106.9 %, seed 90: 106.5 %); `no_wedged_client` fails on 10 seeds.
No fix was attempted.

## ADR-10097: A listen server's uplink is counted on the wire, keeps its measured rate, asks again with a probe and takes its first target from the peers it starves; `path_mtu` is the confirmed size (KI-NT-031, KI-NT-032; amends spec 120 § 4.2 item 8 and § 4.3, ADR-8490, ADR-8733, ADR-10050)
Date: 2026-11-20   Status: proposed
Context: second part of lane v07-net-delay-detector, on ADR-10050's head fab4455f4. The lead's ruling on ADR-10050's
known issue (iii): restore the moved bound of `a_lockstep_link_carries_a_small_ack_frame_for_the_whole_run` unless a
recorded behaviour change justifies it, and make the two red seeded tests green by fixing the code. Then the brief's
listen-uplink items: KI-NT-031 (seconds over the host's uplink, plan N-20), the `SharedUplink` start-up follow-up and
KI-NT-032 (the controller counts packet bodies). Measured on the build server as in ADR-10050: one diag binary per code state,
one environment switch per variant (a scratch overlay, never committed), so "before" is the same binary with this
ADR's changes switched off, and it reproduces ADR-10050's numbers (listen-uplink/64, 20 s, seeds 1-200: 35 seeds with a
second over the uplink, worst 107.5 %). Rows: listen-uplink/64 20 s and 60 s, listen-uplink/32 60 s,
listen-uplink/128 30 s, congested/8, good-wifi/8, mixed/32 and bad-wifi/32 on a listen server, 60 s; the dedicated
rows of ADR-10050.
Decision:
(1) KI-NT-032, by measurement: a link that peers share is counted on the wire; a peer's own controller keeps steering
packet bodies. Counting bytes on the wire inside each peer's controller (targets, delivery rates, the pacer's buckets,
the send allowance less the packets' header rate) was built first and measured against bodies in one binary: congested/8
60 s, seeds 1-400: 162 seeds with a second over the client's link against 117 (40.5 % against 29.3 %); congested/16
60 s, seeds 1-60: 43 against 34; congested/4 20 s, seeds 1-1000: 2 against 0; the smallest snapshot budget on
congested/8 fell from 24 to 19 entities; three window tests of `connection` failed. The headers are a cost per packet
that a rate cut does not shrink (a game sends a packet per tick at any rate), so a controller that scales the whole wire
rate cuts the payload deeper and climbs back steeper than one that scales the bodies; ADR-8301 measured the same
double count. What the wire matters for is a link several peers share or an operator states a rate for. `cc::WireShare`
keeps a tally of a connection's ack-eliciting packets, each weighted by its age (one second of memory): bytes on the wire
(body, endpoint header, 28 bytes of IP and UDP headers, `cc::DATAGRAM_OVERHEAD_BYTES`) per body byte,
`Connection::wire_bytes_per_body_byte`. The server feeds each peer's target and delivery rate times that figure to the
`SharedUplink` and divides the share that comes back by it before it caps the peer. The aggregate, the shares and
`ServerConfig::uplink_bytes_per_second` are now rates on the wire. A dedicated server without a shared uplink sends the
same bytes as before (the default wire's pin did not move).
(2) KI-NT-031: with a crowd (`cc::UPLINK_CROWD_PEERS` = 16 delivering peers) the shared uplink keeps what it measured.
Traced on the three seeds over 105 % and on the seeds under 101 %:
(a) A hold or a cut read the sum of the peers' delivery rates of one update, which drops with every peer that leaves
in it; a crowd reads the mean of 250 ms (`UPLINK_CARRIED_MS`).
(b) Every hold set the estimate to what the peers delivered right then. Peers that leave part of their shares unused
deliver less than the aggregate without the uplink being any slower, and each hold at 97 % of that took the aggregate
down a step: to a quarter of the uplink in 14 s on seed 177. With a crowd the estimate only rises in a hold; a cut
still replaces it.
(c) After 15 s the estimate was dropped and the aggregate grew 8 % a second until a queue stood at the host: the
seconds at up to 101 % every 15 s of a full listen server (25 of 200 seeds at 20 s with every other change of this
ADR in). A crowd asks the uplink again with a probe instead: 12.5 % over the target for 150 ms
(`UPLINK_PROBE_GAIN`, `UPLINK_PROBE_MS`; gain times duration is under the 3 % of headroom, so no whole second with a
probe in it carries more than the uplink does), then 400 ms of watching the median queueing delay of the delivering
peers. A rise of 5 ms is the uplink's rate met: the estimate stands for another 15 s. No rise while the peers delivered
at least 2 % over the estimate during the probe is room: the estimate rises to what they delivered (at most the 12.5 %)
and the next probe follows after a second. A probe the peers did not take says nothing. Two verdicts were measured and
dropped on the way: a fixed 6 % for every probe without a queue walked the estimate over the uplink when the peers left
part of their shares unused (seed 7: a second at 101.1 %; listen-uplink/64 60 s: 4 of 40 seeds over), and reading the
peak of the 250 ms mean against the estimate can never show room at a 150 ms probe unless the peers fill their shares
exactly (the delivery during the probe is the peak mean with the time before the probe taken out).
(d) The start. On seeds 36, 90 and 177 (and seed 36 at 60 s: 18 s without a target, seven clients with nothing
delivered, three involuntary ends in the first build of this ADR) the host offered a quarter more than its uplink while
the 64 clients joined and the aggregate had no target: the median peer read no queue (it joined over the standing queue,
so its minimum round trip sits on top of it) and no loss. The loss is real but not spread: a server flushes its peers
in one burst per tick in a fixed order, a full drop-tail queue takes the burst's head and drops its tail, and the peers
served last lose every packet while the others lose none. Those peers still talk. `Connection::unanswered_ms` is how
long a connection has sent ack-eliciting packets without a new one acknowledged while its peer's packets still arrive
(0 when nothing was heard for a second: that is an outage); four peers over a second of it (`UPLINK_STARVED_MS`,
`UPLINK_STARVED_PEERS`) among a crowd that delivers give an aggregate without a target its first one, 85 % of what the
crowd delivers. A second start rule reads spread drops: the median delivering peer's loss at 10 % for four updates
(`cc::host_loss`, `UPLINK_LOSS_ROUNDS`). It is covered by the fluid-model unit tests only: it fired on no soak row
(switching it off changes no row), because the soak's drops are never spread.
(e) Under a crowd the aggregate keeps its earlier form (a hold at what the peers deliver right now, the estimate
dropped after 15 s, no probe, no start rule). Measured with the crowd rules at every size (on the millisecond
variant's binary): good-wifi/8 on a listen server delivers 392 kbit/s per client instead of 149 (dedicated: 429), but
congested/8 on a listen server has a second
over a client's link on 24 of 40 seeds, worst 126.2 %, against 6 of 40, worst 108.2 %: half of eight peers seeing a
queue at once is their own links, the aggregate engages for no reason, and once it no longer ratchets down it hands a
peer whose own target ran ahead more than that peer's link carries. That needs the host's queue told apart from the
peers' own first (the follow-up below), so the small server is left as it was.
(3) `LinkStats::path_mtu` and `Connection::path_mtu` report the size path MTU discovery has confirmed. They read the
size data uses at that instant, which is the base size for about a round trip whenever a lost full-size packet has the
size in doubt: at 3 % loss a connection is in that state at a given instant on 6 of 100 seeds on wire 5 and 10 of 100
with the arrival stamp, with the confirmed size unchanged, no black hole and full-size data in every second, and
`pmtud_robust::random_loss_never_drops_the_size` read it at one such instant on seed 21. A doubt does not change the
path MTU; only a black hole does. `max_unreliable_bytes` and the packets themselves still follow the size in use.
(4) The moved bound, for the lead's ruling. `a_lockstep_link_carries_a_small_ack_frame_for_the_whole_run` keeps
ADR-10050's form, "9.0 bytes plus the two of the arrival stamp" (measured 9.51 against 7.51 before the stamp): the
behaviour change that moves it is ADR-10050's stamp, two bytes in every frame by design. The way to give a byte back
was built and measured, and is not in: the ack delay in whole milliseconds (RFC 9000 § 18.2 leaves the unit to the
endpoint; a connection's clock is in milliseconds, so nothing is lost) takes the frame to 8.51 bytes and lets the bound
read 9.0 again. But it changes which packets exist, and with it both seeded tests the lead asked green went red on
pre-existing defects, in the full pristine suite (2,425 passed, these 2 failed): `pmtud_robust::random_loss_never_drops_the_size`
seed 23 met a false black hole (`path_mtu 1200 Error probes 88/3 black holes 1`; the loss-burst rule under 3 % random
loss), and `rate_control::listen_uplink_at_64_clients_drops_nobody_and_stays_fresh` read 9 ticks of worst-client
staleness on seed 3 against its 8 (in one binary: the base's uplink rules with only the unit changed read 9 as well,
this ADR's rules with the base's unit read 8). Commit 2403d29df on the lane branch is that variant, whole. It belongs
with fixes for those two defects, not before them.
Rejected, with numbers. (i) Wire bytes inside each peer's controller: (1). (ii) Serving a shared uplink's peers from a
different first peer every flush, to spread the tail drops: listen-uplink/64 20 s has no second over the uplink then,
but each client gets 90 kbit/s instead of 265 and `staleness_p99` fails on 147 of 200 seeds (listen-uplink/32: 115
against 401 kbit/s). A peer's place in the burst is up to 25 ms of serialization at 64 peers, and a place that moves
reads as queueing delay on every peer (815 delay cuts a seed against 168). (iii) The host's queue only when 60 % or
75 % of the delivering peers see it: 41 and 199 of 200 seeds over on listen-uplink/64 (peers that joined over the queue
never see it). (iv) The median over the delivering peers only (a fresh peer votes neither way): 8 seeds over instead of
2, `staleness_p99` fails on 8. (v) No doubt for a lost large packet when a later packet of its size was acknowledged
(path MTU): the pinned seed still ended in a doubt (4 of 100 seeds did). (vi) The ack delay in milliseconds: (4).
Measured, this ADR against the same binary with it switched off (seeds with a whole second over a bottleneck's rate,
worst second; `no_wedged_client` and `involuntary_disconnects` are gating bars):

| Row | Seeds | Before | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| listen-uplink/64, 20 s | 1-200 | 35 over (107.5 %); `no_wedged_client` fails on 10, `staleness_p99` on 2 | 2 over (seeds 30 and 150: 101.1 %, 100.7 %); no other bar fails |
| listen-uplink/64, 20 s | 201-400 | 38 over (124.0 %); `no_wedged_client` 10, `staleness_p99` 6, `involuntary_disconnects` 1 | 5 over (seed 386: 103.8 %, the others at most 101.1 %); `staleness_p99` 1; no other bar fails |
| listen-uplink/64, 60 s | 1-40 | 13 over (113.7 %); `no_wedged_client` 1 | 0 over (100.0 %); no bar fails |
| listen-uplink/64, 60 s | 41-80 | 15 over (108.1 %); `no_wedged_client` 1 | 1 over (seed 53, under 100.05 %); no other bar fails |
| listen-uplink/32, 60 s | 1-40 | 0 over (74.1 %); 394 kbit/s per client | 0 over (74.1 %); 401 kbit/s |
| listen-uplink/128, 30 s | 1-16 | 5 over (101.7 %); `no_wedged_client` 2, `staleness_p99` 11; 91 kbit/s per client | 1 over (100.8 %); `no_wedged_client` 0, `staleness_p99` 14 (156 kbit/s of uplink per client cannot keep 4 ticks either way); 96 kbit/s |
| worst client's staleness p99 over 8 ticks, listen-uplink/64 20 s | 1-400 | 1-200: 57 seeds (over 16 ticks: 21) | 30 of 1-200 (over 16: 6); 30 of 201-400 (over 16: 8) |
| mixed/32 on a listen server, 60 s | 1-20 | 16 over (107.0 %); 212 kbit/s; `no_wedged_client` fails on 4 | 19 over (109.1 %, the clients' own congested links); 338 kbit/s; `no_wedged_client` passes on all |
| bad-wifi/32 on a listen server, 60 s | 1-20 | 0 over; 316 kbit/s | 0 over; 334 kbit/s |
| congested/8 on a listen server, 60 s (under a crowd) | 1-40 | 3 over (113.1 %); 72 kbit/s | 3 over (114.7 %); 71 kbit/s |
| good-wifi/8 on a listen server, 60 s (under a crowd) | 1-40 | 0 over; 148 kbit/s | 0 over; 141 kbit/s (the earlier form now counts headers: 4.5 % less) |
| congested/4 20 s; congested/8 60 s | 1-200; 1-100 | 0 over (99.9 %); 25 over (105.6 %) | the same to the digit (a dedicated server sends the same bytes) |

Consequences: spec 120 § 4.2 item 8 and § 4.3 Built notes; book/user-guide/networking.md, book/agents/net.md;
provenance row; release fragment v0.1.28-v07-net-delay-detector (Upgrade lists the public items). No wire change.
KI-NT-032 is closed for the shared uplink and narrowed to the per-peer controller, where bodies are the measured
choice. KI-NT-031, for the lead's ruling (plan N-20): listen-uplink/64 has a whole second over the host's uplink on 7
of 400 seeds at 20 s (six of them at most 101.1 %, one at 103.8 %; 73 of 400 before, worst 124.0 %) and on 1 of 80 at
60 s (under 100.05 %; 28 of 80 before, worst 113.7 %). The seconds that remain are a rejoin on top of an aggregate that
does not limit: on seed 150 the estimate was read at 2.65 MB/s on a 2.5 MB/s uplink while the clients joined (the
delivery rates of a join wave bunch), the target stood at 102.9 % of the uplink, the clients' own demand sat at 98 %,
and eight clients rejoined in the second that went to 100.7 %. A hold never lowers a crowd's estimate (2 (b)), so a
reading that high stays until a cut. On seed 3 the first reading was 3.4 % low. The estimate is a mean of delivery
rates taken as a queue builds, good to a few percent either way, which is all of the headroom: the next step is a
better reading of the uplink's rate at saturation, not a constant. The bar was not moved.
Known issues: (i) A listen server under 16 delivering peers still throttles itself on its clients' own queues
(good-wifi/8: 141 kbit/s per client where a dedicated server delivers 429; 148 before, the earlier form now counts
headers); the crowd rules fix that and break congested/8 (2 (e)). The follow-up is a host-queue signal that tells a queue all peers share from queues of their own
(their correlation in time, RFC 8382), then the crowd rules at every size. (ii) A crowd's estimate is as good as the
delivery rates it was read from (3.4 % low to 6 % high on the traced seeds); one read low rises only by probes the
peers take (they must deliver 85 % of the aggregate for a probe to start), one read high falls only at a cut. (iii) The
start rule needs four starved peers and a crowd: a server that starves one to three peers of a crowd waits for the
queue signal, as before. A connection that stopped sending with its last packet unacknowledged also reads as unanswered
while its peer talks; a server sends every tick, so the soak never meets it. (iv) `WireShare` counts 28 bytes per
datagram; an IPv6 path costs 20 more, which is not counted. (v) The median-loss start rule has no soak row behind it
(2 (d)). (vi) Two defects the millisecond unit exposed and this ADR does not fix: path MTU discovery can read 3 % random
loss as a black hole (one seed of three with that wire; none of 200 runs on the wires before it), and the worst client
of a full listen server reads over 8 ticks of staleness p99 on 30 of 200 seeds (57 before), so the pinned seed 3 of the
listen test passes with one tick to spare (8 against 8) and has no margin.

## ADR-10157: Random loss on a thin sender: a loss cut without a queue needs two filled rounds, a delivery reading of 32 packets and fresh loss, and its probe is a sequential test against the path's long-run loss
Date: 2026-11-20   Status: proposed
Context: ADR-10096 (lane v07-net-staleness-rtt) left the not-gating soak bar `random_loss_kept` red on
`lossy-fat-pipe/8` at 2 of 5 seeds, green on its base, cause not found. Reproduced (the build server, release, 60 virtual
seconds, smallest snapshot budget of 140 entities, 126 needed): base 775a48bd9 reads 139 at seeds 1592590337, 1, 2, 3
and 4; ADR-10096's head 62abce21f reads 44, 139, 139, 139 and 114. Over the gate's seed and seeds 1 to 364 the base is
red at 4 seeds (146, 158, 248, 307: 84, 58, 9 and 100 entities) and the head at 36. So it is not a staleness or
retransmit rule of ADR-10096: it is a defect of the rate controller's loss bound (`regia_net::cc`, spec 120 § 4.2
item 3) that the base already had, which the clients' shifted timing triggers nine times as often. Traced round by
round, it has two triggers and one amplifier:
(1) A round that holds one tick of sends more than its length. The game sends per 33 ms tick and a feedback round
ends on an acknowledgment at least `max(srtt, 50 ms)` after it began. The server's target for this game sits at the
app-limited bound, 1.5x the delivered rate (77 kB/s; the game sends 52 kB/s, two thirds of it). A round that ends
1 ms after a tick holds three ticks' snapshots in 68 ms: 77 kB/s for that round, "saturating" (80 % of the target).
The loss memory of a sender with five packets a round reads 10 % or more every few seconds on a path that loses 5 %
(seed 36, client 1 at 5,568 ms: 11.9 %), so that round was a loss cut to its own delivery rate (51 kB/s).
(2) The first round of a join. The join's 53 kB burst leaves before the first acknowledgment starts the first round,
30 of its packets are lost in the path's 64 KiB buffer, and the round ends 68 ms later with 4 packets acknowledged: a
"delivery rate" of 50 kB/s under a start target of 256 kB/s, and a loss cut to it. On the base 21 acknowledgments fell
into the same round (delivery over the target, no cut); on the head the acknowledgments' phase moved 17 of them into
the next round. That is the gate seed's case, and by luck of the phase the base's 4 red seeds.
(3) The amplifier. After either cut the game does fill its target, so every later 10 % reading cuts again, each to
ONE round's delivery (two packets lost of five: a 40 % cut), and also the memory of the same loss cuts a second time
when its probe ends, with no packet lost in between. The probe that should give a cut for random loss back compared
the loss of about 20 packets after the cut with HALF THE TRIGGER'S reading. The trigger is the highest of many
readings, so on a 5 % path it reads 10 to 13 % and half of it is the path's own loss: the probe ruled "the loss
followed the rate" for 64 % of such cuts (at least two losses in 25 packets are needed), the cut stood, loss of 2 %
or more held the target for good, and the target went 77 -> 51 -> 26 -> 8 -> 7 kB/s (14 of 140 entities) within five
seconds.
Decision: in `RateController::on_round` (crates/regia_net/src/cc.rs only; no wire, format or settings change):
(a) A round fills its target only when the round before did too (`prev_saturating`): for the loss cut without a queue
and for the startup's "filled" rounds (unless the pacer held data back, which still counts by itself). A round with
an extra tick ends just after a tick, so the next begins just after one and holds none: no two rounds in a row read
high. A connection's first round, or a burst's after an idle stretch, acknowledges packets of no filled round either.
A real saturating sender is cut one round later than before.
(b) Without a queue the cut reads the delivery rate over at least 32 resolved packets of the delivery window
(`LOSS_EVIDENCE_PACKETS`), not over the round. A round of 32 packets or more reads as before; a queue's cut keeps the
round's reading.
(c) One loss event, one cut: another loss cut without a queue needs 10 % loss since the latest one took effect
(`loss_stale`, the part of the loss memory from before it, decays with the memory and is taken off).
(d) The probe compares the loss after the cut with what the path showed before it, unselected: the long-run loss
(`LOSS_LONG_DECAY` 0.98 per round, restarted when a loss cut without a queue takes effect), unless the trigger's count
is over what that loss explains by more than 3 standard deviations of the loss memory's count (`LOSS_SPIKE_SIGMAS`;
variance `n p (1 - p) / (1 + LOSS_DECAY)`), in which case the loss is new and the trigger's reading is the reference
as before. The verdict is Wald's sequential probability ratio test between "the loss stayed at the reference" and "it
fell to a quarter of it" (`LOSS_PROBE_FALLEN`; indifferent at about half the reference, the former rule's line), ruled
at a log-likelihood ratio of `ln 19` either way (5 % error, `LOSS_PROBE_CONFIDENCE`), not before the former minimum
(6 rounds, 2 round trips, 20 packets); after 24 rounds without a ruling it falls back on the comparison with half the
reference.
(e) A "random" verdict covers the path's long-run loss since the probe's cut, not any loss: for the 10 s hold, loss
without a queue is left to redundancy unless the loss since the cut is over that level by 3 standard deviations (a
policer the restored rate ran into, a path that got worse), and it keeps an earlier cut of the same episode owed
(`loss_cut`), so item 5 takes the target back to the episode's pre-cut rate: a probe that ruled wrongly is undone by
the next one that rules "random".
Rejected: judging "saturating" over the 1 s delivery window (tried first: a sender whose rate had just jumped lost 14
of 23 packets per round for three rounds before the window agreed, and `growth_stops_under_the_bottleneck_estimate`
offered 183 kB in a second through a 100 kB/s link); excusing loss at the path's level after a "the loss followed"
verdict too (the loss such a cut leaves can be congestion's own, and item 5 would give the cut back; not measured); a
longer loss memory (it slows every loss decision of every thin sender).
Numbers (the build server, release; the lane report has the per-seed tables). `lossy-fat-pipe/8`, 60 s, the gate's seed and
seeds 1 to 364: base 4 red, head 36 red, fixed 0 red (139 of 140 entities at every seed). `lossy-fat-pipe/32`, the
gate's seed and seeds 1 to 64: 136 of 140 at every seed. The gate plan (61 runs) against ADR-10096's after-run: the
same verdict line (2 failed gating bars, both the base's `reconnect_within_grace` on `asym-bufferbloat`), no gating
bar changed, `random_loss_kept` green; the smallest budgets of other lossy rows rise (`mobile-4g/8` 39 -> 67,
`mobile-4g/32` 8 -> 63, `downstream-loss/32` 83 -> 98 of 140); `tick_p99`, a wall-clock bar, read red on the three
`mixed` rows of this run on a host at load 170 to 190 (green on ADR-10096's quiet-host run; owed a quiet-host
reading). ADR-10096's gains stay: over the 16 rows of its seed sweep (`lossy-fat-pipe`, `congested`,
`congested+bulk`, `rtt-extreme`, `high-rtt`, `asym-bufferbloat`, `wifi-to-cell`, `rtt-step` at 8 and 32 clients) at
its 5 seeds, server ticks without the client's input in time read 136, 119, 141, 128 and 125 (head: 136, 120, 142,
128, 120; base 475 to 508) and corrected predictions 86, 73, 93, 85 and 79 (head: 86, 74, 94, 85, 75; base about
4,400); the staleness p99 of every row is unchanged. Moved, both ways, on rows this change touches through the rate
of lossy paths: over `bad-wifi`, `mobile-4g`, `downstream-loss`, `mixed` and `bufferbloat` at 8 and 32 clients and
the same 5 seeds, missed input ticks 964 -> 998 and corrections 859 -> 895 (+4 %; the bar is 2 % of ticks per client
and the worst client reads 0.5 %), while the smallest snapshot budgets rise (`mobile-4g/8` 20-46 -> 63-86,
`downstream-loss/8` from 24). The gating `involuntary_disconnects` (`protocol_error` on `asym-bufferbloat`, the
base's defect ADR-10096 lists) shows on 1 of the 130 rows on both sides, a different one: `asym-bufferbloat/8` at
seed 4 on the head, `asym-bufferbloat/32` at seed 3 with this change.
Tests (each fails on the head's cc.rs): `cc::tests::a_round_with_an_extra_tick_of_sends_is_not_a_saturating_sender`
(the traced rounds of seed 36 replayed: 81,058 -> 51,352 B/s before, no cut now);
`a_tick_quantized_game_under_its_target_is_never_cut_for_random_loss` (a seeded model of the transport's rounds, 30 Hz
game at 52 kB/s, 5 % loss, 32 seeds x 60 s: 3 to 21 cuts in every seed before, none now);
`a_thin_saturating_sender_keeps_its_rate_through_random_loss` (the same game filling a 52.4 kB/s project rate, 32
seeds x 120 s: mean target 42,737 B/s with every seed's lowest at 4 to 26 kB/s before; mean 51,363 and lowest 38,616
now); regia_net_soak `tests/rate_control.rs`
`lossy_fat_pipe_keeps_the_snapshot_budget_at_the_seeds_that_lost_it` (the gate row at the 6 seeds the head lost and
the 4 the base lost). No existing test changed. The 26 existing `cc` unit tests pass unchanged; two of their printed
readings moved: the 10 % congestive loss test is back at its rate 3,350 ms after the loss clears (3,200 before; the
bar is 5,000), and `a_round_without_a_sample_is_no_queue_evidence` reads a lowest target of 90,625 of 100,000 (75,000
before).
Consequences: no host-visible API change besides four new public constants in `regia_net::cc` (`LOSS_LONG_DECAY`,
`LOSS_SPIKE_SIGMAS`, `LOSS_PROBE_CONFIDENCE`, `LOSS_PROBE_FALLEN`). A saturating sender's loss cut without a queue
comes one round later (two filled rounds). A sender that does not hold data in the pacer leaves its startup's doubling
one round later. Known limits: (1) a thin sender that fills its target on a path with 5 % random loss is still
probed: a cut of about a tenth for 1.5 to 2.5 s at most every 12 s (lowest 74 % of its rate over 32 seeds x 120 s in
the unit model); the soak row's game is under its target, so it is never probed. (2) A probe that rules "the loss
followed the rate" wrongly (5 %) stands until the next 10 % reading starts a probe that rules "random". (3) At 17 %
random loss or more the app-limited bound (1.5x the delivered rate) itself sits within 80 % of the game's rate, so
such a game reads as saturating and is probed (unchanged). (4) A late acknowledgment in a later round does not take
its loss back from the controller's loss memory (the transport nets it within the round only); not changed here.
One existing test is red with this change and is NOT edited (for the lead's ruling):
crates/regia_net/tests/pmtud_robust.rs `random_loss_never_drops_the_size` at seed 22 of its seeds 21, 22 and 23
(`assert_eq!(s.path_mtu, 1280)`: 1200). `stats().path_mtu` is the size data uses now, which by ADR-8300 is the base
for a round trip after every lost large packet (until a confirmation probe answers), and the test reads it at the
60,000th millisecond. Its body over seeds 1 to 150 (3 % loss, scratch copy, release): the size in use is the base
9.94 % of the time on the head and 10.04 % with this change; the assertion fails at 15 of 150 seeds on the head (12,
51, 57, 72, ...) and at 21 of 150 with this change; seed 110 reads a black hole and 19 seconds have no large packet
on both. The rate controller moves the packet schedule (that test's sender is the thin, tick-sending kind this ADR is
about), so which seeds end inside a confirmation moves. Proposed for the ruling: assert the search state and the
black-hole count at the end and the size over the last second, not at one instant; and seed 110's black hole under
random loss is path MTU discovery's own defect.
Specs updated: spec 120 § 4.2 (Built note); book/user-guide/networking.md; one provenance row; release fragment
v0.1.28-v07-net-staleness-rtt-random-loss.

## ADR-10145: The soak splits snapshot staleness into stages; the rate controller drains a deep standing queue and ends a startup on the first round that shows one; the first burst follows the start rate (KI-NT-035; amends spec 120 § 4.2 items 2, 6 and 7, ADR-8490, ADR-8534)
Date: 2026-11-20   Status: accepted (lead 2026-11-20: R1 (d) through ADR-10156 and R2 accepted as a physics bound; applied by ADR-10200)
Context: lane v07-net-staleness-queueing, on integ-v07b 318ea3a6c with v07-net-delay-detector (b06deec36) merged.
`staleness_p99` fails on every queue-driven row of the gate plan since ADR-8592: congested/8 22 ticks (limit 8),
congested/8 on a listen server 20, congested+bulk/8 22, asym-bufferbloat/8 and /32 20 (limit 4), and the congested
members of mixed/32 and mixed/40 18 and 23. The brief: find where the ticks go, stage by stage, fix the dominant
stage, and where a row is bounded by its own queue write the physics with numbers for a bar ruling. No bar is moved
here. Every number below is from seeded virtual-time runs (`crates/regia_net_soak/tests/staleness_stages.rs`, 30 Hz
ticks; the base's numbers were the same to the sample on aarch64 macOS and x86_64 Linux).
Decision:
(1) The soak reports where staleness goes. The bar's sample is the client's tick estimate minus the tick of its newest
snapshot, every client frame. The impairment net now keeps a trace with every datagram (when its sender's socket took
it, what it waited in the bottleneck queues, its own transmission time, when it reached the receiver:
`impair::DatagramTrace`, virtual wire only), the server notes when it made each tick's snapshot, and each client traces
its newest snapshot to the datagram that carried it (of the datagrams the frame read, the first sent at or after the
tick was made). A sample then splits into seven stages that add up to it to the microsecond (`workload::STALENESS_STAGES`):
`sender_hold` (made to leaving the server's socket), `queue`, `serialize`, `path` (latency, jitter), `receiver_hold`
(socket to the frame that handed it over), `wait` (that frame to the sample: the snapshot interval and every snapshot
that did not arrive) and `estimate` (the bar's whole-tick count minus the true age: the tick label, rounding, and the
error of the client's tick estimate). Every run's `result.json` carries `measures.staleness_stages` (per limit group:
the mean stages of all samples and of the judged tail, the samples at or over the p99; the samples over the limit; and
`settled_p99_ticks`, the p99 of the samples 5 s or more after their connect), and `summary.md` has a table of the groups
over their limit. It is a report: no bar reads it.
(2) Where the ticks went at the base.
| Row (seed) | p99 | Samples over the limit | Tail: queue | serialize | path | wait | estimate | Settled p99 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| congested/8, 60 s (gate seed) | 22 | 1,371 of 29,205 | 13.67 | 0.93 | 0.59 | 0.34 | +6.91 | 3 |
| asym-bufferbloat/4, 30 s (7) | 20 | 6,089 of 6,416 | 29.88 | 0.06 | 0.18 | 3.93 | -13.98 | 20 |
`sender_hold` is 0.00 to 0.01 ticks everywhere (an unreliable message leaves in the poll after its send or expires a
tick later) and `receiver_hold` 0.2. congested is not a steady state: its settled p99 is 3 ticks. Each of its nine
joins (eight clients, one scripted rejoin) is one episode of about 2.4 s over the limit: the server sends the 16 KiB
world blob and full snapshots at the 256 KiB/s start rate into a 256 kbit/s downlink behind a 16 KiB buffer, 28.8 kB
in the first 134 ms round, so the buffer (512 ms, 15.4 ticks) is full before the first acknowledgment returns; the cut
then took the target to 0.85 of the delivery rate and held it while the queue stood (item 2), which empties a full
buffer at 15 % of the link's rate, 3.4 s. The dominant stage is the bottleneck queue, and what kept it was the
controller.
(3) A deep standing queue is drained (`cc::RateController`, `DRAIN_*`). When a delay-driven cut finds 100 ms of queue
or more (`DRAIN_QUEUE_MS`, four standing-queue thresholds: under it item 2's cut is unchanged), or such a queue stands
for two rounds while the sender fills its target (whichever signal cut the rate, or none: a loss cut leaves the target
at the delivery rate, which holds a full buffer full), the controller answers with a drain rate for a bounded time:
`1 - queue / 400 ms` of the bottleneck's delivery rate, between 0.25 (`DRAIN_GAIN_MIN`) and 0.85, for
`queue / (1 - gain)` plus a round, at most 1.5 s. The queue is read on the round's own smallest round trip, and on the
one-way delay of wire 6's arrival stamps when that is smaller (the way back is not this sender's to drain). A deeper
reading rescales a drain in force (the queue keeps growing for a round trip after the cut); a round whose packets met
under 12 ms of queue ends it; at its deadline a queue that fell but still stands is drained again, and one that stayed
at 80 % of its depth or more is not this sender's (cross traffic): no drain starts for 15 s. `target` itself is not
touched, so the sender returns to the rate the state machine holds (0.85 to 0.97 of the bottleneck) as soon as the
queue is gone, and a peer under a shared uplink's share is never drained by its own controller. An app-limited sender
is not drained. BBR drains its startup queue at 0.35 of the bottleneck rate until the flight fits the path (Cardwell
et al. 2016); here the gain follows the measured depth and the drain is bounded in time instead of by a flight size.
(4) A startup ends on the first round that shows a deep queue: the smallest sample of one round 100 ms over the
minimum (round trip, and one-way when stamped), where two rising rounds over 25 ms cost one more round of sending at
the start guess. This is the delay-increase exit of HyStart++ (RFC 9406 § 4.2) with this controller's thresholds. Its
drain starts at the lowest gain, because the reading is a round trip old and the sender has offered several times the
path's rate since. The peers of a shared uplink keep the two rounds (the queue they read may be the host's, ADR-8733).
(5) After a drain the slow-draining queue ADR-8534 read is gone: four clean rounds at the headroom no longer say the
congestion was transient, and giving the pre-cut rate back refills the buffer. A second deep queue within 15 s of a
drain that emptied the first confirms the bottleneck for 15 s (`BOTTLENECK_HOLD_MS`): a loss cut's recovery then ends
at the headroom. The first time the rest is still owed, so DO27 A4's transient loss recovers in full as before.
(6) The first burst follows the start rate: at most 300 ms of `rate_control.start_bytes_per_second`
(`cc::START_BURST_MS`, `RateConfig::start_burst_bytes`), never fewer than four packets. At the default 256 KiB/s that
is 78.6 kB, above the 64-packet initial window: the default first burst is what it was. Lowering the start rate used
to leave the 64-packet burst in front of it, so it could not protect a thin link; at 32 KiB/s the first burst is now
eight packets. No default changes in this ADR.
Amended in the lane's second session (2026-11-20): the start rate at its maximum, 256 KiB/s (the default), sets no
bound at all (`start_burst_bytes` answers `usize::MAX`), so the first burst is the initial window as the link is
configured. "The default first burst is what it was" held only for the default 64 packets a poll: a link with
`max_packets_per_poll: 512` has an initial window of 614 kB, the first session's bound cut it to 78.6 kB, and
`connection::unify_tests::a_capped_acknowledgment_train_never_skips_a_range` (240 kB of unreliable messages in its
first four polls) failed with `queued: Backpressure(108)`. Found by the full `regia_net` suite, which the first
session had not run to the end. A lowered start rate still bounds the first burst at 300 ms of itself.
Measured after (3)-(5), default start, congested/8, 60 s:
| Seed | p99 before | p99 after | Over the limit before | after | Tail queue after | Settled p99 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| gate (0x5EED0001) | 22 | 14 | 1,371 | 447 | 10.58 | 3 |
| 1, 2, 3 | not run | 14, 13, 14 | not run | 437, 431, 442 | 10.50, 9.50, 10.49 | 3, 3, 3 |
A join is now about 0.8 s over the limit (2.4 s before). asym-bufferbloat reads the same to the sample (no drain
starts: its queue is in the minimum round trip from the first packet). The bar still fails on the congested rows.
The gate plan (61 runs, light driver, the same numbers on x86_64 Linux and aarch64 macOS): congested/8 22 to 14,
congested+bulk/8 22 to 14, congested/8 on a listen server 20 to 15, the congested members of mixed/32 22 to 13 and of
mixed/40 21 to 12, asym-bufferbloat/8 and /32 19 and 19; no other row's staleness p99 moves, and the verdict is the
same (59 rows pass their gating bars; the two asym-bufferbloat rows keep their inherited `reconnect_within_grace`).
`rate_vs_bottleneck` is not worse: over seeds 1 to 40 of 60 s, seeds with a second over the link go 13 to 14 on
congested/8 (17 seconds to 16), 16 to 9 on congested+bulk/8 (20 to 13, worst 108.4 % to 104.7 %) and 3 to 0 on
congested/8 on a listen server; on the gate's own seed the one failing row moves from congested/8 to
congested+bulk/8.
Rulings asked, with the physics:
(R1) congested, and the congested members of mixed. With the default start the join fills the buffer in its first
round whatever the controller does afterwards: the world blob alone is 16.4 kB, 0.51 s of the link and the whole
buffer. A full 512 ms queue cannot empty in under 0.51 s with nothing sent, 0.63 s with the smallest snapshots (19 %
of the link) still going; the limit is crossed back at about 170 ms of queue, 0.42 s into the drain, plus 0.13 to
0.23 s to fill and detect. The bar's budget is 1 % of the row: 292 samples, 0.52 s per join. So no drain passes it;
only a start that does not fill the buffer does. Measured with `start_bytes_per_second = 32 KiB/s` (the essential
floor; decision (6) makes the first burst eight packets): congested/8 p99 7 ticks on all four seeds (252, 260, 254
and 255 samples over the limit), the bar passes. The price, time from the connect to the world blob, median/largest
ms at 256 KiB/s against 32 KiB/s: clean 0/0 against 208/208, good-wifi 0/16 against 192/208, transatlantic 0/0
against 336/336, high-rtt 16/784 against 240/1,008, congested 944/992 against 688/848 (the thin link joins
faster). Options: (a) make 32 KiB/s the default start rate (spec 120 § 4.2 item 6 says 256 KiB/s
and `cc::tests::ten_percent_loss_reaches_the_floor_in_three_seconds_and_recovers_in_five` pins 262,144, so it is the
owner's or lead's to rule, not this lane's); (b) keep 256 KiB/s and judge `staleness_p99` from 5 s after each connect,
as `rate_vs_bottleneck` already does (`RATE_SETTLE_MS`): the settled p99 is 3 ticks on every congested run above; (c)
carry the path's measured rate in the resume ticket so a rejoin starts under it (the rejoin only). This lane's
recommendation is (a): a join that costs a good link 0.2 to 0.35 s once is cheaper than one that costs a thin link
most of a second of stale state on every join, and a project can raise the rate again in `config/net.ron`.
Option (d), added by ADR-10156 in this lane's second session and now the lane's recommendation over (a): a first
flight (eight packets and the floor's rate until the path has answered once, then a startup from what the first
round delivered when the path fell behind the flight), built and off by default: 7 to 8 ticks at the default start
rate, the bar passes, a good link's join 0.10 to 0.11 s later.
(R2) asym-bufferbloat is bounded by a queue that is not the game's. Cross traffic offered at 4.4 Mbit/s keeps the
500,000-byte buffer of the 4 Mbit/s downlink full, so every snapshot that gets in waits 29.9 ticks (0.997 s; a second
of buffer is 30 ticks at 30 Hz, 60 at 60 Hz) whatever the sender does, and lowering its rate drains nothing. The bar
reads 20 and not 31 because the client's tick estimate halves a round trip whose delay is all on the way down: it runs
15 ticks behind the server, which no exchange of timestamps can see without a common clock. The limit of 4 ticks
cannot be met on this profile by any sender. Options: skip `staleness_p99` on it with the reason, give it the limit
its buffer implies, or judge what the sender adds (`sender_hold` 0.00, `wait` 0.6 mean).
Consequences: `regia_net::cc` gains `DRAIN_QUEUE_MS`, `DRAIN_HORIZON_MS`, `DRAIN_GAIN_MIN`, `DRAIN_DONE_MS`,
`DRAIN_MAX_MS`, `DRAIN_UNMOVED`, `DRAIN_RETRY_MS`, `START_BURST_MS`, `RateController::{draining, drains}` and
`RateConfig::start_burst_bytes`; `RateController::target_bytes_per_second` answers with the drain's rate while one
lasts. `regia_net_soak` gains `impair::DatagramTrace`, `ImpairedNet::{trace_reads, take_read_traces}`,
`workload::{StalenessStages, STALENESS_STAGES, STALENESS_SETTLE_MS, Knobs::start_bytes_per_second}`,
`ClientRecord::{staleness_stages, staleness_ticks_settled, world_after_connect_ms}` and
`report::{StageTicks, StalenessStageGroup, Measures::staleness_stages}` (additive in `result.json`: an older file
reads with an empty list). No wire change, no format change. Spec 120 § 4.2 has a Built note; `book/agents/net-soak.md`
and `book/user-guide/networking.md` describe the stages, the drain and the start rate. Known limits: (i) without
arrival stamps (a peer before wire 6) the drain reads round trips, so a queue on the way back starts one drain, which
does not move it and is then refused for 15 s; (ii) a peer whose clock runs slow reads a one-way delay of 0 (ADR-10050),
so no drain starts and the plain cut stands as before; (iii) a startup whose loss shows before its queue is cut by
the loss bound first and owes its start guess back once: a second fill before decision (5) confirms the bottleneck;
(iv) two deep queues within 15 s that were both transient stop a loss cut's recovery at the headroom until the
confirmation lapses; (v) a path whose latency steps up by 100 ms or more reads as a deep queue for the ten seconds the
minimum takes to follow: one drain of about 0.6 s at three quarters of the delivery rate, which does not move it and
is then refused (the gate's rtt-step rows: 31 more samples over the limit of 89,226 at 8 clients, 64 fewer of 356,736
at 32, p99 6 on both as before); (vi) the judged tail's `estimate` stage reads +2.7 ticks during a join's queue (+6.9 at the base,
+0.7 settled): the client's tick estimate runs ahead while the downlink queue stands. Feeding the clock filter the
minimum round trip instead of the smoothed one did not change it (444 against 447 samples over the limit); the cause
is not found and is left to the clock's own lane (v07-net-staleness-rtt works in `client.rs`).

## ADR-10156: The first flight: until a path has answered once its sender offers it the floor's rate and eight packets, and the startup begins at what the first round delivered (off by default; option (d) of ADR-10145's ruling R1; spec 120 § 4.2 items 6 and 7)
Date: 2026-11-20   Status: accepted (lead 2026-11-20: R1 (d); revised the same day: built and opt-in, off by default for v0.7, see "Revised ruling" below and ADR-10231)
Context: lane v07-net-staleness-queueing, second session, on ADR-10145's code. ADR-10145 drains the queue a join
leaves on a thin link, and `staleness_p99` on the congested rows still fails with the default start rate (13 to 14
ticks, limit 8): the server sends 28.8 kB (the 16.4 kB world blob and full snapshots) in the first 134 ms round into
a 256 kbit/s downlink behind a 16 KiB buffer, and no drain empties a full 512 ms buffer inside the bar's 0.52 s per
join. Its ruling R1 offered (a) a default start rate of 32 KiB/s (7 ticks; a join on a good link 0.2 to 0.34 s
later), (b) judging the bar from 5 s after each connect, (c) the path's rate in the resume ticket. (a) holds every
link to 32 KiB/s after the join too, until the startup has doubled its way back, to protect a link the sender could
have measured. What the sender lacks at its first packet is not a better guess; it is one answer from the path.
Decision:
(1) `RateConfig::first_flight` (off by default; not serialized, so `config/net.ron` and every recorded config read
and write as before). When it is on, a controller is in its first flight until a feedback round has acknowledged
one of its packets (`RateController::first_flight()`; a round that acknowledged nothing is no answer): the rate in force is the smaller of the target and
`RateConfig::first_flight_bytes_per_second()`, the essential floor (32 KiB/s down, 16 KiB/s up; never over the start
rate), which is what the transport sends blind in any state, and the connection's first burst is 300 ms of it
(`START_BURST_MS`): 9,830 bytes, eight 1,200-byte packets, toward a client. RFC 6928 allows a sender ten segments
before the first acknowledgment and RFC 9002 § 7.2 ten datagrams (14,720 bytes); the engine's default first burst is
the 64-packet initial window (ADR-7995), 77 kB.
(2) The first round measures the path, and a round sent at the floor's rate can say one thing: whether the path fell
behind even that. What the flight sent, less what its last round trip cannot have acknowledged yet (1.25 times the
rate in force over the minimum round trip plus the 25 ms queue threshold), was due. If the sender filled the round
(the pacer held data back, or it sent 80 % of the rate in force) and the path acknowledged under three quarters of
what was due (`FIRST_FLIGHT_BEHIND`), the path is slower than the flight: the startup's target becomes the delivery
rate of that round, never under the first flight's rate and never over the start rate. BBR starts the same way, from
the delivery rate of its initial window (Cardwell et al. 2016); the gain is 1, because the first burst still stands
in a thin link's queue when the round ends. The soak's 256 kbit/s link acknowledges under half of what is due. A
path that kept up with the flight (a fat link, with or without random loss: it acknowledges all but its losses) has
shown no limit: the start rate stands, without the doubling a round at the floor's rate would have earned. A first
round the sender did not fill says nothing either, so a connection with little to send behaves as before from its
second round on.
(3) Every later round is the startup's own: it doubles while the path keeps up, ends on ADR-10145's deep queue, and
a queue it leaves is drained.
Measured (seeded virtual time, `crates/regia_net_soak/tests/staleness_stages.rs`
`a_first_flight_keeps_congested_under_its_staleness_limit_at_the_default_start_rate`, the knob
`workload::Knobs::first_flight`; the same numbers on aarch64 macOS and x86_64 Linux), congested/8, 60 s, start rate
256 KiB/s:
| Seed | p99 off | p99 on | Over the limit off | on (the bar's budget is 292) | Settled p99 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| gate (0x5EED0001) | 14 | 7 | 447 | 262 | 3 |
| 1, 2, 3 | 14, 13, 14 | 7, 8, 8 | 437, 431, 442 | 263, 267, 273 | 3, 3, 3 |
`staleness_p99` passes on all four seeds with no end and no wedged client. Three variants of (2) were measured and
dropped: the start rate back at once after the first round, whatever it showed, reads 10 ticks (354 to 368 samples
over the limit); twice the delivery rate reads 10 ticks (340 to 350); and the delivery rate after every filled first
round, behind or not, reads the same 7 to 8 ticks but holds a path that kept up to what the floor-rate flight itself
carried (a good link's join 144 ms instead of 112, 304 instead of 272 across the Atlantic).
The price is the join's world blob on a good link: its tail waits for the first round. Time from the connect to the
world blob, median/largest ms, by default, with a first flight, and with ADR-10145's 32 KiB/s start (option (a)):
| Profile (8 clients, 30 s, seed 7) | Default | First flight | Start 32 KiB/s |
|---|---|---|---|
| clean | 0/0 | 112/112 | 208/208 |
| good-wifi | 0/16 | 96/112 | 192/208 |
| transatlantic | 0/0 | 272/288 | 336/336 |
| high-rtt | 16/784 | 240/1,008 | 240/1,008 |
| congested | 944/992 | 688/848 | 688/848 |
The gate plan with the setting on by default (61 runs through the light driver on x86_64 Linux: the pushed code with
only `RateConfig::default().first_flight` flipped in a scratch tree, against the same driver's run of the pushed
code): `staleness_p99` fails on 11 rows instead of 15. congested/8 14 to 7, congested+bulk/8 14 to 7, the congested
members of mixed/32 13 to 7 and of mixed/40 12 to 6 now pass. congested/8 on a listen server reads 11 (15 off) and
still fails: its peers keep the two-round startup exit (ADR-8733). The ten other rows are the path's and the cross
traffic's (high-rtt, rtt-step, rtt-extreme, wifi-to-cell, asym-bufferbloat at 8 and 32) and read the same. No row's
p99 rises, and 59 rows pass their gating bars, as before. Three things move the other way and belong to the ruling:
(A) `random_loss_kept` (not gating) fails on lossy-fat-pipe/8 and /32 with `the snapshot budget fell to 80 of 140
entities`. The bar reads the smallest allowance toward any connected client after 5 s, and the profile's scripted
rejoin flies its first flight then: for that round the allowance is the floor's rate, which carries 80 entities. It
is the flight's own rate, not a loss cut (`a_first_flight_dips_the_snapshot_budget_to_the_floor_and_no_further`: 139
and 136 entities with the setting off, 80 with it on, the floor's budget is 80). With the default on, the bar would
have to read from after each connect's first round, as `rate_vs_bottleneck` reads from 5 s after each connect.
(B) The groups with a limit of 4 ticks keep their p99 and gain samples over the limit where many clients join at
once: mixed/32 128 to 157, mixed/40 179 to 200, bufferbloat/32 20 to 31, lossy-fat-pipe/8 0 to 8 and /32 0 to 35 (of
about 28,000 samples at 8 clients and 110,000 at 32): a join's first snapshots are sized to the floor.
(C) `rate_vs_bottleneck`'s one seed-sensitive second moves from congested+bulk/8 to congested/8 (102.9 % of the link).
Why it is off by default, and the ruling asked: R1 of ADR-10145 gains option (d), `first_flight` on by default. It
needs a ruling and not a lane's commit because tests on the base pin the blind first burst of a default connection:
`connection::uplink_cap_tests::a_capped_connection_sends_no_first_burst_over_its_share` (its control: an uncapped
default connection's first poll sends 30,000 bytes or more),
`connection::uplink_cap_tests::a_saturating_sender_from_a_fresh_bucket_earns_no_message_burst` (the initial window
leaves in one poll: over 20,000 bytes), and `cc::tests::ten_percent_loss_reaches_the_floor_in_three_seconds_and_recovers_in_five`
and `cc::tests::startup_is_bounded` (a fresh default controller's target reads 262,144). With the default flipped in a scratch tree, the whole
`regia_net` suite (x86_64 Linux) fails 34 tests that pass with it off: 18 in the library (`cc::tests` 7,
`connection::{tests, unify_tests, uplink_cap_tests}` 11) and 16 in eight integration targets (`ack_poll` 3,
`ack_poll_conditioned` 3, `timeout_policy` 3, `transport_unify` 3, `reassembly_stall`, `transport_streams`,
`transport_v2`, `wire_bytes` 1 each). They build default connections as fixtures and send a burst in their first
poll; three of the 18 are this lane's own tests of the default. Switching the setting on where sessions build their
links (`ServerConfig::link`, `ClientConfig::link`, `RateSettings`) instead of in `RateConfig::default()` would leave
the transport's fixtures alone; which session-level tests that changes was not measured.
A lane never edits a pinned assertion to make its change pass, so the code ships off, the tests above switch it on
through the setting, and the default is the ruling's. This lane's recommendation is (d) over (a): both pass the bar;
(d) costs a good link 0.10 to 0.11 s of its join where (a) costs 0.19 to 0.21 s, and keeps the spec's 256 KiB/s
from the second round on for every path that kept up with the flight, where (a) holds every link to 32 KiB/s until
its startup has doubled back. If (d) is ruled in, `session.rate_control` can carry the switch as a `config/net.ron` key inside format
batch 2 (before 11-28) or the switch can go; that is part of the ruling.
Consequences: `regia_net::cc` gains `RateConfig::first_flight` (a new public field: a struct literal of `RateConfig`
without `..` no longer compiles), `RateConfig::first_flight_bytes_per_second()`, `RateController::first_flight()` and the constant
`FIRST_FLIGHT_BEHIND`;
`RateConfig::start_burst_bytes` reads the first flight's rate when the setting is on, and
`RateController::target_bytes_per_second` answers with it during a first flight. `regia_net_soak::workload::Knobs`
gains `first_flight`. Off, nothing changes: the gate plan through the light driver reads the same staleness groups
and stage tables on all 61 rows as before this ADR. No wire change, no format change. Spec 120 § 4.2 has a Built note;
`book/user-guide/networking.md` and `book/agents/net-soak.md` describe the setting and the knob. Known limits: (i) the
price on a fast path is the first feedback round, which starts at the first acknowledgment and lasts at least 50 ms
(`MIN_ROUND_MS`): about 110 ms as measured at 30 Hz ticks, in which the full snapshots a new client needs compete
with the blob's tail for the floor's rate. Ending the flight on the first acknowledgment, with the bytes it names
over the time since the first packet as the rate, would cut that to about a round trip; not built or measured;
(ii) on a long path the first round's delivery rate reads low (the round includes the path's round trip), so the
first round itself is long: across the Atlantic the join's blob arrives 0.27 s after the connect;
(iii) a rejoin flies its first flight again: a resume ticket that carried the path's rate (ADR-10145 R1 (c)) would
skip it; (iv) `rate_vs_bottleneck` on congested keeps the seed-sensitive second at 102 to 103 % of the link that
ADR-10145 measured at the base (with a first flight: the gate seed and seed 3 of the four); (v) the flight covers
what a connection opens with (the soak's server queues the world blob as it accepts the client). A transfer that
starts after an idle first round meets the start rate as before, without the initial window's burst (the pacer's
buckets are at their depth by then), on a path whose round trip is known and whose rate is not.
Revised ruling (lead, 2026-11-20 21:4x; recorded by lane integ-v07-net, ADR-10231): for v0.7 the first flight stays
off by default. It stays built and opt-in: `RateConfig::first_flight`, and the `config/net.ron` key
`session.rate_control.first_flight` of format 4 (format batch 2), default `false`. The ruling R1 (d) had turned it on
(ADR-10200 (1)); the A/B on the merged v0.7 net line (integ-v07c with delay-detector, random-loss, queueing,
reassembly-stalled and far-tier-record; the same seeded runs with `Knobs::first_flight` `Some(false)` and on) is why
it was revised. With the first flight off every test below passes; with it on by default they fail:
| Test | With the first flight on | Cause |
|---|---|---|
| `regia_net_soak` `rate_control::lossy_fat_pipe_keeps_the_snapshot_budget_at_the_seeds_that_lost_it` | budgets 63 to 123 of 140 entities on 6 of 10 seeds (bar 126) | a rejoin's first round ends with (2)'s "the path fell behind" verdict on a 100 Mbit/s path: the due bytes leave out the receiver's acknowledgment delay, the startup begins near the floor with the pacer holding, and an early loss cut holds it (ADR-10200 (7) (i)); open |
| `staleness_stages::a_first_flight_dips_the_snapshot_budget_to_the_floor_and_no_further`, as ADR-10200 pinned it (the bar passes outside the flight) | 123 of 140 at the gate seed | the same; the test is back to this ADR's assertions (the flight's own dip is the floor's and no deeper) |
| `rate_control::congested_keeps_headroom_under_the_bottleneck_over_seeds` | seed 2: 2 of 13 s at 106 % of the 256 kbit/s link | known limit (iv), on more seeds |
| `rate_control::congested_recovery_keeps_headroom_over_more_seeds` | seeds 50, 51: 2 and 1 s at 104 to 108 % | known limit (iv); seed 50 reads 97 % with the first flight off |
| `capture_replay::{a_bad_wifi_capture_replays_to_the_same_corrections_and_digest, a_failing_run_writes_captures_that_replay}` | the replayed client's early input one tick lower (16 captured, 15 replayed; 30 and 29) | not traced: `workload::replay_client` replays with the defaults; green with the default off (ADR-10231) |
| `regia_net` `cc::tests::a_tick_quantized_game_under_its_target_is_never_cut_for_random_loss` (ADR-10157) | cut on 6 of 32 seeds | the app-limited bound read the flight's floor-rate rounds as the game's demand; fixed by ADR-10200 (7) and kept covered with the first flight on (`a_tick_quantized_game_after_a_first_flight_is_never_cut_for_random_loss`) |
The gate plan passes either way (61 runs, 0 gating reds); on: `staleness_p99` fails on 11 rows and `random_loss_kept`
on lossy-fat-pipe/8 and /32; off: see ADR-10231. A v0.8 lane fixes the rows above (the acknowledgment delay in the
first round's verdict first) and then turns the default on; until then a project opts in per ADR-10231.

## ADR-10125: The cause of `reassembly_stalled` behind a full byte-limited queue: a loss repair leads its poll, repairs are spread over a long round trip, and state waits for them
Date: 2026-11-20   Status: proposed
Context: ADR-8902 measured, and ADR-10088 reduced, connections lost to `reassembly_stalled` on the soak profile
`asym-bufferbloat` (a 4 Mbit/s downlink behind a 500,000-byte drop-tail queue that 4.4 Mbit/s of constant cross traffic
keeps full) once the scripted rejoin presented the wire-6 credential: 3 of 12 rows, then 1 of 72 with ADR-10088's
repeat-repair stagger. ADR-8902 read it as unrelated to the resume and it is: nothing is keyed by the old link, no
window fails to reopen, no fragment is misnumbered. The client really is waiting for one fragment of its join snapshot
(16 KiB on the replication stream, 15 fragments) for its whole stall deadline (spec 120 § 5.2: 18.6 s on that path)
while the server repairs it once per round trip and the queue drops every repair. This ADR is the cause of those
drops. **Where (base b3607bd51).** `crates/regia_net/src/connection.rs`, `Connection::poll_transmit`: (a) line 2754
plans the credit and essential records first into every packet; a full fragment is exactly a packet's budget
(`fragment_bytes`, line 1725), so the size check at line 2942 ends the packet in front of the repair, the bulk phase
fills that packet with the tick's state, and the repair opens the poll's second packet; (b) line 2718 lets one poll
send `MAX_RESEND_PACKETS_PER_POLL` (8) packets of repairs back to back; (c) line 2171 (`fragment_due`) then makes each
lost repair wait a round trip. The queue is `crates/regia_net_soak/src/impair.rs` line 506 (`DirState::pass`): a
datagram is admitted only if the whole of it fits the room that drained since the last arrival. **Measured.** The
trace of the residual row (32 clients, seed 2213; lane v07-wire6-soak-bars' instrumentation, the queue's free room at
every arrival and every repair's place in its poll): of 2,056 full-size repairs (1,227 bytes on the wire) 1,006 left as
the first packet of their poll and 49 % of those were admitted; 523 left second, behind a 1,117-byte packet of an
essential record and state, and 4 % were admitted; 527 left third or later and none was. The room swings below 2,864
bytes (one cross datagram plus what drains between two of them), so it never holds two full packets; the first flight
of every join snapshot, 15 fragments in one poll behind the tick's records, is lost whole (0 of 120 admitted in the
8-client gate row). The server's own state packets (1,055 and 815 bytes every tick, to every client) take the room
whenever it reaches their size, so at tick instants it sits just above 1,055 bytes and under the 1,227 a repair needs
far more often than chance (a tail-drop queue measured in bytes favors small packets, RFC 7141; here the sender's own
smaller packets lock its largest one out). An offline model of that queue (the same arithmetic as `DirState`, 40
seeds, about 22,000 repairs per policy) gives the admission of a full-size repair as 0 to 2 % behind the tick's
records, 47 to 50 % as the first packet of its tick, 57 to 59 % when the tick before it carried no state, and 94 to
96 % for a packet of half the size; a round of 12 due repairs delivers 0.03 fragments as one burst behind the tick's
records, 5.5 one per poll in first place, 7.0 with the state waiting. One fragment repaired per round trip of 1.04 s is
what the join snapshot times showed: over 96 rows (48 seeds, 8 and 32 clients) the median join snapshot took 9.3 s,
the 99th percentile 17.5 s, against a stall deadline of 18.6 s. The stalls are the tail of that distribution, not a
separate fault.
Decision: sender only, no wire change. **1. A loss repair leads its poll.** When the poll's first foreground
candidate is a loss repair (or a probe) that the pacer, the repair budget and the window let leave, and the credit and
essential records planned in front of it would not leave it room in the packet, the first packet carries the repair
and those records ride the second packet of the same poll (`Connection::lead_repair`, `repair_leads`). New data never
leads. **2. The lead is paid for.** With rate control on, the repair leads only a poll whose pacing buckets hold its
packet and more, so the packet behind it still leaves in that poll: on a link held to about a packet per tick (a
listen host's fair share of its uplink) the tick's records keep the first place, as before. Without this,
`listen_uplink_at_64_clients_drops_nobody_and_stays_fresh` went from 6 ticks of worst staleness to 11 (limit 8): every
repair cost a state frame. A poll of one packet (`max_packets_per_poll` 1) keeps the spec's order too. **3. Repairs
are spread over a quarter of the round trip.** A poll sends `MAX_RESEND_PACKETS_PER_POLL` packets of repairs divided
by the ticks in a quarter of the round trip, at least one (`Connection::repair_packets_per_poll`,
`REPAIR_SPREAD_ROUND_TRIP_DIVISOR`): all 8 under 8 ticks of round trip (every profile but the bloated ones: nothing
changes there), 4 and 2 between, one per poll from 20 ticks on. A repair's fate is not known before a round trip has
passed (RFC 9002 § 6.1), so the last repair of a burst loses at most a quarter of a round trip, and each meets the
bottleneck at an instant of its own instead of behind its neighbors (RFC 9002 § 7.7: a sender should not send in
bursts). Polls less than half a tick apart share one budget (a server that polls on receive and on tick would send
the second repair 2 ms behind the first). **4. State waits for spread repairs.** While repairs leave one per poll,
ordinary unreliable data waits: a repair whose previous tick carried state waits one poll, which is then the quiet
one, and the polls that carry a repair send no state; after a quarter of the round trip of waiting
(`REPAIR_QUIET_ROUND_TRIP_DIVISOR`), one poll's state rides behind its repair and the wait starts again. Essential
records never wait. The state of a tick that waited is dropped by the one-tick lifetime, as any stale state is.
**5. The soak records join snapshots** (`ClientRecord::join_snapshots`, connected and arrived times), the measure
this fault moves. ADR-10088's stagger, the once-per-round-trip bound of ADR-7995, the receiver's stall deadline
(ADR-8521) and every existing bar are unchanged.
Consequences: measured with the soak's workload over `asym-bufferbloat`, 8 and 32 clients, 200 seeds (400 rows,
9,000 joins and rejoins, virtual time; `regia_net_soak` test `reassembly_stall`, `join_snapshot_sweep`): rows
that lose a connection: 4 before, 0 after; join snapshots that never arrived: 133 of 9,004 before, 1 of 9,000 after;
join snapshot time (median / 90th / 99th percentile / slowest): 9,264 / 13,728 / 17,568 / 27,664 ms before,
3,888 / 6,384 / 9,728 / 15,664 ms after; rows whose slowest join snapshot took more than 15 s: 252 before, 3 after
(before = lane v07-wire6-soak-bars' transport, a09349835, built in the same tree with the same tests). Rules 1 and 3
alone, measured on 96 of those rows before rules 2 and 4 were written: none lost, 5,936 / 9,264 / 12,800 / 17,504 ms;
the shared budget and the waiting state bought the rest. `listen_uplink_at_64_clients_drops_nobody_and_stays_fresh`
reads 6 ticks of worst staleness before and after. `cargo test -p regia_net` and `-p regia_net_soak` are green.
The gate plan has no red gating bar on two seeds, before and after (61 runs each; against lane v07-wire6-soak-bars' tables no gating bar and no verdict moves; the one-second overshoots that failed the non-gating `rate_vs_bottleneck` bar on `congested/8` and `congested+bulk/8` are gone; `asym-bufferbloat`'s non-gating `staleness_p99`, red before, reads 20 ticks instead of 19 on both rows and both seeds: the state that waits for repairs). What this does not fix, and what
would: the queue admits a full-size packet at best about six times in ten, and a fragment cannot be repaired in a
smaller packet than it was first sent in, so a join snapshot behind such a queue still takes several round trips and a
stall is unlikely, not impossible (3 of the 400 rows still had a join snapshot that took more than 15 s of the 18.6 s). Three follow-ups, none built: (a) repairs in smaller pieces, a wire
shape (a part record carrying an offset into a published fragment), which the model puts at 94 to 96 % admission and
which must ride wire 6 before its freeze; (b) pacing the first flight of a connection over the handshake's round trip
(today the 15 fragments of a join snapshot leave in one poll before any round trip is measured, and behind this queue
all of them are lost: one round trip wasted on every join); (c) bulk-stream repairs, which stay in the bulk class
behind state and can meet the same fate. Host-visible API (release fragment v0.1.28-v07-net-reassembly-stalled,
Upgrade): `Connection::repair_packets_per_poll`, two public constants in `regia_net::connection`, one field of
`regia_net_soak::workload::ClientRecord` (`join_snapshots`, `#[serde(default)]`). Behavior: on a path whose round trip
is 8 ticks or more a burst of repairs takes up to a quarter of the round trip longer to leave; from 20 ticks on state
frames can wait for repairs, up to a quarter of the round trip at a time; a poll that resends a full fragment sends it
before the tick's essential records instead of after. No wire, content-format, agent-method or CLI change. Specs
updated: spec 120 § 5.3 (Built note); book/user-guide/networking.md; a provenance row.

## ADR-10124: The far-tier record as built: state record kind 3, a coarse position that is a function of the server's position alone, never a transform baseline (amends ADR-10052 (1))
Date: 2026-11-20   Status: proposed
Context: ADR-10052 (1) designed the far tier's reduced record (spec 120 § 8.3: position only, 5 bytes) and left it
unbuilt. Building it showed three faults in that design. (a) The lead bit: it put one `far` bit on every update of a
profile with `rate_tiers` and assumed both sides know the profile. The client does not: a record carries the position
step, not the profile, and the profile name arrives as a component after the record is read. (b) The baseline rule
("both sides store the coarse integers as the new baseline; rotation and velocity keep the baseline's") is not sound
on an unreliable channel. Two far records of one version coded against two baselines decode to two rotations, an exact
